year term. In 1959 he was awarded the first Honorary Master's Degree
ever granted by Chico State College.
He was raised in Chico Lodge No. 111 on December 3, 1940. and
served as Master of Chico Lodge in 1946. In 1958 he was appointed
Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge of California by M. W. Phil N .
Myers. He served as a member of the Policy and General Purposes
Committee of the Grand Lodge in 1960 and 1961, and of the Masonic
Information Committee in 1961. It was as a member of this latter committee that he authored the widely d istributed pamphlet "If Freemasonry Is Good Let Us Talk About It.'' He was elected Junior Grand
Warden in September. 1961, Senior Grand Warden in October, 1962.
Deputy Grand Master in October, 1963, and on October 16, 1964, he
was elected Grand Master. He is a member of the York Rite Bodies
in Chico and of the Scottish Rite Bodies in Sacramento, and belongs
to Ben Ali Temple of the Shrine, Sacramento. He is also a member of
St. Francis Conclave of the Red Cross of Constantine, San Francisco.
In addition to membership in Chico Lodge No. l 11, he holds plural
membership in Sincerity Lodge No. 132 at Greenville.
Theodore "Ted" Meriam has been an active Mason and a firm
leader in Grand Lodge affairs. He has been an outspoken advocate of
individual responsibility by all Master Masons for the welfare of
Freemasonry, present and future. He believes in the fundamental
tenets of Masonry, and in the rightness of the entire institution of
Freemasonry. He bas always stressed that Freemasonry is an institution of Quality, of Dignity and of Substance - and to the author of
this biographical sketch he has said, "If, as Grand Master, I added
a bit to the improvement of our quality, to the support of our dignity,
and to the recognition of our substance. then I feel that it has been a
good year."

The Very Reverend Edgar F . Magnin, Gra nd Chaplain

Most Worshipful and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
The first thing I want to say is that I am highly appreciative of the
great honor be~towed upon me _by our Grand Master Theodore Meriam
in having appointed me Chaplain.
I have the very highest respect and regard for him. He is a fine
human being and a dedicated Mason. It has been my pleasure to come
to know him and to serve under him.
My interest in the Masonic fraternity dates back to my childhood.
My maternal grandfather was devoted to our order. An emblem
dangled from his watch chain. It was a gold keystone. At the time I
did not know what it meant. When I grew older and became a member
of the fraternity . .. which was one of the first things I did when I
came to Los Angeles ... I came to learn its significance.
The keystone holds the arch together. The arch of a civilized
society must be held together if we are to prevent anarchy ... chaos .. .
nihilism.
Masonry. based on the Hebrew-Christia n tradition, is an important
factor in preserving our civilization and improving it in order that it
may survive and all men and women live in peace, justice and good
will.
Today we are living in a sick society. Thomas M ann pointed this
out many years ago when he wrote " MAGIC MOUNTAIN."
This novel is symbolic ... allegorical. It depicts a group of invalids
in a sanatorium on top of a high mountain, indulging in theoretical
discussions and debates while the world is going to pot. Each one has
a single point of view and cannot see that of the others. They are
deciding the fate of the world while they themselves are dying . . .
and in the valley below preparations are being made for the First World
War.
Today the world is sicker than it was when Thomas Mann wrote
this book. We have had another world war worse than the first and
are threatened with a third which could destroy millions of lives of
innocent men, women and children and poison the atmosphere of a
large part of the earth for years to come.
Rebellions and revolutions are going on in every corner of the
world.
Violence and riots have taken the place of law and order.

IO

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

The tragedy of Watts is a warning of what can happen in any
city . .. anywhere ... any time.
Crime is growing especially among juveniles. The increase of sex
promiscuity among adolescents is shocking.
Avant-ga rde plays and novels depict the worse side of life in the
name of realism.
The feeling of despair .. . hopelessness ... helplessness is rampant
everywhere.
Sanity seems to have flown out the window.
Pornography in books and plays either directly or indirectly. as
well as in popular songs, has become so common that it doesn't shock
people anymore.
The arts have become nihilistic. Abstraction has its place but in
some cases it is ridiculous. It is a rejection of man and the meaning of
life.
Twisted and contorted facial expressions suggest that everybody
and everything are crooked.
Te~n-agers have become hysterical and go into coma over silly
male s~ngers who wear long hair like girls and hop around with a grin
on their faces to the strumming of electric guitars and the banging of
drums.
If Bach and Beethoven came back to earth, they would hardly meet
with such a reception.
This in a day and age of free education!
Frustrated people seek publicity and healing for their shrunken
egoes. They march in picket lines in behalf of every cause good or bad.
Sometimes they lie around in lobbies of hotels and buildings impeding
normal ingress and egress ... all in the name of progress.
Freedom and license are two separate things. There is a difference
between self-expression and individuality on the one hand and impudence and stupidity on the other. Some people have nothing to express
except nonsense. They haven't a single idea in their heads.
Liberalism once a respected term now stands for bread and circuses
... bureaucracy ... pork barrels. On the other side of the fence are
the reactionaries who think they can save democracy by acting like
fascists.
Thus we see that the keystone of the a rch is crumbling. It threatens
to fall and with it the collapse of our best hopes for a government "of
the people, by the people and for the people" under God Almighty.
Much of this malaise which I have described only in part is due
to fuzzy thinking.
As far back as the fifth century, B.C .. Socrates emphasized the
necessity for clear thinking. Unless we know what we are talking about

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

11

and face life realistically. we get nowhere fast . Slovenly thinki ng
encourages confusion and hostility. There are no substitutes for logic
and plain common sense.
We have confused wishful thinking with practicality . . . built up
vague and unrealistic Utopias by enacting silly laws. We have clung
6rmly to a number of fallacies and illusions that are nothing but soap
bubbles.
Among them are the following:
t. We can cure all ills and change human nature by legislation.
2. There are solutions to every problem.
3. The solutions can be achieved quickly and easily.
4. Everybody is entitled to something for nothing.
5. Economics is the key to most problems. A full belly and a big
house and at least one automobile will make everybody happy
and virtuous the rest of his life.
6. Work is evil and the more leisure we have the better off we
will be.
7. Saving is silly. Buy as much as you can whether you can afford
to pay for it or not.
8. Materialism rather than idealism is the source of happiness.
9. Status is important. If you would be somebody. try to impress a
lot of nobodies.
10. Commercial deception is not lying. It is "public relations."
11. Freedom of sex has nothing to do with morality. It is the
individual's privilege to do what he pleases w hatever, wherever
and whenever.
12. Religion is passe. Its day is done. Better substitute modern
superstitions for ancient ones.
13. Educate students to challenge everything whether it is logica l
or not ... to defy every convention irrespective of whether it
is good or bad. This is known as existential education.
14. Accept existentialism as the la test philosophical fad. It teaches
that man amounts to nothing, life has no meaning, so do anything that you want to do to anybody or everybody as long as
you are able to get away with it.
15. Moral responsibility is a fiction. There are no bad people in
the world . .. just those who have erred because they lacked
parental love during infancy.
16. Children should be spoiled.
17. Criminals should be pampered.
Much of this fuzzy thinking is a result of confusing the social
sciences with real science. Physics and chemistry deal with objects • . .

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

roe say that I feel confident in reporting ~o you that .this Grand Lodge
is in an ascending posture and I trust that it ever remams so.
The many activities of this past year would not have been possible
f achievement had it not been for the splendid and untiring support
~f the Grand Lodge Officers and the Inspectors t~roughout the J urisdiction. Our lnspectoral corps can never be suffic1e~tly com~e~ded .for
the unselfish devotion to Masonry and the seemingly unlimited h~e
contributed to Masonic work. I want to especially call to your attention
the tremendous service provided to Masonry in this Jurisdiction by the
Grand Secretary and his staff. In Edward H. Siems this Grand Lodge
possesses a n executive of great ability and a Mason of unusually hig.h
caliber. Through his leadership the Office of the Grand Secretary is
rapidly becoming one of the most efficient service organizations of its
sort anywhere and I want to personally. and before all of you. express my deep gratitude for the outstanding work that is do ne for us
all by the Grand Secretary.
During this past year we received with great regret the resignation
of Very Worshipful Donald G . Campbell as Grand Lecturer. Bro~her
Campbell had served this Grand Lodge as Grand Lecturer smce
January 1, 1960, and I want to quote from his letter of resignation
because I believe his words contain a philosophy about Grand Lodge
service that is most appropriate. These are his words:
"This resignation ... is based solely on my steadfast belief
that no man should occupy any position in the Grand Lodge
beyond a reasonable length of time. The tendency to stay on.
to seek re-appointment or re-election, ha-s. in the past. prevented
and is now' preventing. good younger men from finding a place
in which to grow and develop in our Grand Lodge. Potential
leaders have undoubtedly turned their energies to other paths
because of this. So. I must. in good conscience, move aside to let
the chain of advancement and appointment bring new opportunities for service to other men."
Following acceptance of Brother Campbell's resignation, it was my
great pleasure to appoint the V ery Worshipful Harold N. Richards as
Grand Lecturer of the Grand Lodge of California and I feel that no
man, experienced in the affairs of the Grand Lodge of California, was
better qualified to assume the important duties of this office than
Brother Richards.
Following the passing o f John R. Moore. P.G.M., who was Chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee on Jurisprudence, I selected
Elbert W. Davis, Past Grand Lecturer, as his s uccessor on this
important Committee and I asked Brother Wakefield Taylor. long
a member of that C ommittee, to succeed to the Chairmanship of the
Committee.

THEODORE MERIAM, Grand Master

To say that this has been a busy year for the Grand Lodge of
California is almost an understatement. Those who ha ve been familiar
with the schedule of Grand Lodge ceremonies and special events are
well aware that the 1I6th year of the Grand Lodge of California has
been one of great activity. First. however, let me extend a very hearty
and fraternal welcome to all present this morning as the I 16th Annual
Communica tion of the Grand Lodge of California convenes. Many of
you have attended Grand Lodge previously - some a great number
of times. Others of you are here for the first time and to these brethren
we especially extend a warm welcome. This can be a busy and exhilarating week for you as you become acquainted with, and participate in ,
the procedures of our Annual Communication. I am sure that you will
each discover very clearly that the Grand Lodge of California is composed of all of the delegated brethren in attendance at each Annual
Communication.
It is the duty of the Grand Master to report on the general condition of Masonry within the Jurisdiction and I am pleased to say that
the past year has been another good year for Masonry in California and
Hawaii. Various statistics supporting this statement will be presented
in the reports which you will hear during this week. H owever, statistics
alone are not the measure of the condition of the Craft. Rather, what
should be reported is the reaction I have experienced through my many
Masonic visits in all parts of this great Jurisdiction during the past
year. I am confident that I have sensed a decided strengthening of
serious interest in the purposes of Freemasonry. I believe that a great,
great many of our brethren are devoting more time. more thought, and
more energy to Masonic activities which are designed for strengthening
our Lodges and thus our total stature. Many of you have, on previous
occasions, heard me use the three words "Dignity, Quality and Substance" and I think I have detected a renewed application of individual
Masonic effort in strong support of these three essential factors. As
each of our brethren applies himself to the responsibility of supporting
our dignity, improving our quality and understanding our substance.
there can be no doubt that this great institution will continue to grow
and command the respect of not only those who are members of it, but
also those who come in contact with it. Throughout this year I have
attempted to stress the individual responsibility that rests upon each
Master Mason to be the instrument of Masonic influence on the lives
of all with whom he comes in contact. I believe there is considerable
understanding of the vital responsibility that each individual Mason
has to apply the teachings of our Craft in his daily life. In short, let

In the death of Brother James Leo Halley, the Board of Trustees
of the Masonic Homes of California lost a devoted and able member
and in his place I appointed P.G.M. Phil N. Myers who had resigned
from the Homes Board several months previously beca use of having
moved to San Francisco . Thus, the Masonic Homes Board was able
to continue to use the wise counsel and devoted service of this highly
respected Mason. With the appointme nt of Brother Myers to the Board
of Trustees of the Masonic Hornes of California , there occurred a
vacancy on the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Memorial Temple
and I was very pleased to appoint Brother Howard M. McKinley .
P.M. of California Lodge No. 1, to serve the unexpired term of
Brother Myers.
One of the most enjoyable experience s for any Grand Master in
his year of service as Grand Master is the opportuni ty to visit our
brethren in Hawaii. Theoretic ally, the visit of the Grand Master to
Hawaii is intended to inspire the brethren of our Lodges in that State
to be more active and more enthusiast ic in their practice of Masonry.
Actually though, this visit must surely be of greater inspiration to the
Grand Master because of the warmth and sincerity of the hospitality
extended by all of the Hawaiian brethren and their families. You have
all heard of the Aloha spirit but one must be present in Hawaii to
really understan d just what this means, because there is such a definite
spirit of brotherho od permeatin g the entire scene in this beautiful island
State. It was my privilege while in Hawaii to place a wreath at the
U.S.S. Arizona Memorial in Pearl Harbor, and also at the Nationa l
Punch Bowl Cemetery in Honolulu on behalf of all of the Masons
of this Jurisdiction. This was both a sobering and thrilling experience .
During this year there have been many outstandin g events in
which your Gra nd Master has participate d. To attempt to describe to
you all of these events would not be possible in the time available
but I do want to comment on three which were particular ly outstandin g.
I attended the 75th Anniversa ry of Porterville Lodge No. 303. This
Lodge held an open banquet in the largest available room in the City
of Porterville and every seat was taken . This provided the Grand
M aster with the opportuni ty to talk about "What Is Freemaso nry?"
to approxima tely 500 men and women of that city. The response of this
group was an inspiration to all of the Grand Lodge Officers who were
present and it was our unanimou s conviction that this type of observance, wherein there is the opportuni ty to describe and explain both the
heritage and purposes of our Craft, can be of great service both to Freemasonry and to the communit y.
In mid-Janua ry we were invited by our Grand Chaplain , the Very
Reverend Edgar Magnin, to join with the congregat ion of his Wilshire
Temple in a special Masonic Night held as a part of their regular
Sabbath service. The attendanc e in this beautiful temple far exceeded

the capacity of the building and I know that both Rabbi Magnin and
myself were tremendou sly pleased by the wonderful response of the
M asonic brethren and their families, of all denomina tions, as well as
the members of Brother Magnin's congregat ion. I was accorded the
privilege of speaking briefly about Freemaso nry and our Grand Chaplain 's message that evening was an inspiration to all. To me this was
one of the very outstandin g special events of this past year and I felt
that it was of great value to Freemaso nry in California .
In April I joined with the Grand Master of Oregon in a special
evening at the home lodge of the Grand Master of Oregon in Ashland.
This was a particular ly friend ly and cordial interstate gathering and
I felt that for the brethren of the far northern Lodges in California
and the far southern Lodges of Oregon a further tightening of the
strong fraternal bond between these two areas was accomplis hed. We
were pleased a nd honored to have the Grand M aster of Nevada also
present with us on this memorable evening.
These are but three of many fine events which we have been
privileged to participate in during this past year, and it is impossible
for me to adequatel y express to a ll of you my deep appreciati on for
this opportuni ty of participation on behalf of our Grand Lodge.
I want to particularly urge each and every one of you to listen
carefully to the reports of the various Grand Lodge Committe es as they
are presented to you during this week. These reports portray the many
areas of service and work of the Grand Lodge of California . and your
understan ding of these activities is most important for the welfare of
the Lodges which you represent. Some of our Committe es have had an
outstandin g y~r of activity and as each year unfolds there is a lways
the opportuni ty for even more activity and greater service, but this
can only be with the enthusiast ic support of the Lodges of this great
Jurisdiction. I know that your pride in, and your understan ding of.
the operation of the Grand Lodge of California will be all the greater
when you thoughtfu lly consider the reports which will be provided
for you.
Each Grand Master has the responsibi lity of making recom mendations which he thinks may be helpful for the welfare of the Cra ft and ,
in the course of his service as a Grand Lodge Officer, he necessaril y
has had the opportuni ty to observe that which he thinks might be
improved upon and thus recomme ndations are made by every Grand
Master. As the years go along, many of these recommen dations lead
to changes in our pattern which tend to strengthen us, but the determination concernin g any recommen dations by a Grand Master is in
the hands of the Grand Lodge and I urge that each one of you give
thoughtfu l considerat ion to these recommen dations. In addition to the
recommen dations, there are decisions which have been made by the
Grand Master on behalf of the Grand Lodge during the interim be-

PROCLAMATION -

D EM OLAY W EEK

M ARCH I 5-20. 1965
The Code of D eMolay consists of fo urteen precepts, the fourteenth
of which is that " A DeMolay by precept and example must preserve the
high standards to which he has pledged hi mself." The Order of DeMolay, founded on M asonic principles , is of immeasurable value in
helping to mold and develop the character of the youth privileged to
participate in DeMolay.
The young men of DeMolay have indeed pledged themselves to a
code of high standards. and it is incumbent upon all Masons to encoUiage
and support them in t heir resolve. To do otherwise is to default in our
own practice and exemplification of Masonic ideals.
Our encouragement and support of D eM olay should be more than
mere endorsement; we must also help "preserve by example" the high
standards to which the Order of DeMolay subscribes by continuously
providing the example of ourselves as good men, as good citizens. as
good Masons. This is leadership for our youth-leadership of the highest
sort.
Each Master Mason in this jurisdiction should become well acquainted with De Molay. its purposes. its activities and its members. As Grand
Master I urge you to "Let the DeMolay know who the Masons are: and
let the Masons know who the DeMolay are." I. therefore, hereb y proclaim the week of March 15-20. 1965. as DeMolay W eek in this jurisdiction and I urge that this special week be embraced by each constituent
Lodge as an opportunity week in w hich to become better acquainted with
DeMolay, and I further urge that each Master of a Lodge arran ge for
suitable ways in which to accomplish this.
I direct that this procla mation be read at the February and March
Stated Meetings and, if possible, that it be included in Lodge bulletins
for M a rch.
Dated : January 25. 1965
Fraternally yours,
THEODORE MERIAM
Grand Ma ster
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand S ecretary

PROCLAMATION
FORTY-SIXTH ANNUAL PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
In 1920, Charles Albert Adams said: " As M asons we unqualifiedly
subscribe to the belief that an educated and enlightened citizenship is
the fir·st great care of the progressive State; and that upon our Public
Schools depends the hope for the perpetuity of a free and untrammeled
democracy.''
We cannot be too often reminded of this statement by the founder of
Public Schools Week. It is perhaps more applicable today than it was
forty-five years ago.
As M asons, we have a responsibility to be in the front ranks of an
intelligent citizenry dedicated to sound and sturdy support of our public
schools. We need to provide leadership and example for all people to
understand the purpose and function of all of our schools. Public Schools
Week draws attention annually to our public schools. but more than
cursory attention during a single week is needed. Let us all resolve to be
better informed concerning the problems, the goals, the policies, the
needs-and all that involves the acquirement of ever-better schools and
an ever-finer product of our schools. Understanding will not be brought
to us: rather, we must seek it, and it is important that we do so.
The week of April 26 through 30, 1965 is proclaimed as Public
Schools Week in CaHfornia- the 46th Annual Observance. The year
1965 also marks the Centennial Celebration of the American Asssociation of School Administrators. It is a time when we should salute and pay
tribute to th e d edicated me n and women who have the awesome responsibility of administering the operation of our schools. The theme of Public
Schools Week for 1965 is-HELP BUILD A BETTER AMERICASUPPORT OUR PUBLIC SCHOOLS. May all unite in active, intelligent and sincere support of our public schools and of those who
serve America in the vital role of education.
I direct that only Stated Meetings or those for Public Schools Week
observance be held during Public Schools Week.
This Proclamation is to be read at the Sta ted Meetings held in the
months of March and April. 1965.
Dated: February 23 , 1965
Fraternally yours.
THEODORE MERIAM

PROCLAMATION
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
Alexander Pope ( 1688-1744) once wrote"In faith and hope the world will disagree,
but all mankind's concern is charity."
The great charitable concern of California Freemasonry is the continued and adequate support of our Masonic Homes. The facts of rising
costs and rising needs combine to make our concern ever greater. There
is need for a PLUS EFFORT for our Homes.
Following long established tradition, I hereby proclaim the month
of May as "Masonic Homes Endowment Month." I urge that each
Master Mason in this Jurisdiction join with his brethren in strong and
unanimous financial support of our Masonic Homes Endowment Fund.
Let us make this a year in which each of us does a little more to help
with the " plus effort'' that is so vital a part of our responsibility as
Masons.
I direct that this Proclama tion be read at the March or April Stated
Meeting. and urge that a copy hereof be sent to each member.
Dated: Februery 15, 1965
Fraternally yours,
THEODORE MERIAM
Grand Master
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

PROCLAMATION
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

When the Constitution of the United States of America was written
so many years ago, one of the great concepts of human relations and
self-government was reduced to writing. Based on the dignity and rights
of the individual. this Constitution was one of the greatest documents
ever penned by the hand of man.
For the last thirty-four years, we have celebrated in California the
birth date of this great document, bringing to the attention of all Californians the importance of the principles and ideals which all Americans
enjoy and live by.
It is incumbent on all Californians to cherish this Constitution and
rejoice in its creation whereby the dignity and freedom of the individual
American is forever secured.
Therefore, the celebration of this important event in American history, in fact in the history of all mankind. should be a joyous occasion
and recognized as such by all the people of California. I therefore proclaim the month of September, 1965, to be Constitution Observance
Month and direct that all constituent Lodges hold public celebrations
commemorating the signing of the Constitution of the United States,
and I further request that if at all possible no such celebration shall be
held in a Masonic building in the various communities unless such
Masonic building is the principal meeting place for the public in the
community.
This proclamation shall be read at the August and September Stated
Meetings.
Dated this eighteenth day of June, 1965.
THEODORE MERIAM

Grand Ma ster
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS

LIBRARY

As Grand Librarian, I have worked closely with Chairman David R.
Lane and members of the Board of Library Commissioners. This year,
for the firs t time, we have managed to keep the Library "manned" and
open to Temple visitors nearly five days of each week througho ut the
year. Most of our books have been properly accessed, and our lending
program of books to members of the com:;tituent Lodges has continued
to grow. We are indebted to our faithful volunteers who have been
developing this work for the interest of the entire membership.

Eight years ago Grand Lodge purchased a set of white velvet. goldtrimmed aprons and collars for use by the Grand Lodge Officers in their
various functions and especially our Annual Communication. The
regalia previously used for the Annual Comm unication was used as
traveling regalia._ With repeated packing, shipping and use, both sets
of regalia have become disreputable and are now held only for emergencies. Last year a set of blue and gold aprons and collars, which have
now become the " traveling set," was purchased and, although they are
still in excellent condition, time will soon begin to take its toll. A second
set was purchased, therefore, and will be held in reserve for special uses
only. We are wearing them for the first time during this Communication.
In their turn they will become our ''traveling set" and subsequently
relegated to non-use.
A gold jewel has been made this year for the Grand Chaplain. This
makes a total of eight Grand Lodge Officers jewels now completed.
Gold for the Grand Lodge jewels has been gradually accumulated from
gifts of old rings, etc. received from residents of the Masonic Homes
and. from others. As time progresses we hope to accumulate enough to
complete the set for each of the Officers of Grand Lodge.
OFFICE OF SERVICE

We have considered the basic purpose of our office to be that of
service to our constituent Lodges and their members. With that in mind
we are continuously aware of any techniques which might make o ur

GRAND LODGE PERSONNEL HISTORY

Combined with the recent survey and clean-up of the membership
records an effort is being made to establish a complete file on membership of this Grand Lodge. A discussion of this program with our Grand
Master, Deputy Grand Master, a nd the two Grand Wardens brought
immediate and complete endorsement for the program. It is contemplated, as soon a s cards can be printed after the close of this Annual
Communication , they will be placed in the hands of the Master of each
Lodge with the request that he deliver cards to each of his Wardens
and to each Past Master. It is the sincere hope of our elected Grand
Lodge Officers that each member of Grand Lodge will furnish the information requested and return the card in the self-addressed postage paid
envelope provided for that purpose.
This information of personnel history should prove invaluable to the
incoming Grand M aster when he considers committee and line appointments. A s names are suggested to him through the usual sources he will
have at his finger tips certain basic information on every member of
Grand Lodge. The information will be kept current by having the Junior
W a rden, after his election and installation , complete a personnel history
card.
The program is introduced a t this session to alert members of Grand
Lodge to the purpose of the program and to solicit your complete
cooperation.

CALIFORNIA FREEM ASON

A challenge was given to this office as a result of the decision at the
last Annual Communication that this magazine be distributed to every
California Master Mason of the jurisdiction. W e were again gratified
by the support of the Secretaries in their extra effort to make this distribution effective. An operating program for the magazine's distribution
is now functioning. With the continued assistance of each member, and
of the Secretaries of the Lodges, every California Master Mason should
continue to receive quarterly his copy of the California Freemason.
SECRETARIES Assoc1AT10Ns

Representatives from this office have continued to meet at periodic
intervals with the numerous voluntary Secretaries Associations throughout the State. At least one of these groups is over fifty years of age.
Thjs effective area of liaison between our office and the con stituent
Lodge Secretaries. particu larly with respect to those functions pertaining
to the operation of the secretarial job, has proven of value both to the
constituent Lodges and to this office. Masters, W a rdens and Inspectors
are always welcomed at these association meetings. There are presently
four such associations in Southern California which meet at quarterly
intervals and one which meets annually. In Northern California there
are four such association groups, two of which meet on a quarterly basis,
one biannually and one annually.
With the multiplicity of forms, notices, reports, etc. which each
Secretary is required to complete, we feel that an effective area of service is advanced by these contacts. It is our conviction, based on actual
practice, that where we have Secreta ries Association meetings that are
well attended, correspondence between this office and the Lodges in the
area is reduced to a minimum.
W e welcome invitations from other areas in which Secretaries Associations have not been formed to make visitations to assist in organizing
such groups a nd to discu ss w ith the Lodge representatives those a reas
of Lodge operation in which we are best q ualified and in which we may
be of most service.
CONCLUSION

This concludes my fifth year as your Grand Secretary. It has been
a rare privilege to give full a nd loyal support to each Grand M aster
during that period. Each Gra nd Master has been different in his per~
sonal approach to the problems of this Grand Lodge. To have experienced their leadership first ha nd in such close rela tionship with each
of them has been a ~reat factor in effecting the procedural cha nges in
the Grand Secretary s Office. They have a ll been understanding. patient
and considerate. For the entire staff, we express our sincere thanks.

and appreciation.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
In a fraternal institution such as ours, the quest for, and efforts
toward, uniformity in the ritualistic work of our constituent Lodges is
an ever present challenge. The importance of uniformity has been recognized by our Grand Lodge constantly since it came into being in the
year 1850. Our system, whereby the Grand Lecturer and the Assistant
Grand Lecturers, constituting the Ritual Committee, constantly review
the work, then in turn instruct the Inspectors who are responsible for the
instruction to the officers of the Lodges of their respective districts,
has long been recognized for its efficiency in working toward uniformity
and perfection in the exemplification of our three degrees.
This Grand Lodge has been most fortunate to have had the services
of a series of highly capable and sincerely dedicated brothers to serve
our Grand Lodge in the capacity of Grand Lecturer. I know that the
brethren here assembled will join with me in recognizing our three living
Past Grand Lecturers-Most Worshipful Leslie E. Wood, 1934-39;
Very Worshipful Elbert W. Davis, 1952-59; and Very W orshipful
Donald G. Campbell, 1959-64. Each ha·s contributed significantly toward
thte goals of the office of the Grand Lecturer, the Ritua l Committee, and
the Grand Lodge of California, and I extend to them my heartfelt thanks
a nd gratitude.
The entire Ritual Committee, as now constituted, is determined that
the retention of the purity of our ritual. as handed down to us by these
distinguished Masons who have preceded us. is a sacred trust. We
pledge ourselves to this trust, and the following is a resume of our
activities in this regard during the past year.
The importance of constant review of our ritual as a means of
retaining the purity of our work is recognized by the Ritual Committee:
and, in accordance with established practice. the Grand Lecturer and the

In recent years there have been more and more requests for our
Grand Lodge Cornerstone Ceremony throughout the State. It is
particularly necessary, because of our public contact and exposure
in these instances, that careful planning and proper arrangements be
made. The procedure followed by our recent Grand Masters has pla~ e?
responsibility in the hands of the Assistant Grand Lecturer of the D1v1sion. to the Inspector, and then to the local Lodge. In o~der to pro_vide
greater efficiency and thoughful planning for these functions'. the R1~ual
Committee is now in the process of developing a set of detailed gmdelines and instructions for the guidance of the Inspectors and the brethren
of the Lodges. We feel that such a set of detailed instructions, w~th a
degree of flexibility in some areas of detail. will eventually contnbute
g reatly toward the growth and enhancement of the public image of
Masonry in our various communities.
At last year's Annual Communication. the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommended that the Grand Lecturer be instructed
to prepare a suitable ceremony to be used as an alternate w.hen n~cessary
in the placing of a plaque in lieu of a cornerstone. T~1s s u?iect has
been explored at some length, and in the course of cons1derat1on many

questions as to scope and feasability confronted us. Additionally. our
exploratory work in this field raised questions as to the functionability
of our present Cornerstone Ceremony in our present day application .
Our Cornerstone Ceremony was written for situations wherein the
stone was an actual cornerstone, and functional in the erection of the
building. However, the laying of the cornerstone of public schools and
public buildings, at the present time, usually takes place after the building has been completed. Because of this, there is a growing sentiment
that optional phraseology should be included in certain segments of
the ceremony to better flt the circumstances of the laying of the corner~
stone under these conditions.
We propose that s uch optional material be developed. with the intent
that ~uch optional _rhraseology may then render the ceremony appropriate to the placmg of a plaque as well as for the laying of a cornerstone un~er .p resent day situations. This will require further study before flnal1zat1on, and we shall continue to work toward this end.
It is gratifying to report this year that the education of our Candidates through the Candidates ' Coaches Handbook program, is being
adopted by an increasing number of our Lodges. Our Inspecto rs and
Masters of Lodges report that the educational program, adopted at the
1962 ~ommunication , and based on the Handbook created by Very
Worshipful Don Campbell. is catching on, and is bringing forth better
informed Masons. The Ritual Committee is well aware of the importance
of this responsibility, and is determined that it shall expand to greater
effectiveness.
During the year it was called to my attention that there were a few
Lodges. seven to be exact, that were presenting to their candidates a
la~skin apron displaying symbols and emblems in blue. In keeping
with long established tradition, references in the C a lifornia Masonic
Code, and our adopted rituals, I issued a directive to the Inspectors
that none but all-white aprons are to be used for this purpose. and
that no symbols, insignia, nor trim in any color other than white, shall
be permissible.
. Also, upon investigation of a report that a so-called " Table Lodge"
ritual of another Grand Lodge was being used by one of our chartered
Lodges, I issued a directive to the Masters of the Lodges concerned.
and the Inspectors of the jurisdiction, that the use of this ritual is
c~ntrary to _the California M asonic Code sections having to do with
~tual. that 1t shall not be utilized by our constituent Lodges, and that
it shall be discontinued where such program had a lready been utilized.
. The Grand Lecturer a nd the Ritual Committee recognize the extreme
importance of Ritual. its teachings of the great moral truths, virtues,
and tenets of Masonry, in the building of a strong fraternal institution
such ~s ours. !"nd _while we recognize the previously acknowledged
necessity of umform1ty and the preservation of the purity o f our work

- the ritual and lectures - we also firmly believe that in order to be
effective the rituals and lectures of our three degrees must be characterized not only by perfection, but by excellence as well. Careless and
slip-shod ritual, and lectures delivered merely by rote. are repugnant to
us. We shall. through the Inspectors, and in turn through the officers
of the Lodges. strive for more meaningful presentation of our. degrees
for our candidates. Our Ritual, both monitorial and esoteric. when
presented with thoughtful and conscientious effort. can make a deep
and lasting impression on the mind of the can~idate that may become
a life-long inspiration. Our Ritual has been tried and proven. and we
are determined that the Ritual as handed down to us by our predecessors.
and which we cherish, needs no periodic revisions, innovations, or
embellishments - past, present, or future.
Our Inspectors have been referred to, in a most s incere and kindly
manner, by our Grand Masters of the past, as the workhorses of our
Grand Lodge. From my experience during the past nine years, working
in close association with the Inspectors - first as one of them, then
as Assistant Grand Lecturer. and this year in my present capacity I wholeheartedly subscribe to and agree with this assessment by our
Grand Masters. Their assignments. the duties to be performed, and
the unstinting discharge of their responsibilities. merit all the recognition, thanks. and appreciation that the Grand M aster. the Grand Lecturer. and the members of this Grand Lodge may expre-ss.
Our Grand Secretary. Most Worshipful Edward H. Siems , h<ls been
most helpful to our efforts during this past year. His courtesies, the
availability of his store of knowledge, and the help and assistance of
both he and his staff.has been much appreciated.
Shortly before the convening of this Annual Communication, Worshipful Arthur J. Kahn. Assistant Grand Lecturer. Division III. indicated to our Deputy Grand Master that he desired to be relieved of his
duties at the close of this Communication. He has served our Grand
Lodge in his present capacity since 1952, and during his years of service
he has a chieved a commendable record of service to the Fraternity, and
displayed his love and devotion to the ideals and principles of Masonry
that have been ispirational to those who know him best - the Inspectors
and brethren with whom he worked, and his collegues on the Ritual
Committeee. We express our sincere thanks for his year of unstinting
service, and wish him Godspeed in his future interests and the relaxations
of his retirement.
In closing. may I pay tribute to my predecessor in this office.Very Worshipful Donald G. Campbell. Past Grand Lectu~er. Durmg
the earlier years of his tenure in this office, he was handicapped by
physical misfortunes that would have brought to a close the careers of
many lesser men. But, with indomitable courage, a fighting heart, a
fortitude beyond description, and with an unswering faith in God, he

rose above his misfortunes and travail, eventually to resume his duties
and establish a shining example of determination. service, and accomplishment in the interests of Masonry and the Grand Lodge of California. I shall always cherish his friendship, and the confidence that
he displnyed in recommending me as his s uccessor upon his resignation
last winter. I shall look to him, and to Very Worshipful Elbert W. Davis,
who preceded him, for wise and thoughtful counsel during my tenure in
office.
To our Grand Master and friend, Most Worshipful Theodore
Meriam. goes the hope that our efforts during the ye;lr have been
creditable and acceptable, and our thanks and appreciation for his
demonstrated trust and support.
Respectfully submitted,
HAROLD N. RICHARDS,

CITY

We feel we must again stress the grea t need of the Board for closer
cooperation on the part of the Lodge committees in the matter of investi~ating applicants for admission to the home in Union City. The records
will sh~w that during the pas t year we turned down a greater proportion
of applicants than in any previous year. This was not due to any change
of admission requirements or any change of heart on the part of the
Trustees: It was d~e s~lely to the presentation of applications which
clearly d1~ not qualify either from a financial or physical standpoint. If
the constituent lo~ges will give greater heed to our admission requireme~ts before p~ssmg upon an application, substantial savings in investigation costs will be realized. Please remember, too, that admission to
th~ ~asonc Homes is a charity and that years of satisfactory membership m a. lodge .does n~t. necessarily qualify applicants for the privilege
of spending their remammg days in our Home, unless there is a financial
need, and unless they are physically qualified by being ambulatory and
able to care for themselves.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is interesting to note how the State of California Department of
Social Welfare requirements have become more and more s tri ngent.
For years we have taken care of our senior guests in the Union City
Home in a normal manner even after they might, after admission, become
dependent upon mechanical aids such as canes. crutches, wheel chairs,
etc. Now we are advised that these people will have to be segregated
and a special building or floor of a building be especially equipped to
permit their continued residence. This is cited only to acquaint you with
the manifold and increasing problems continuing to confront the Board,
all of which increase the cost of our already expensive charitable operations. Our next report will undoubtedly outline our method of meeting
this latest requirement.
We are advised that the Medicare program as administered in California, will be the subject of a special legislative session in October. It is
expected that at that time legislation will be adopted outlining the scope
of service available to the indigent residents of California. Your Board
of Trustees are keeping in close touch with developments as they may
apply to our medical and hospital expenses in our Union City home.
We are pleased to report that there have been no changes in the key
personnel of Union City. so that again the sincere thanks of the fraternity is expressed to them by the Board of Trustees on behalf o f all the
Masons of the Jurisdiction. The positions of Superintendent, A ssistant
Superintendent, Matron and Hospital Supervisor would indeed try the
patience of a saint, and we of ten feel as though the positions are indeed
filled by such. Service beyond the call of duty seems to be an everyday
occurrence. and our expressions of thanks are inadequate to let them
know of our gratitude for their devoted labors.
The appended Superintendent's report will give some idea of the
complexity of the opera tions with which he· is charged.

COVINA

For the past several years the report of this Board of Trustees has
mentioned that it is giving serious consideration to the acquisition of a
new location for our Children's Home, inasmuch as the urbanization of
our present location seriously impairs its desirability for our use. It goes
without saying. also, that half-century old buildings are not in keeping
with modern standards and are of course costly to maintain. While the
Board is not yet in a position to make a definitive recommendation,
exhaustive studies are being continued in relation to this important
problem.
Our camp at Big Bear Lake is serving us well and almost continuously
through the various seasons. Our improvements are practically com.pleted and we find that the facility is fulfilling a real need and the benefits
surpassing our fondest expectations.

REP0R T OF SUPER INTEN DENT - MASON IC HOME
AT UNION CITY (Decato )
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic H omes of California:
Brethren:
It is a sincere pleasure and privilege to submit my ninth annual
report for the fiscal year ending June 30. 1965.
The populatio n as of July 1. 1964 was 149 men and 213 women,
including 20 mar.ried couples. The average age of the 362 residents
was 82.09 years.
During the year, 23 men. average age of 80.80 years, and 18
women. average age 75.22 years. entered the Home. We laid to rest
30 men. average age 84.80, and 21 women, average age of 86.20 years.
On June 30, 1965, there were 340 residents in the Home. consisting
of 136 men and 204 women, including 17 married couples. The average
age of the 340 residents is 82.50 years.

The hospital on June 30. 1965, containe d 103 patients, of whom
88 were considere d permane nt because of their inability to complete ly
care for themselves. On occasions our hospital has been nearly filled
to capacity, with a daily average througho ut the year of approxim ately
116 patients.
We continue to receive the same medical services as mentioned
in our report last year. The Palo Alto Clinic furnishes visiting doctors
five days a week, and on call 24 hours per day.
We are happy to report there has been no chan ge in the administrative staff during the past year. Mrs. Eleanor Farris, the Hospital
Supervisor, Mrs. Betty Dagger , Matron. and Brother Hugh Herring,
Assistant Superint endent, continue their respective duties. They cannot be praised too highly for the excellent work they are doing and
their devoted effort to the Home and the residents. M y sincere thanks
to them for their assistance and cooperat ion.
During the year we have made good use of our bus on weekly
outings to Carmel. Santa Cruz, San Francisco. and along the Sacramento River to Stockton . Also, many evening trips were made to San
Carlos and the Circle Star Theatre, who so gracious ly invited our group
as their guests for various musicals. Larger buses were chartered
for ball games and the ice follies.

64

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

To the many groups that have visited the Home and entertained
the residents, we extend our thanks and appreciation. These include
the many Masonic Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters, and groups from
the Masonic Club House in Berkeley. DeMolay boys, Job's Daughters,
Rainbow Girls and the Musicians' Union of San Leandro, and many
other groups and individuals. The various booking companies furnished us with movies throughout the year on a gratis basis for which
we are very appreciative.
We are grateful to all the Masonic Lodges and others for their
generous contributions to our Christmas Fund, which helped to make
it a Merry Christmas for the residents. To the various groups and
individuals we extend our thanks and appreciation for all other contributions, such as T.V.s, radios. clothing. etc.
Our annual reception for the Grand Master was held on Friday,
January 8, 1965. This was in conjunction with the regular quarterly
meeting of the Trustees. This visitation was a pleasure enjoyed by
both the residents and staff. The Grand Master and Trustees were
entertained that evening by the residents with several skits.
Another large day was the third Saturday in August, it being
the annual reception for the Grand Matron of Eastern Star by the
Past Matrons of the East Bay. There were a pproximately 800 visitors
on this day. We extend to the organization our sincere thanks for
a year' s supply of jams and jellies and many miscellaneous items.
We greatly appreciate their continued interest in our Home and the
fine work their sewing clubs are doing in supplying us with hospital
gowns, etc. This also applies to the Eastern Stars throughout the
State.
Our Grand Lodge held its annual visitation on October 14, 1964,
and there were approximately 1500 visitors. They were served a box
lunch, then toured the Home. The formal dedication of our new building. the Charles Albert Adams Hall, was held that afternoon in the
entrance to this building.
We began moving into the Charles Albert Adams Hall on June 1,
1965, with six couples occupying apartments, and they are quite happy
with their new quarters.
Our maintenance program has been quite extensive this year. The
painting of the dining room and kitchen was completed in January.
We have kept our own painters busy painting rooms, hallways and
furniture. The roads were all gone over and repaired where necessary.
Our guest register was signed by 4,220 visitors, representing 525
Lodges in California and Hawaii, 28 other jurisdictions as well as two
foreign countries.
To all the residents, on behalf of the staff. our sincere appreciation
for your cooperation during the past year. It has been a pleasure to
work with you for your happiness.

To vary ~e pattern of institutional living, the children at Covina
:nurg~d to sign up for ~chool and extra-curricular endeavors. Placet o the Home Family according to grade level is as follows:

66

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

twenty-two children in high school. fourteen in junior high, and twentyfive in grade school.
Within the Home structure we offer a program designed to keep
the young people healthy and fit through the medium of school sports,
intra- and inter-Dorm athletics. and Southern California Boys' League
competition. Included on the agenda are swimming and lifesaving,
camping, water- and snow-skiing, surfing, boating, track, horseback
riding, and hiking. Where cultural opportunities arise for trips to art
galleries, museums, or scientific institutions and demonstrations , it is
arranged for the young people to attend. Additionally, in keeping with
their inclinations and personal qualifications, it is possible for them to
join the Rainbow for Girls. Job's Daughters, or De Molay; Girl
Scouts, Boy Scouts. Campfire Girls; school choirs or choruses; and
other organizations for youth groups which will contribute to their
character development or spiritual growth. This past year. ballet
lessons have once again been offered for the young ladies here.
Recognizing that lack of family identification may produce a parallel
lack of motivation in maintaining high scholastic standards at school,
we continue to make supplementary instruction in the form of a special
tutoring program available for the residents. Thus, emphasis is
placed upon aiding the children to keep up with their peers in classes
at all levels. Usually, additional help is made available in math and
languages at the high school levels to insure grades which will make
it possible for the college candidates to qualify.
In general health and well-being, the children of the Covina Home
would disparage any similar or individual family group anywhere. Our
aim has always been to keep the young people at a high peak of
health. Magan Clinic in Covina supervises this program for us in
the form of regular annual examinations, with additional examinations
and consultations when necessary. We continue to provide dental
hygiene and care at the Home hospital. with specialized problems
being handled at the dentist's or orthodontist's offices. Specialists are
consulted for ophthalmology , dermatology, surgery, etc. Psychiatric
testing and treatments are included in the program.
Because the only home many of these graduates have ever known
is the Masonic Home at Covina , a particular effort is made to maintain an active contact with the Alumni. Four Masonic Home Reunions
bring the Alumni together: a picnic in Sacramento on the first Saturday in June; a dinner in San Francisco on the Saturday preceding
the Annual Communicatio n; a picnic in Covina on the second Sunday
in September; and a Dinner Dance near Covina in April. Further,
recent graduates with no relatives in the area may write in and request
permission to stay at Covina during a Service leave or school vacation.
This bridges the gap between residence here and such time as is required
to build a life of their own.

On the eve of its fiftieth anniversary, the Home at Covina is an
island of serenity_ in a sea of problems, most of the problems intrinsic
withi~ ~he changing. face of th~ city of Covina itself and the rapidly
urbanrzmg community. around 1t. Under the circumstances, we have
been very successful m maintaining an orderly, disciplined heavily
'
parental stability.
The retur~ "Home" by Alumni throughout the year, the various
Alumni Reunions throughout the State, and the hundreds of contacts
by letter and telep~one continually remind me of the responsibility
and challenge that 1s afforded by being a part of the Masonic Home
Family.
It w.ould be impractical to endeavor to set forth the numerous
accomplishments and honors achieved by Alumni of the "Home." It
would be even more difficult to evaluate them individually in this respect
here in this report. . However, when they are reflected upon, one
cannot help. but realize the tremendous contribution that has been
made to society by the Masonic Fraternity of California and by the
Board of Trustees through the medium of the Covina Home Family.

Bequests in the amount of $153,029.00 were received into the Homes
Endowment Fund during the past year. This is in addition to a similar
amount of bequests which were received by the Homes Board of
Trustees, which did not specify the Endowmen t Fund in the Will.
An ever~increasing number of our brethren and their families are
providing in their Wills for a bequest to the Masonic Homes and/or
the Homes Endowment Fund. Such bequests become a final and lasting tribute to Masonic Charity, and truly leave Masonic "foot-prints
in the sands of time."
INDIVIDUAL PARTICIPATI ON

123,854 brethren made contribution s to the Homes Endowment
Fund this year, for an increase of 5,658 above a year ago. This is 51 %
participatio n-up from 18 % the previous year.
The number of contributors has been steadily increasing each year,
and this is the first time it has passed the "half-way" point, percentagewise.
IND!VIDUAL CoNTRIBUTI ONS THROUGH LooGES

Individual contribution s this year amounted to $846,895.0 0-for an
increase of $63 .555.00 above a year ago. This is a percentage increase
of 8%.
The average amount per contributor was $6.84-up from $6.63 the
previous year. The over-all average per member was $3.16--up from
$3.20 a year ago.
The total amount contributed is particularly gratifying when it is
remembered that this is a voluntary program, and that each brother
decides for himself if he shall give and how much he shall give.
HoNoR RoLL STATUS

Honor Roll status of $2 per member average was attained by 652
Lodges this year, or 92 % of all Lodges. However, the $2 Honor Roll
is considered as only a minimum achievemen t. obta inable by all Lodges.
It is a base or foundation from which to build to greater heights. It is
a starting-poi nt or "stepping~stone" or "mile~pos t" from which to meas-ure the distance between a minimum and maximum accomplishm enL
$3 OR MORE AVERAGE PER MEMBER
A much higher achievemen t is for the Lodges to be in the special
listing of Lodges which average $3 or more per member, listed according to average, and to be as high as possible on that list. To these
Lodges we give our extra s pecial thanks a nd congratulati ons. Last yeta
there were 397 Lodges on this list. This year there are 451, as follows:

PRINTED ITEMS FOR PUBLICITY

. Again this year, the Lodges ordered more than 1Yi million printed
items from the Endowment Board , for sending to the members, to

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

"inform the brethren" about our Homes and encourage them to make
periodic contributions to the Homes Endowment Fund. These items
are furnished to the Lodges, upon their order only. without a direct
charge to the Lodge.
Primarily, these printed items contain factual information about our
Homes and authentic pictures of the Homes and the children and
elderlies who live therein, on the assumption that an "informed" membership will become a "giving" membership.
In addition to disseminating information, the items serve as reminders to contribute and some, such as the contribution envelopes, make it
easier for the brethren to contribute. A large percentage of the budget
allotted to this Board is used in the printing and distribution of the
printed items.
SPECIAL HOMES E NDOWMENT MEETI NGS

Again this year, a number of " District" or "area" meetings were
held throughout California, and arra nged by the Inspectors and local
Lodge Officers. In most such meetings, M .W . Edward H . Siems, Grand
Secretary and Secretary of the Endowment Board, was the principal
speaker and members of the Endowment Board also participated.
In each meeting the entire time was devoted to information about
the various phases and activities of our Masonic Homes, much of which
information is difficult to include in printed information.
Some of the meetings were primarily for Lodge Officers, Lodge
Endowment committeemen and other interested brethren, but some of
them were "family night" meetings w ith the ladies present, that they
too might learn more .about our Masonic Homes.
These meetings were very enlightening and helpful. and it is hoped
that more of them will be arranged for the coming year.
IN CONCLUSION

It is obviously impossible to give due credit and adequate thanks to
everyone who participated in some way in the Homes Endowment program during the past year but we do give an all-inclusive and sincere
thanks and express our appreciation to all in general and to a few in
particular :
To M .W . Theodore Meriam, Grand Master, who expressed his
interest and support of the Endowment program at every opportunity:
To M.W. Edward H. Siems, Grand Secretary and Verne W . Hendrix,
Assistant Grand Secretary, together with all members of their staff, all
of whom have so willingly and ably given their support all year;
To Harold N . Richards, G rand Lecturer, who always showed an
enthusiastic interest and support of the Homes Endowment in his
Division while he was an Assistant Grand Lecturer, and has now been
extending that interest and support to the whole Jurisdiction since his
elevation to the Office of Grand Lecturer last January;

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

75

To the A ssistant Grand Lecturers and Inspectors who assist so
greatly in the Endowment program by giving encouragement, counsel
and advice to the Lodge Officers and otherwise assisting them in attaining a higher achievement for the Homes Endowment;
To the Masters, Wardens, Secretaries and Lodge Endowment committeemen. for it is they who have the direct contact with the Lodge
members, and upon whom falls the very great amount of work and
responsibility for the success of the Endowment program in their Lodge
in particular and in the Jurisdiction in general, and especially the devoted
work of the Secretary of the Lodge who, in many cases, sends out most
of the printed matter and receives the contributions, issuing the receipts
and making the reports thereof;
To the Board of Trustees of the Homes, and to Superintendents
Robert M. Henry and Gail H . David and their wives and staff members,
who cons tantly administer to the daily needs, comforts and happiness
of the children and the elderlies-the end result of the H omes Endowment program;
And last. but certainly not least, to the I 23,854 brethren who made
cash contributions to the Endowment Fund this year: and still others
who have remembered the M asonic Homes in their Wills.
All of the above have shared in one way or a nother in the responsibilities and sacrifices of the Endowment program and now may sha re
in the rdlected Glory of True Masonic Charity.
Respectfully submitted,

. REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
This is the Eleventh Annual Report of the Board pf Trustees of the
"'\
California Masonic Memorial Temple.
At the close of the 1964 Annual Communication of Grand LOOge
the Trustees of California Masonic Memorial Temple m!ft in Annual
Meeting. The President. Ralph H . Head, reported the election of Myron
E . Smith as Deputy Grand Master, Laurence E . Dayton as Senior
Grand Warden, and John F. Porter as Junior Grand Warden. On
proper motion they were duly elected members of the Board of Trustees
as provided in the California Masonic Code.
The Board then proceeded to organize with Ralph H . Head as
President, Samuel I. Jacobs as Vice-President. Paul A. Pflueger. Grand
Treasurer, as Treasurer, and Edward H . Siems, Past Grand Master
and Grand Secretary. as Secretary.
The terms of the appointed members of the Board were as follows:
Expiring in 1965, ~alph H . Head and Lyle Patton, expiring in 1966,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

T. Galt Atwood and Chester T. MacPhee, and expiring in 1967 Samuel
I. Jacobs and Phil N. Myers, Past Grand Master. During the year Phil
N. Myers was appointed to the Board of Trustees of Masonic Homes
and Howard M. McKinley was apopinted to serve in his place.
In his letter to the Phillipians, the Apostle Paul wrote "This one
thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth
unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark."
No words could more eloquently express the dreams, the hopes, the
planning. and the determina tion which has brought to fruition the California Masone Memorial Temple. The goal was set by Past Grand
Master John R. Moore in his message to Grand Lodge in 1947. It was
implemented by the resolution s of the 1951 Communica tion of Grand
Lodge which supported the Report of the Committe e on Memorial
Temple, Chairman of which was Past Grand Master Edward H. Siems.
On October 26, 1955, ground was broken. On Septembe r 19, 1956,
the cornerston e was laid, and on Monday, Septembe r 29, 1958, California Masonic Memorial Temple was dedicated at the 109th Annual
Communi cation of the Grand Lodge of California .
Your Trustees have chosen in this Report to pass briefly in review
that which started as a dream and ended in fulfillment because in the
year ahead we will arrive at another important milestone in the history
of California Masonic Memorial Temple.
Before Grand Lodge meets again in 1966 all of the outstandin g debt
will have been retired. As of the preparatio n of this report in the first
week of Septembe r, I 965, the amount due on loans amounts to $221 .790.00 and the way is now crystal clear for the complete retirement of
this remaining debt by this time in 1966. It will then be the privilege of
your Trustees to deliver to this Grand Lodge at its I 17th Annual Communication evidence that this Temple, erected to God and dedicated to
those members of the fraternity who gave that last full measure of
devotion, intrinsical ly valued at more than six million dollars. is free
of all financial incumbran ce.
Thus will have passed nineteen years of hopes and aspiration s, planning and preparatio n, accomplishment and culmination. Truly as Paul
wrote "This one thing we do."
Since the last Annual Communi cation seventeen Lodges have gained
Merit Roll status. 0 f 709 Lodges, only 109 have yet to attain the goal.
When they do so, as could well happen during the next year with the
horizon of debt retirement close at hand, $I 66.084 .00 will have been
added to the financial stability of the Temple. We wish to highly commend Districts 220 and 528 on becoming " Honor Districts" during the
past year as all of the Lodges in those inspectoral districts became
Merit Roll Lodges.
The Trustees have high praise for the efficiency and good judgment

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M . of California:
The Board of Control herewith submits its annual report incorporating the activities of our Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus.
"To relieve the distress is a duty incumbent on all men but particularly on Masons." That doctrine with its implications has existed in
Masonry from time immemorial and yet, my Brethren, how star tling
it is to find so many of our Brethren who had little or no knowledge of
its perpetuation through the efforts of our Boards of Relief!
As a remedial measure the Board of Control will continue its planned
"educational program" of disseminating information relating to Boards
of Relief in order that our Brethren may become more enlightened as
to the purposes, functions and objectives of our Boards. To implement
this program the Secretaries of our Boards of Relief have prepared
monographs on "Why a Board of Relief" which have been edited by
the Board of Control into an abridged treatise which we hope soon to
have released in the California Freemason.
It has long been the concern of the Board that many Lodges are
receiving benefits from the Boards of Relief without contributing their
share of responsibility. The geographical location of Lodges within our
Grand Lodge jurisdiction has been converted to map form. These colored maps make easily discernible the non~member Lodges of Boards of
Relief and have been use ful instruments in the study and analysis of
services rendered by Boards of Relief within their territorial environment. It is hoped that by means of our visitations and addresses to
Lodges throughout the jurisdiction, and the distribution of pertinent
materials, they will be encouraged to join existing Boards of Relief or
form new Boards. A Board of Relief is not an autonomous organization;
each Lodge has equal representation in its government and operations.
A program such as instituted will also serve a twofold purpose. It will

BOARDS OF RELIEF

The Boards are established to perform those duties and obligations
which have been so clearly defined by Grand Lodge in the matter of
relief to the distressed or needy worthy brother, his widow and orphans.
By custom and procedure in the matter of charity they are en.dea~oring
to create a virtual California Masonic landmark. We now mamtam and
operate twenty Boards of Relief composed of 359 active and enthusiastic
Lodges with an aggregate membership of 152.369. Five of the Boards
also operate Employment Bureaus. During the past year one new Board
of Relief has been organized in the Southern Alameda County area. The
Lodges and their Brethren comprising the Board have embarked upon
their new undertaking with an enthusiasm and determination which
can only bode a long and successful association together.
The continued migra tion into California with its accompanied pro~
portion of sojourning Brethren, together with the much publicized recession throughout the country have caused considerable increased activities in our Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus. Notwithstanding
this additional work that has been thrust upon them these devoted brethren and their employees continue to go far beyond the call of duty, on
foot and out of their way, in carrying out their work. No money can
buy that kind of devotion and dedication. Brethren, it can only be acquired by the applications of the tenets of Freemasonry to the hearts
of men. It is their unselfish labors that have earned for them and all of
us an enviable reputation among all Grand Lodge jurisdictions.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Board of Control assures you that relief as a dministered in
this jurisdiction conforms in every detail to our ancient and honored
custom. Long practice in administration of relief has permitted us to
develop businesslike methods without detracting from proper consideration, understandin g and courteous attitude in the granting of relief.
Changing conditions of prosperity. depression , peace or war have not
permitted any deviation from our established practices. A review of the
rulings will show that relief as administered within the jurisdiction of
California has kept to the spirit and intent which our ancient Brethren
so wisely and care fully established. It is also worthy to note that the
San Francisco Board of Relief has taken on the added responsibility of
acting as trustee in the disbursement of funds to aid some sixty unfortunate Eureka flood Masonic family victims.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Since filing our report for 1964, there have been changes in the
payroll tax laws and the Federal Admissions Tax which apply to our
various Masonic organizations.
As has been our custom in past year.,s, we present, for reference purposes. the usual schedule of tax rates and wage bases for the various
payroll taxes which will be in effect during the calendar year 1966 and
thereafter.
Now pending before the U. S. Congress is Bill H. R. 8282 which
would effect major changes in both Federal and California Unemployment Tax possibly effective January I. 1966. The Federal taxable
wage base would be increased to $5,600.00 for 1967-1970 and $6,600.00
thereafter, and the net rate would be increased to 0.55% from the present 0.4%. The bill would also instigate changes for California purposes. It is quite possible that this legislation will not pass at least
this year. Mention thereof is made to post you on possible future
developments.
We again present in our report a section on Federal Admissions
Tax.

FEDERAL UNEMPLOYMENT TAX

Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if they employ four or
more individuals who are paid $50 or more per calendar quarter. providing they have first qualified as an "employer" by employing four or
more employees-on at least one day in each of 20 or more weeks during
the calendar year. For this purpose, all paid employees of the Lodge.
including the Secretary and those who are performing ritualistic services
(Tiler, Organist, Soloist). should be counted if they receive $50 or
more per calendar quarter.
Federal Unemployment Tax at the rates shown below will be applicable to the first $3.000 of wages paid to each employee during the
calendar year. However, Lodges which are subject to the California
Unemployment Insurance Tax law, and which meet certain requirements, will be entitled to a credit up to 2.7%. Only the employer pays
