THE GEORGE W ASI-IlNGTON
MASONIC NATIONAL MEMORIAL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
It is again my privilege to bring to this Grand Lodge a report on the
Great Memorial on Shooters Hill, high a bove the Potomac River in
Alexandria, Virginia and overlooking the Nation's capitol - a memorial
erected by Masons to the memory and in honor of their distinguished
brother. George Washington, Master Mason , the first President of
his beloved country which he served so well as citizen, soldier and statesman.
We. as members of the Craft. can rejoice that those who comprised
the Grand Lodges of the United States in the early 1900' s caught the
vision of this memorial, then implemented their dreams by their efforts
and produced the great structure that now stands on Shooters Hill as
a beacon to all Americans who would pause and partake of the inspiration which ,s prings from being in the presence or atmosphere surrounding the memory of our illustrious brother.
In my report last year, there was the opportunity to give the background of the memorial. statistics on operating income and expense,
contributions to and condition of the Endowment Fund, and what you,
as a visitor. could expect to see should you be fortunate enough to visit
the Memorial. For you who may not have read it, may I suggest that
you refer to the 1964 proceedings. pages 173 to 176, for the report of
last year. Suffice it to say that the Grand Lodge of California with contributions totaling $537,324 plus $7.903 from York and Scottish Rite
Bodies stands third in total contributions to the Memorial and, for the
last fiscal year, we contributed $6.195 derived from the $1.00 contribution by each applicant for the degrees of Masonry. I can repeat that
the management of the Memorial is in the hands of able, competent men.
devoted to the task of keeping the Memorial in the best condition pos~
sible; making capital improvements as rapidly as possible - all this
with the somewhat limited funds available each year.
In this report, I want to tell you about the George Washington
Museum which is now being completed on the fourth floor and which
will be dedicated at the next annual meeting of the association to be
held at the memorial on February 22, 1966. As previously related, the
Memorial Building contains the Great Memorial Hall in which stands
the heroic bronze statue depicting brother George Washington as Mas~
ter of his Lodge, and in which are the two large murals presented by
the Grand Lodge of California. Other points of interest are the
Assembly Room housing the outstanding dioramas of events in the
life of our brother; the Replica Lodge Room; the Alexandria-Washington Lodge Room; rooms furnished by other Masonic Bodies; a fine
Masonic Library sponsored by the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania; and
other interesting and significant exhibits.

109

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Noting one floor yet to be completed, the northern and southern
jurisdictions of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, through their
sovereign Grand Commanders, have made available sufficient Funds
with which to complete what will be known as the George Washington
Masonic Museum.
The intent is that exhibits or memorabilia to be displayed in the
Museum must be related directly to George Washington or the Washington family. From Alexandria-Washin gton Lodge No. 22 will come
important items. Four flags of the revolutionary period have been placed
at our disposal. Tattered and torn, damaged by the ravages of time. the
flags are being restored at substantial cost. They are:
1. The Lafayette Flag showing Washington on one side and an
eagle on the other.
2. A Flag o f the Alexandria Independent Blues.
3. Flag of the XI Virginia Regiment, bearing the date I 776.
4. Flag of General Washington's Life Guard.
Now let me tell you about a heart-warming event which took place
at our last annual meeting held at the Memorial on February 22. 1965.
Negotiations had been under way for some time with the Misses Anne
and Patty Washington, fifth generation descendants of John Augustine
Washington, a brother of George Washington. These charming
ladies, in their mid-eighties, had expressed their desire to give certain
extremely valuable possessions to the Memorial Association, chief of
which was the Washington family bible appraised at $25 ,000. But with
a true value of about $50.000. Also to be donated were the Chapman
portrait of the Augustine Washington family and numerous books.
These gifts are now ours and in the hands of expert craftsmen for
ne-cessary restoration before being pla ced on display in the Museum.
To quote Miss Patty Washington, who addressed those present at the
annual meeting, "It is a great satisfaction to us to know that these things
are where they will be so wonderfully cared for always. We are most
grateful to you all for what you are doing and I speak not only for
my sister a nd myself. but for all the other members of our family." It
was. indeed, a delight for all present to meet these spry and charming
ladies as they joined us at lunch that day.
The notable bronze statue of George Washing ton which stands
in the Memorial Hall was created by Bryant Baker. sculptor. A fine
bronze bust of Brother Washington, also created by Mr. Baker, is being
obtained for the Museum Room.
Yes, in due course of time, the Masonic Fraternity will offer as a
part of the Masonic Memorial a Great Washington Museum for all
Americans to visit and we expect to be able to exhibit items from Mt.
Vernon, the Smithsonian Institute, and, on occasion, from the Library
of Congress. And, my brethren, beyond the importance of rare exhibits

ill the Museum and in other rooms of the Memorial. is the hallowed

108

tmosphere which permeates the building, standing so close by Mt.
Vernon and the tomb of our beloved brother.
Recognizing that not every one can visit the Memorial. sets of colored
slides, 50 in number, with an appropriate script, are available on request
to brother Marvin E. Fowler, secretary-treasurer, of the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial Association, Alexandria.
Virginia, Zone 22301. There is no charge for the use of the slides only the requirement that they be returned promptly after use so that
others may have the pleasure of viewing them. For Lodges looking
for an excellent program when wives, children and friends are present,
I can recommend most highly an evening devoted to the story of the
George Washington Masonic National Memorial.
Being on the board of directors of the Memorial Association, I find
myself. when on the Eastern Seaboard, searching out places. paintings.
sculptures. etc .. related to brother Washington. Last year, I visited the
National Cathedral on Mt. Alban in Washington, D . C.. particularly
wanting to see the statue of George Washington presented to the
Cathedral by the Supreme Council of the Southern Jurisdiction, Scottish
Rite. The Cathedral has a number of Memorial Bays and in the Washington Bay with walls, ceiling, mouldings and carvings patterned after
his beloved Mt. Vernon, stands this beautiful statue. 7 feet 6 inches
tall. carved of pure white Vermont marble-a statue intended to show,
not the soldier, not the President. but the man Washington, coming into
the church - Christ Church at Alexandria- pausing a moment before
going down the aisle to his pew. On the center front panel of the eightsided base of th~ statue are these words: "First Citizen; Churchman:
President; Statesman; Farmer; Soldier; Patriot; Free Mason." And on
plaques on the walls are likenesses of the Holy Bible. Square and Compass with words, "F redricksburg Lodge No. 4, 1752 where brother
Washington was obligated." Then there is a direct impression on a
Plaque of brother Washington's Past Master Jewel which is on exhibition in our Memorial at Alexandria, and there are several other
plaques with Masonic Symbols. The formal dedication of the Washington statue in the National Cathedral will take place within a few
days - on the twenty-first of October and the Washington Bible will
be taken from the Memorial to the Cathedral for the dedication
ceremony.
I am sure you will agree that the Masonic Fraternity is benefited by
the Washington Bay in the National Cathedral. seen by thousands of
visitors each year. We would like, of course, to have all who are interested in the life and story of George Washington to visit our memorial
in nearby Alexandria, particularly Masons who should fully realize
their Masonic heritage and what a great memorial has been created in
the name of the fraternity.

The right to a charter is governed by Article IX of our Constitution,
which is Sec. 62 C.M .C .. and by Sec. 311 found in the Ordinances.
Article IX provides that "no charter shall be granted to any Lodge
until it shall have worked a time under dispensation, and shall have
exhibited to the Grand Lodge satisfactory evidence of its Masonic
capability...."
Sec. 311 requires that for a charter to be issued it is necessary that "an
examination of its work and proceedings shall prove satisfactory. . . . "
Among other sources of information the Committee must have
recourse to (a) the records kept by the Lodge. and ( b) discussions
with the delegates to Grand Lodge and other members of the Lodge
who attend.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
At the 1964 Communication of Grand Lodge. the dispensation of
Frank S. Land Lodge U.D. was continued for the succeeding year. Mar
Vista Lodge U .D . was instituted before the 1964 Communication but
after October 1, 1964, hence the dispensation continued in effect without action by Grand Lodge. Since the 1964 Communication one more
Lodge, Gateway Lodge U .D .. has been instituted.
The three Lodges under dispensation have petitioned for charters.
They have submitted their records for examination and their delegates
and inspectors have appeared before the Committee. While there have
been errors and omissions in the records of all these Lodges. those
occurring in the records of Frank S . Land Lodge and Mar Vista Lodge
are of a minor nature. and the Committee has received assurances from
the respective delegates that such errors and omissions would be
corrected.
The two Lodges last referred to have demonstrated to the Committee a Masonic maturity, work and proceedings that are satisfactory.
and these Lodges otherwise are fully qualified under Section 311
C.M.C. The Committee on Charters, therefore. unanimously recommends that charters be granted and numbers assigned to these two
Lodges as follows:

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

we find an entry which reads, "The Secretary read the list of audited
bills and there was a motion made and seconded that the audited bills
be paid. The motion carried." The bills are not itemized. the total is not
recorded, and whether they were proper Lodge expenditures does not
appear.
The foregoing is a sampling reflecting the general unsatisfactory
administration of the affairs of the Lodge.
While the Secreta ry has the initial responsibility for these records,
the Master has a duty to see that the requirements are met. Yet in each
of the instances mentioned above regarding the minutes. the Master's
signature appears, with the implication that he has endorsed them as
approved.
These and other discrepancies were discussed with the Master,
Wardens, and Secretary of the Lodge. From the explanations given,
or lack of them , this Committee can only conclude that proper administrative attention to the affairs of the Lodge suffered in the respects
noted.
The Master, Wardens. and Senior Deacon, are Past Masters, thus
experience is not lacking. No doubt extenuating circumstances are
present, possibly involving personal problems and relationships. We
are satisfied that these can be solved, and that if the Lodge is given
another year, it will solve them by the exercise of proper Masonic
relationships; adjustments. if necessary; a closer supervision by the
Inspector and regard for his instructions and advice. It has been our
experience that under circumstances such as prevail here another year
under dispensation invariably results in strengthening the Lodge.
Moreover, we find a compulsion in the Constitution and Ordinances,
cited above, to report that Gateway Lodge U .D. has not exhibited to
the Grand Lodge evidence of its Masonic capability. and that an examination of its work and proceedings has not proved satisfactory.
These, Brethren. are the factors that control.
We do not overlook ample evidence of worthwhile Mas onic activity
by Gateway Lodge. The Lodge is to be commended for its charitable
pursuits and work with the public schools, participation in Constitution
Month Observance, and its financial s tability. Those, and ot her attributes are what justify the continuance of the Lodge. But our commendations of these things, and any sentiment or personal sympathy
for the officers and brethren involved or our admiration for their ambitions and zeal cannot substitute for the basic requirements under our
Masonic Law.
The Committee, therefore, unanimously recommends that the dispensation of Gateway Lodge U.D. be continued for the ensuing
Masonic Year.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC fflSTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
On October 4, 1960, Past Grand Master Leon 0. Whitsell. who
served so ably and faithfully as chairman of this Committee, caused a
letter to be sent to the Master and Brethren of each constituent Lodge
o~ the Grand Lodge of California requesting information to complete the
history of Freemasonry in California for the ten year period from 1950
thr?ugh 1960. He wrote that the history is to include the following events
which have taken place in your Lodge within the ten year period above
stated:
1. Observance of a Centennial and other Anniversaries, including
the entire programs thereof.
2. Lodge dedication.
3. Corner<Stone laying.
4. Formation of a Lodge made up of members from your old Lodge.
5. New Temple.
6. Mortgage burning.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

7. Unusual and distinctive events and unusual happenings in the
history of your Lodge and its members.
It was sugges ted also that each Lodge appoint a "Lodge Historian"
to assist in this task by obtaining and forwarding to the Committee the
pertinent material.
Approximately a year later Grand Secretary Edward H. Siems
wrote to the Masters of each Lodge informing them that the responses to
Brother Whitsell's request were as follows:

past. Cicero recognized the necessity of studying history when he said:
"Not to know what has been transacted in former times is to be always
a child. If no use is made of the labors of past ages, the world must
remain always in the infancy of knowledge."
Finally. to reinforce the view of the Committee that the achievement
of the assigned task is significant. reference is made to the learned essay
entitled "History" by the famed American poet and essayist Ralph
Waldo Emerson:
"Of the works of mind history is the record.
"The world exists for the education of each man. There is no
age or state of society or mode of action in history. to which there
is not somewhat corresponding in his life. Every thing tends in a
wonderful manner to abbreviate itself and yield its own virtue to him.
He should see that he can live all history in his own person .. , ,
"By surrounding ourselves with the original circumstances , we
invent anew the orders and the ornaments (of the past) . . . .
" Yet every history should be written in a wisdom which divined
the range of our a ffinities and look at facts as symbols . ...
"Broader and deeper we must write our annals,-from an ethical
reformation, from an influx of the ever new. ever sanative conscience ,
-we would trulier express our central and wide-related nature ... ,"
The recording of history is a never ending mission. The Committee
on Masonic History now is faced with the preparation of the history of
the constituent Lodges of the Grand Lodge of California for the years
1950 through 1965. It is essential to the fulfillment of the mission that
each Lodge collaborate. It is only with their participation that the undertaking may be brought to a successful conclusion and, incidentally, insure a proper and accurate record of each Lodge.
A suggested letter, which is incorporated as a part of this report,
has been prepared for transmittal to the Master of each Lodge and it is
hoped that each of the Masters will respond promptly.

116

Satisfactory reply received .............................. 96 Lodges
Reply received but not complete ...................... 114 Lodges
No reply received ................................. ........... 476 Lodges
Brother Siems requested fuller coopera tion of the Lodges in order to
accomplish the purpose of the Committee. About fifty additional Lodges
responded, still leaving the Committee without the information required
to complete the job.
During the past year all of the material received has been assembled
and examined. However, we must recognize that the four volume
treatise, "One Hundred Years of Freemasonry in California" written
under the direction and supervision of Brother Whitsell, covering the
century 1850 to 1950 may not be supplemented effectively unless ALL
of our Lodges provide informa tion of their significant events so that the
review of each Lodge contained in the treatise may be augmented.
Five years have elapsed since Brother Whitsell's letter of October 1,
J 960. and there now is fifteen years of history of the Lodges unrecorded
in the annals of the Grand Lodge. Thus, if the history of one hundred
years is to be brought up to date it will be necessary to accumulate information of consequential occurrences for the past fifteen years. This
imposes upon the Lodges an obligation and upon the Committee considerable labor in order to complete the assignment.
The value of devoting so much time and effort in recording episodes
of the past may not seem of importance to some of the brethren. They
may be convinced. however, by the realization that enlightenment in the
future is provided by an understanding of the past. The roots of Freemasonry are growing deeper and deeper and its history may symbolize
the firm foundation of our Craft and the salutary influence upon its
members.
History is the story, or biography. if you prefer. of happenings of
mankind, or a particular segment thereof. If intelligently conceived it
may be an instrument of progress. It may suggest dynamic capacities yet
unexplored and may give new direction to self criticism and creative
energy which may aid in generating a richer plan, design or ideal.
Human evolution has proven that soundness of the philosophic and
historic truth that in order to understand the present we must study the

117

For the future. it seems advantageous to compile information of
significant events of the Lodges annually. This will make it less difficult
for each Lodge and the History Committee to keep current the record
of history. Accordingly. it is recommended that the retiring Master or
Historian of each Lodge be required to submit to the Grand Lodge at
the end of each calendar year a report containing the happenings of the
particular Lodge involved for inclusion in periodic supplements of the
history of the Grand Lodge of California.
The Committee respectfully requests that the su m of $500 be appropriated for use during the coming Masonic Year to cover the expense of
meetings, secretarial aid and materials, and incidentals, to enable the
effectuation of its work.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the M ost W orshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Lodge Financing respectfully submits, for your
approval and adoption, this ·report indicating its activities and transactions rela ting to the financial matters of Lodges and T emple Associations operating temple properties within the jurisdiction. A review of the
activities reveals continuing and definite progress in the construction,
maintena nce and financial operation of these properties. During the year,
282 T emple Associations and Lodges have ·submitted to the Committee
for information, s tudy and review a statement of financial status as required by Section 200 of the Masonic Code. These statements disclos.e
that each year more interes t is being taken in proper financial and business operations of Masonic properties and the preparation of proper,
concise, accurate financial reports thereof.
Ever looking to the future, greater effort is being made to establish
cash and depreciation reserves to provide for the replacement, repairs
and maintenance o f the temples which will be required in the future.
In the past year the Committee acted upon 94 applications relating to
the purchase of property, construction, maintenance, and other matters
affecting the financial operation and conduct of their Lod ge facilities:
The Committee approved 24 applications for the transfer of funds
from Lodges to Temple Associations for use in various matters regarding temple construction and maintenance; 15 requests for consent
to purchase property for future temple sites; eight requests to start
construction on new Masonic temples; I 9 requests for capital improvements; 19 requests to borrow funds; five requests to form
non-profit temple corporations; three requests to enter into satisfactory lease agreements; three requests to purchase stock in temple
associations and other various items; these. with other miscellaneous
requests, requiring necessary action of the Committee in more than
I 20 proceedings. During the year numerous visitations were made
to various Lodges throughout the jurisdiction to advise and counsel
with the brethren concerning problems affecting Lodge and temple
association financial affairs. These visits, made upon the invitation
of the brethren, were most satisfactory and in all instances resolved
the problems confronted to the satisfaction of all concerned.

119

The Committee again wishes to call to your attention the importance
of keeping the Masonic temples in proper order and repair. Good housekeeping, both within and withou t the temple, does much to maintain
the impressive, highly regarded and respected ima ge that the Fraternity
enjoys within the communities and the State. So much can be done with
some thought and with very little effort and financing.
The Committee further recommends that Lodges and Temple Associations constantly review their insurance programs in order to be
assured that they are properly covered in all requirements necessary
to protect their property. It is further recommended that occasional
examination be made as to their status relating to tax requirements of
local. state and federal agencies. The requirements as to tax exemption
should be strictly adhered to in order that the individual Lodges, Temple
Associations and the Fraternity conform to all existing laws relating
to tax matters.
Yearly activities of the Committee are contained in detail on the
following pages of this report and will be included in the published
proceedings.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
For the forty-sixth annual Public Schools Week observance our
Grand Master adopted a truly timely theme. HELP BUILD A BETTER AMERICA ... SUPPORT OUR PUBLIC SCHOOLS. And
in his Proclamation he reminded us of our Masonic responsibility, " ...
to be in the front ranks of an intelligent citizenship dedicated to sound
and sturdy support of our public schools." Our Grand Master also
quoted our late, beloved Past Grand Master, Charles Albert Adams,
who founded Public Schools week in 1920 and set forth our purpose in
these words: "As Masons we unqualifiedly subscribe to the belief that
an educated and enlightened citizenship is the first great care of the
progressive State and that upon our Public Schools depends the hope
for the perpetuity of a free and untrammeled democracy." Having thus
given the necessary instruction, the Grand Master tendered Public
Schools Week 1965 into the custody and care of the Craft.
How well we have individually discharged our duty, each Master
Mason must answer for himself. The purpose of this report is to summarize and to present a general assessment of this year's program, as
reflected by all activities witnessed within this Grand Jurisdiction. In
so doing, your Committee finds it impossible to properly pay tribute to
each and all of the thousands of our brethren who have rendered,
individually and collectively, outstanding service during this past year.
Any listing of acknowledgements, no matter how extensive, would, at
best, be incomplete and its only justification is that it serve to illustrate
the entire scope of our program and likewise allow your Committee
an opportunity to share with you the fraternity's portfolio on public
schools. This portfolio reflects a long-term investment of time, money
and much energy. It has, in turn, paid and continues to pay the highest

127

passible dividend - the prosperity and well-being of the free public
schools of America.
Our Committee records confirm that special recognition together
with sincere appreciation has been earned by and must be extended
by this Grand Lodge to each of the following:
The Most Worshipful Theodore Meriam, Grand Master, who has
given in great abundance of his time, his enthusiasm, and his great
knowledge to counsel. guide, and foster the work of this Committee. As
our Grand Master is a distinguished member of the Board of Trustees
of the California State Colleges. we have been doubly privileged this
year to have shared our work with one so well informed, so personally
concerned, and so totally dedicated to the task at hand. As an example
of this interest and devotion. we would recall our Grand Master's appearance of April 23, 1965, on KCOP's television program, "The
Intelligent Parent." The bright light of Masonry was never displayed
to better advantage, than in the capable hands of our most eloquent
Grand Master.
On this same occasion and on behalf of this Grand Lodge. the
Grand Master presented a walnut scroll to the show's producer-hostess
in appreciation of the area-wide coverage annuaHy given by this station to Public Schools Week. This is but one example of our Grand
Master's devotion to duty. We regret that time does not permit review
of the complete register of his activities, but we can and we do take
this opportunity to join with all the citizens of C alifornia in commendation of Most Worshipful Theodore Meriam, who through leadership
and by example has given each of us a clearer understanding of both
... " the purpose and function of all of our schools."
To the Grand Secretary, the Assistant Grand Secretary and to the
Grand Lodge staff, who performed above and beyond the call of duty,
my bretheren, in processing and shipping well over two tons of posters
and stickers within one day of receipt. Each of these dedicated workers
continues to earn. merit and deserve the gratitude of this Committee and
of the entire Grand Lodge.
To the former Committee Chairman, Right Worshipful John F.
Porter, for his sustained interest and continuing activity. Your Chairman has been privileged to observe and to benefit from the Junior Grand
Warden's dedicated labor on behalf of one of the most important programs of Freemasonry in California and Hawaii.
To the California Teachers Association, for their fine brochure and
ac"<:ompanying publicity releases, all of which were based upon the
Grand Master's theme. We would note that this cooperating association
has consistently given full and proper recognition to Masonry's role in
Public Schools Week.
To the faculty and student body of Los Angeles Trade-Technical

128

College, who each year design and produce our posters and stickers
and this year accepted the added responsibility for the milk carton art
work. How fortunate we are to have both facilities and craftsmen of
such excellent quality within our school system. This internationallyknown school well deserves its reputation and our especial gratitude.
To the local School Districts, Boards and Administrators for their
support and encouragement. This year your Chairman requested the
active help of the 58 County Superintendents of Schools in developing
a state-wide program of milk carton imprinting. A very good beginning
was made with nearly half of these busy administrators taking time to
personally respond and to implement the suggestion. This preliminary
success gives us confidence that future efforts can produce a million or
more half-gallon milk ·c artons to carry the message of Public Schools
Week into every family-home within the length and breadth of our
jurisdiction.
To the related bodies and organizations, the Scottish Rite, York Rite,
Shrine, Order of Eastern Star. Job's Daughters and Order of Rainbow,
for their cooperative spirit. Particular mention should be made of the
Masonic Press Club of Los Angeles for preparation and release of two
write-ups in a national newspaper. which devoted an entire issue to Public Schools Week. And to the Order of DeMolay for offering to help and
then accepting and distributing 25.000 car-window stickers and for
countless other services performed for individual Lodges.
To the Inspectors, Masters, Wardens. Secretaries and local Lodge
Public Schools Chairmen and their Committees. For it is here. upon the
level of the local Lodge, that the credit and success must finally come
to rest. It would be a monumental task to mention all within this group
who are entitled to recognition and therefore your Committee asks that
you accept the following as both reflective and representative of the
individual efforts-we would acknowledge and give recognition to:
those who prepared and presented radio and TV announcements
and press copy, the latter resulted in over 500 articles, carried in
newspapers with a total circulation of over 7 million subscribers
(several papers published a special edition or a separate section};
those who imprinted shopping bags and distributed them in major
markets within their communities-what a practical and effective
way to announce Public Schools Week schedules;
those who arranged for Proclamations by their Mayor or other
public officials;
those who participated in our poster project by distributing over
19,000 posters and 100,000 stickers to attract public interest and
gain public support;
those who honored both teachers and students through luncheons,

dinners, theater parties, picnics, cook-outs. song festivals, and essay
contests;
those who presented attendance trophies to encourage every school
within their area to attain the highest possible attendance records;
those who arranged for and then decorated window space along
Main Street to display student work and to further call attention to
Public Schools Week;
those who planned and executed new, different and untried programs
which aroused new interest and resu lted in a better and a bigger
Public Schools Week in their communities;
and finally, to those who would share their success and experience
by telling their story and by making their report a part of the exhibit
which is now on display at this Annual Communication.
To each and to all of the above we say Thank you.. The files of your
Committee attest to the untold labors of Masonry on behalf of our free
public schools and the annual increase in the number of invitations for
both School Dedications and Cornerstone Ceremonies offers indisputable evidence that we have indeed united in a ctive and intelligent support of our schools.
This constitutes the full and final report for 1965. To continue,
sustain and amplify this program, your Committee on Public Schools
requests that the sum of $1,500.00 be appropriated for its work during
the coming year.
Each member of· this Committee joins your retiring Chairman in an
expression of gratitude to each Master Mason who has taken the time
to personally participate. Whether the individual Mason's activity has
been large or small, the aggregate effort has produced results which
places us ever-closer to the attainment of our goal-to that day when
we can announce that we now possess an enlightened citizenship wmking in concert to ", .• Build a Better America .. ," through the continuous and sustained support of our free public schools.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON COMMERCIALISM

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Commercialism is pleased to report that during
the year just ended there have been no serious infractions of our laws,
rules or regulations. This reflects no change from recent years and is
a further indication that in most instances before embarking on any
venture. which might be considered as of a questionable nature, the
promoters are seeking clearance,
Quite naturally everything has not gone along smoothly and strictly
in accordance with the law. Our Craft being composed of human beings
is bound to have a member occasionally get out of line but when called
to our attention, and by whi,spering good counsel, correction usually can
be affected before anyone is hurt. This we believe to be far better for the
sake of peace and harmony within the Craft than to allow a real serious
situation to develop.
Your Committee does not embark on "Witch Hunts." Complaints
come to us through the Grand Lodge officers and occasionally from
individuals.
This year in only one instance has a Lodge been involved in a situation which could have been a serious one, but prompt action with the
assistance of our Grand Master enabled the matter to be brought to a
close without leaving any wounds.
We have had no problems with the concordant organizations the
past year.
In regard to the appendant or prerequisite organizations. we have
received the fullest cooperation of all.
During the past several years certain of the Shrine Temples have reestablished circus performances under permission of the Grand Masters
and in accordance with our regulations. As authorized ticket sales are
limited to their membership, to Master Masons or to members of prerequisite organizations, no sale to the general public; no advertising in
their programs, profits if any are for their general operating funds and
tickets sold so state thus removing any implication that the affair is a
charitable one. Other charitable Shrine activities such as sporting events
in the several areas of our jurisdiction have been carried out in accordance with our regulations with beneficial results to the hospitals.
Publications-Late last year attention was called to the incorporation
of "Masonic Publishers, Inc.,'' headquarters San Jose. In our investigation it was learned that the sponsors were not members of the Craft, also
that they had formed another organization titled "Catholic Publishers,
Inc." In discussions with their attorneys court decisions, also registration
of the name and symbols under the corporation code were pointed out

131

Associated Publishers , Inc.
In September last year a newly obligated Brother was solicited by
phone for an ad in the Trestle Board, a publication we had not heard
from in quite some time. Because of the phone caller's intimate approach
the Brother agreed to place an ad, thinking it was a Masonic publication,
and issued his check for $300.00 in payment w hich was picked up with
the copy and a receipt given. The same day the Inspector of the Lodge
learned of the transaction and advised the brother to s top payment of
the check but it was too late, the check had been cashed almost immediately. Unfortunately when this came to our attention we could not be
of any help in recovering the money.
We were in correspondence with the Grand Lodge of Illinois in
regard to an advertising list of books put out by the Charles T. Pawner
Co. of Chicago. This list offered many books on Masonic and prerequisite rituals and history, including one of the ineffable word. So far
as we could learn. the owner of the concern was not listed as a member
of the Craft in Illinois, further that approximately 95% of their business
was with Prince Hall affiliates.
Every once in a while a spate of circulars advertising "The Great
Message" is received by our members. The past year was one of these
occasions. The publisher is an expelled Mason.
Our attention was called to a book, Secret Societies and Sub uersive
Mouements. Throughout the book there is much said abou t Free
Masonry - in connection with subversive activities in Europe, much of
which is attributed to the Grand Orient of F rance . a clandestine a nd
non-recognized atheistic spin-off from French Masonry.
Another book. The Secret in Your Heart, written by a member of a
Lodge in this jurisdiction , has been the cause of concern by reason of
the solicitation circular sent to a number of Lodges and to Grand Lodge
Officers. The matter is still under investigation.
MISUSE OP MASONIC EMBLEM

We have had called to our attention a number of instances of business cards carrying the Square and Compass. Investigation developed
that three of the persons involved were members of a non-recog nized
group. one of whom had left the state; the other two agreed to coopera te
and discontinue the use of the emblem - a fourth was a member of a
regular Lodge in Tiajuana, Mexico. We were told that Mexican Lodges
encourage such use, believing that it helps the cause. The member who
has a business in San Diego was using the emblem on book matches and
business cards and was unaware of our law and offered to destroy the
match books and cards, but was told to confine the distribution to south
of the border. The fifth person was a member of a Lodge in this Grand
Jurisdiction who claimed he did not know that he could not use the

132

133

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

emblem. The appropriate section of our law was pointed out to him, after
which he stated he would discontinue its use.
A privately owned cemetery, which at our request several years ago
had removed a square and compass from its sloping lawn where it could
be seen by those driving by, lost by death the Brother who had had the
emblem removed. Shortly after his passing the emblem reappeared. On
being contacted by a member of this committee, the responsible party
(an attorney and member of the Craft) strongly remonstrated, insisting
that it would remain. A pparently he sought advice for shortly thereafter
the emblem disappeared, but was replaced by a ··shrine" emblem, thus
observing the lang uage but not the spirit o f the law.
There have been a few other matters coming to our attention, nothing serious, but which were satisfactorily concluded within our law.
Continued vigilance is the keystone necessary to hold in place those
who through inadvertence, willfulness, or ignorance would violate our
law, rules, and regulations.
Our sincere thanks to our Grand Secretary and his staff, also to the
other Grand Officers and to those Inspectors who, when called on, gave
generously of their time and counsel - a ll were most helpful.
To the M ost W orshipful Theodore Meriam. our Grand Master, for
grateful thanks. It was an honor to have worked with and served under
him.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
To the Most W orshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee concludes its fifteenth year o f activity,
and herewith renders its report for the 12 months ending June 30
1965. Each year's report gives a certain amount of historical background and basic information, which should be helpful to those attending Grand Lodge for the first time.
The Prudent Man Rule in modified form was adopted by and for
Grand Lodge at the 1950 Communica tion. For the Constituent Lodges
a Prudent Man Rule was adopted in 1951.
The Investment Committee o f Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California was formed for the purpose o f administering the investable
funds of Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes of California, and the
M asonic Homes Endowment Fund.
The Committee does not supervise the investments of Constituent
Lodges, but Grand Lodge makes the services of its investment advisor

By Ordinance, under Section 246 (formerly 86) with respect to
investment of Grand Lodge funds, and Section 403 (formerly 152.l)
respecting investments by Constituent Lodges, the following provisions,
U briefed, prevailed as of June 30, 1965. (See Sections 246 and 403,
C.M.C.):
GROUP I. At least 20% of the funds available for investment must
be in:

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

134

A) Cash and/ or bank accounts.

B) Obligations of the United States.
C) Obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions .

D) Such other securities as are legal investments for savings
banks in California or Hawaii (as amended 1959).

GROUP II. Up to 20% may be invested in:
A) Other evidences of indebtedness, which are or will be fully
listed and registered on an exchange registered with the
Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that this listing requirement shall
not include railroad equipment trust issues ( 1955).
B) Preferred stocks. which are or will be fully listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that full listing and registration of preferred stock shall
not be required whenever the common stock of the corporation issuing such preferred stock is fully listed and registered
on such an exchange. provided that such preferred stock is
traded on such an excha nge ( 1956).
GROUP Ill. Up to 60 % may be invested in : (As amended 1959)
A) Common stocks, which must be fully listed and registered
on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission as a Nationa l Securities Exchange. except that
this listing requirement shall not apply to bank and insurance stocks.
B) Shares of Investment Trusts.
C) Shares and / or certificates of insured Federal or State Savings and Loan Associations ( 1957 and 1959). The amount
invested in any one Association shall not exceed the amount
covered by insurance.
With respect to the authority to invest in Groups II and Ill. the
Ordinance reads as follows: "No such investments, however, shall be
made which at the time of purchase will result in the total market value
of the securities ref erred to in this section exceeding twenty per cent
or sixty per cent (as the case may be) of the total market value of all
the cash, bank accounts and securities held.'' - the controlling point
being that there cannot be more than 20% or 60 o/o invested in Groups
II and Ill. at the time of purchase. ( 100% may of course be invested in
Group I).
At the 1959 Communication certain amendments were passed with
respect to the percentages which could be invested in Groups I and III.
Group I was reduced to 20% and Group III was increased to 60% . In
this connection, it is very important to call attention to the following ,

which is contained in the Reports of the Committee on Juriprudence
and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
"Your Committee on Jurisprudence respectfully calls attention to
the fact that this proposed amendment is permissive only and is not

"Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends

"~) The autho~ity granted is permissive only and is not suggested
as an investment gmde under present economic conditions.

"C) And that they strictly comply with the provisions of the last

individual Lodge."
The above comments are included in the reports of the Committees
as they appear on page 282 of the 1959 Proceedings.
At the 1960 Communication Section 403 was amended, as follows :
"Th~ provisions of this section requiring securities to be fully listed
and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange, shall not apply
to the Honolulu Stock Exchange. This exception is confined to Lodges
located in the State of Hawaii." (The Honolulu Stock Exchange is
not as yet a National Securities Exchange, as defined by the Securities
and Exchange Commission).
. We ~ould also like to call your attention to the fact that there is a

Constituent Lodges, which is available at the Grand Secretary's office.
At this time the Committee desires to call to the attention of Grand
Lodge that Group II of the above investment regulations is very restrict~d and consequently minimizes our opportunity to make certain sound
mvestme~ts. The Investment Committee is therefore proposing certain
changes m Group 11, as set forth in Resolution No. 8 presented to this
Grand Lodge for its consideration. We unanimously seek your approval
of this change in the law.
Since its formation the Investment Committee has met regularly
every three months. Between quarterly meetings the business of the
Committee is conducted by correspondence or telephone.

We have no particular case history to report this year. We still have
several very interesting items which will mature in time - Santa Rosa
Savings & Loan Association, Corona Foothill Lemon Company, Ramona
Savings & Loan Association (Fillmore)-to na~e a few.
The entire portfolio is listed in the Grand Treasurer's and Auditors'
Reports, and therefore is not included herein. The securities are held in
safekeeping for account of Grand Lodge by the Trust Department of
the Crocker Citizens National Bank, at its One Montgomery Street
Office, San Francisco.
We have had excellent attendance at our Investment Committee
meetings during this year, as has been the case since this Committee
was organized. We were very pleased to have M.W. Grand Master
Elmer W. Heald attend our August, 1964 meeting.
Again we come to that portion of the Investment Committee report
when we try to summarize in few words the financial and investment
outlook as we see it.
We are presently pursuing an even more conservative course, as
already indicated by the figures. With what we believe to be a greatly
changed investment atmosphere, we have the objective of obtaining
the greatest amount of protection for our funds, under trying conditions
and changing circumstances.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges has
had under consideration for several years the request of the Grand
Lodge of Turkey for recognition by the Grand Lodge of California.
We have delayed action to allow sufficient time to make sure that the
Grand Lodge of Turkey is well established and entirely regular. It
now appears that the Grand Lodge of Turkey meets these standards,
and we therefore recommend that the Grand Lodge of California extend
fraternal recognition to the Grand Lodge of Turkey. The official address
is Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of Turkey, Nafiz Ekemen, Grand Secretary. Nuruzlya Sok. No. 25, Istanbul, Turkey.
From information furnished us, it appears that Masonry in Egypt
was forbidden in 1961 by a formal decree of the Egyptian Government.
"'!e have heretofore carried a reference to E gypt in the list of recog~•zed Grand Lodges, though we have not been in touch wi th any Lodges
m that country for some yea rs. For all practical purposes. any Grand
Lodge has ceased to exist in Egypt.
We therefore recommend the formal withdrawal of recognition from
the National Grand Lodge of Egypt.
Respectfully submitted,
PHIL N. MYERS
ALFRED F. BRESLAUER
WILLIAM RHODES HERVEY, JR .

Adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
Your Constitution Observance Committee is pleased to report to the
Grand Lodge that, through the splendid support, enthusiasm and efforts
of the Craft as a whole. we are able to report an outstanding year of
accomplishment on this most worthwhile project. Your Committee has
endeavored to implement and carry out the theme for this Masonic
Year as set forth in the Grand Master's Constitution Observance Proclamation that the celebration of this important event in American
history. in fact in the history of all mankind, should be a joyous occasion
and recognized as such by all of the people of California and that all
constituent Lodges hold public celebrations commemorating the signing
of our Constitution of the United States.
The ultimate success of this year's program must certainly be
ascribed to the cooperation and enthusiasm of everyone associated with
this work; first, the Committee expresses its sincere appreciation to the
Grand Master who conceived the theme for the year, and for his continued support of the program; our thanks are extended also to the
Grand Lecturer and the Assistant Grand Lecturers who permitted members of this Committee to present and explain our program to the
Inspectors as a group, and to the Inspectors for their cooperation and
enthusiasm when we presented the aims and purposes of this program
to the Masters and Officers of the Lodges. But more especially we
express our appreciation to those Masters, Officers and Brethren of the
Lodges who, by·their enthusiasm and splendid efforts, actually presented
this program to the California public. The Grand Secretary's office
certainly was of constant assistance to the Committee"s work. Therefore, any accomplishment or progress reported here was due to the
combined support and efforts of the entire Craft at all levels of Masonry
in California and Hawaii.
This concept or approach of presenting these celebrations to the
public at large in our communities is in its infancy in many areas. and
your Committee feels that the continued success of this approach depends upon the incoming Masters of our Lodges appointing chairmen
within their Lodges who are aggressive as well as cooperative and enthusiastic in this program. In this connection, this Committee unanimously feels that the real aim and ideal of this program are to encourage
the California public as a whole to an added awareness and a better
understanding and appreciation of our constitutional form of government.
Your Committee has found that a dedicated and aggressive chairman
within the Lodge usually produces a successful, worthwhile as well as
Masonically proper celebration out in the community.
With the advent of this technique whereby this program was pre-

In conclusion, your Committee makes the following recommenda tions:

Standing Committee of this Grand Lodge, since the activities of this
Committee deal with one of the most important and worthwhile programs of the Craft.
2. That future Constitution Observance programs of this Grand
Lodge be celebrated as public gatherings, in public places other than
Masonic buildings, except in those instances where the local Masonic
Temple is the chief meeting place in the community.

REPORT OF COMMIT TEE ON CORRESP ONDENC E
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California:
Your Committee has completed the twelfth year of the publication
of the quarterly California Freemason. The Committee has also continued to review the proceedings of sister jurisdictions and to print
extracts which may be of interest to California Masons.
At the 1964 Communica tion of Grand Lodge it was voted to send
the California Freemason at Grand Lodge expense to every member.
This required setting up a mailing list of nearly a quarter of a million
names which proved to be a tremendous task. It was first necessary to
determine whether address plates or a computer system be utilized. A
comparison of the cost and efficiency of the two systems indicated the
new and modern method be employed. The post office requires zip
codes on all addresses and it was necessary to obtain these data. It soon
became apparent that it would not be possible to start the new distribution until the Spring issue. The address list is now completely established and, with .the cooperation of the Lodge Secretaries, will be kept
up to date.
This is our financial report for the year ending June 30, 1965:
Expenditure s of Committee during fiscal year. This
includes putting out two issues to approximate ly
90,000 subscribers and two issues of 250,000. It also
includes the cost of setting up the address list on
computer tape from which the magazines are

Also the erectio n of alta rs. or similar structu res. in such areas,
either

that
order.

ons

gave title and trusteeship to the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California.
A survey of the site was made by a registered surveyor and th~ boun~a­
ries set up in proper form. We were then ready to proceed m fencing
the plot, clearing the land and repairing the graves. Our hope was to
immediately start this work but late rains in the a rea prevented any
thought of work until late in May. Then , when the weather became
favorable, all local contractors were too busy to immediately put any
of their local men on the cemetery project. To hire extra crews would
have made the work far too expensive. Bids, therefore, for this work
came in too late for consideration during this past fisca l year. Our
budget for this year will reflect this in the amounts requested. V'f e have
suggested one change from the work as planned by last year s .Committee report and that is that the material to be used to fen~e m the
cemetery be wood in the form of a Cedar Rail fence. We belte~e such
a fence , having two gates--one for pedestrians and one for equ1pmen~,
is more in keeping with the historical background of the. a:ea and 1f
properly treated and installed will last for many years. S1m1~a_r fences
in the same climate and in adjacent locations are in good condition af~er
seventy- five and eighty years. Our budget request has been made with
this type of fence in mind and if Grand Lodge feels that we should
still go to a wire fence the budget will have to be increased to cover the
additional expense.
FIDDLETOWN : This cemetery, as reported by this Committee last
year, is a credit to the fraternity. Through the efforts of Broth~r Adrian
Taylor, our committeeman in that area, it has been further 1mpro~ed
this year with fencing completed and additional clean-up work bemg
done. A bronze plaque, to be mounted on a large natural granite bo~lder
at the gate of the cemetery, was dedicated by the Most Worshipful
Theodore Meriam, Grand Master, on April 24th in a late afternoon
ceremony. During the next year work pl~nn:d for this cemetery in
addition to general care will include the tnmmmg of all trees, removal
of limbs and mistletoe. Also there will be work. unable to be completed
this last year, on headstones, curbs and grave sites. V:Ve sincerely. hope
that by the end of the coming year all restorative work will be
completed.
The second part of our report deals with a phase of cemetery ca~e
in which a great amount of work is yet to be done. Past. re~orts of this
Committee have called attention to a number of cemeteries m a state of
neglect that are under the care of individual Lodges or should be under
the care of such Lodges in the vicinity. We are fully aware of the f~ct
that this phase of our activity is of a very sensitive nature ~nd w.e sincerely hope that the Lodges, when contacted, will also realize this and
full cooperation can be obtained. We also hope tha t the Lodge officers
and the membership of such Lodges will accept the basic fact that our
cemeteries are one of our most important "public" faces. Our ceme-

teries a re seen by people from. possibly, the entire world and their
neglect or abandonment reflects on all M asons.
During the coming year more time will be spent on those cases now
before us and on others still to be looked into for possible action. In
view of the fact that no firm solutions have been yet reached on the
specific problems we are working on they will not be detailed in this
report.
Thirdly, we have been called on twice this year to approve the
erection of altars in Masonic sections of already established cemeteries.
Brother Frederick Chapman, Committee member in Los Angeles, after
considerable correspondence and work, was able to obtain for the
Committee the plans for a proposed altar to be placed in El Camino
Memorial Park , San Diego. These plans were forwarded to the Grand
Master and approved. The altar is now in the process of construction.
The altar planned for Memory Garden Memorial Park at Brea, C alifornia and discussed in last year's Committee report has been completed and Brother Chapman reports that the Masonic section of tha t
cemetery is in excellent condition.
Last November a request was received by the Grand Master tha t
an altar be authorized for a Masonic section of the Sacred Gardens
Cemetery at Farmington near Stockton. After correspondence with
Brother E . J. W illett, Worshipful Master of Stockton Lodge No. 498
and with Brother Charles W. Heck, Worshipful Master of Delta Lodge
No. 471, plans were obtained for the G rand Master and were approved.
This altar is now being constructed and, we believe, will set aside a
section for Masons in the cemetery that will be a credit to the Craft.
In last year~s report this Committee was requested to make a
further study of the old cemeteries at Red Dog and Omega. These
cemeteries are in Nevada County and are all that remain of once
populated mining towns. Brother Leslie Woodworth and his friend,
Lisle White, have again this year, as they did last year, worked at
these two cemeteries . Three of our Committee have been able to visit
Red Dog this year. As a result of these visits the Committee would like
to make the following recommendation to Grand Lodge. That the Committee be empowered to solicit as a gift the site of the Red Dog
Cemetery from the present owner of the land with an irrevocable rightof-way thereto. That the Committee then arrange for the removal of
those trees uprooting graves, repair the fence surrounding the plot and
repair those graves that are repairable. We also ask that we be authorized to place the three remaining headstones at Omega in a concrete
slab. This will save these from destruction. We have permission from
the owner at Omega to do this and as it only entails an area of about
seventy-two square feet no title would be sought. We believe the cost
of these two projects will come to one thousa nd dollars with the future
upkeep of the Red Dog Cemetery costing one hundred dollars a year.

NEW ACQUISITION POLICY

Heretofore your commission has considered its first duty, after
preserving what books we have, to be the acquisition of books suitable
for the use of the ordinary Mason. In doing this we have purchased
principally new books as they were published.
Now we feei it is time to go aggressively into the market and
broaden our acquisitions so as to make available to the brethren books
suited to more advanced ,s tudy. For this purpose the financial section
of this report will contain a request for additional money to purchase
books.
MUSEUM ACQUISITIONS

Gifts of museum items this year have been numerous and valuable.
Some leading items are:
A beautifully constructed Chippendale "Master's Chair" used for
many years by an old English Lodge, presented by M. W . Brother
Alfred F. Breslauer.
An autograph book in which President Lincoln wrote an encouraging message for a wounded soldier. With this gift from Bruce A and
Ruth Austin Cameron came two Lincoln pictures and other items.
A Masonic apron of the Civil War era, with a romantic history,
gift of Ruth M. Murdock.
A number of books and three volumes of photographs of Masonic
meeting places, gift of Brother Leslie Woodworth.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DeMOLAY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. o A. M. of California:
Masonry in California has a tremendous opportunity to combat,
through the Order of DeMolay. some of the evil forces causing unrest
in the minds and lives of our youth.
As we carried on our duties with the Committee during the past
year. we have found again that the young men busy in the activities
of a DeMolay Chapter are far removed from the juvenile delinquents
making the headlines. A boy of fourteen tends to follow the crowd;
he may well be as good or as bad as his associates. However, when
he follows the example of an older DeMolay boy, guided by a group
of advisors who are Master Masons, we soon find him knocking at the
door of a Blue Lodge, still emulating that which he has learned in
De Mo lay.
H erbert Hoover once said, "Words without action are the assassins
of idealism." Words of help and assistance for the Order of DeMolay
are coming from the entire institution of Masonry. However, definite
meaningful action is coming mainly from the Grand Lodge officers
and from the administrative officers and advisors of DeMolay. The
appendant Bodies of Masonry are helping but a more effective action
could be obtained if there were closer coordination and liaison with
the Grand Lodge. Past and present Grand Lodge officers. in their
visitations have done a splendid job of spelling out to the Lodges every
encouragement to participate in the affairs of DeMolay. but despite
this effort, many Blue Lodges still hesitate to sponsor or encourage a
DeMolay Chapter. Presently there are approximately 280 DeMolay
Chapters in this Grand Jurisdiction. Our observation shows that there
are many areas open for additional chapters and we suggest that each
Lodge investigate this potential in its jurisdiction.
There is no hesitation on the part of this committee when we say
that DeMolay is good for the youth of California and America, and

We have been welcomed enthusiastically on our visits to various
Chapters and especially at DeMolay conferences and conventions.
Strenuous efforts are being made by the DeMola y administrators to see
that every Chapter lives up to the laws and edicts of this Grand body.
On these visitations there is a constant feeling that the entire organization of DeMolay is looking to Masonry and especially the Grand
Lodge for definite leadership. Each committeeman has asked the question, "What are we doing for DeMolaly?" and "What more can we do
to insure the future of Masonry and the generations of the future?"
The Grand Master, several Past Grand Masters. and the Grand
Secretary have been most helpful by sitting in on the deliberations of
your committee, and making it possible to meet with other Grand
Lodge committees.
A word of thanks is certainly due all DeMolay Chapters for their
civic activities. and especially for their help to the Blue Lodges during
Public Schools Weck, Constitution observances, installations and other
activities that help to build the image of Masonry in every community.
In fact, DeMolay Week in March and DeMolay Traffic Safety Week
in October are becoming outstanding examples of youth on the march
and are setting an example of exemplary action for other youth to
follow.
'
We recommend and have requested the Finance Committee for a
budget of seven hundred and fifty ( $750) dollars for the work of the
committee next year.
With all due regard for the progress that has been made to date, and
the desire of Grand Lodge to help in every way possible, there still
remain several basic problems that need immediate attention. We therefore recommend that a special committee be appointed to study in
depth and to make recommendations concerning the following:

1. Improved communication and liaison between DeMolay and the
various Masonic Bodies.
2. Method of establishing a liaison between appendant Masonic
Bodies and the Grand Lodge with respect to DeMolay.
3. Need for obtaining more interest and active participation in
DeMolay by the Master Mason.
4. Method of insuring adequate support for DeMolay administrative organization.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

5. Problem of assisting the young man reaching his majority in
making the transition from DeMolay to Master Mason.
6. Need for making DeMolay available to every eligible boy.
As the Committee proceeds with its study. other problems may be ·
discovered and should be included in the report. The above list should
not be considered restrictive or all inclusive.
We wish to thank each of you for the helpfulness and cooperation
we have received this past year.
Respectfully submitted,

BROTHERLY LOVE
''By the exercise of Brotherly Love we are taught to regard
the whole human species as one family-the high and the low, the
rich and the poor-who, as created by one almighty parent, and
inhabitants of the same planet, are to aid, support and protect
each other. On this principle Masonry unites men of every country. sect and opinion; and causes true friendship to exist among
those who might otherwise have remained at a perpetual distance."
"We love because he loved us first. But if a man says, 'I love God.'
while hating his brother, he is a liar. If he does not love the brother
whom he has seen, it cannot be that he loves God whom he has not seen.
And indeed this command comes to us from Christ himself; that he who
loves God must also love his brother." I John 4: 19-21
We know what Brotherly Love means, although it is most difficult
of definition. Imperfect it may be in its manifestations, and not always
displayed by us; yet it is the cement which hold<s together the social
edifice of this world.
Brotherly Lov.e is the divine element that advances society; it is the
solar ray that brightens the heavens, thaws the ice-bound districts.
vitalizes its soil, and quickens its germs of life. Love breaks the seal of
the apocalyptic books, and leads all the powers of the soul to join in
their hallelujahs.
Masonry is Brotherly Love. It is the heart of a system of principles
which underlie the w hole fabric of Freemasonry. Heaven-taught
brotherly love has been the distinguishing characteristic of every true
Mason from time immemorial, and should continue to be so characteristic
of Masons that the enemies of Masonry should be compelled to say
now, as did the enemies of the Christian believers of old : "Behold how
they love one another."
Brotherly Love is a task, a kingly task-quite the greatest, the most
important, inside the whole compass of life. Just as man must be in right
relation with the food he eats in order to maintain health, ·s o must he
likewise be in right relation to his fellows if he would live in happiness.
Practical men of affairs are today thinking of brotherhood in terms
of cooperation, and this is perfectly legitimate. Freemasonry is organized
cooperation. Because we can do together what we could never do alone,

practice of brotherhood in their own lives, but also in the life of the

The spirit of fraternalism. in all its aspects, is a spirit of cooperation.
There can be no constructive progress without cooperation. There can
be no cooperation without proper regard for duly constituted authority
which is the very cornerstone of the social compact. If. therefore, the
Masonic Order is to fulfill its high mission as the great exponent of
brotherhood. every Freemason must be taught not only to be a lawabiding citizen, but that he must cast his influence on the side of law
and order.
Wherever in the world there is a lodge of Freemasons, there should
be a focus of civilization, a center of the idea of fraternity, making for
the peace and ha rmony that should prevail in this great lodge of the
world.
I like to think that our Fraternity is a sort o f great school in which
men learn brotherly love by practicing it toward Masons, because he
who begins by practicing it toward his brethren will come sooner or later
to practicing it everywhere.
Masonry teaches Brotherly Love. This is one of its leading lessons.

It is this which has given it a place among the social organizations of
the past and present ages, which has reared its temples among all
nations, and scattered the seeds of civilization and progress over the
surface of the globe. It is this which brings peace. harmony and decorum
to our Lodges; which banishes the talebearer. censor and reviler; which
guards the character of a brother, and brands calumny and s lander as
detestable crimes. It is this which brings to a common altar the
Israelite, the Christian. the Mohammedan and the Hindu, and joins
their hands in the strong grip of a Master Mason. It is this which exalts
society, disarms feuds and sectional hatred; which cements republics,
and produces international comity. It is this which ma kes Masonry the
world's great peacemaker.
Do you who have joined Masonry realize tha t each and every step,
obligation and lesson you have experienced has been personal. in that it
is you who have professed your faith in our principles and teachings.
and you who have solemnly promised, in the name of God , to perform
those duties of moral and material assistance to your brethren. to those
of their household, and to the whole human family?
Do you recall the lesson that you might some time become entirely
dependent upon the benevolence of others? Do you realize that you
have specifically obligated yourself to assist your brethren, their widows
and orphans? Do you feel the tremendous significance of the inter~
pretation of the " five points of fellowship?" ls it fixed in your mind that

TRUTH
"Truth is a divine attribute and the fou ndation of every virtue.
To be good and true is the fir·s t lesson we are taught in Masonry.
On this theme we contemplate, a nd by its dictates endeavor to
regulate our conduct. Hence, while influenced by this principle,
hypocrisy and deceit are unknown among us; sincerity and plain
dealing distinguish us, and with hear t and tongue, we join in
promoting each other's welfare and rejoicing in each other's
prosperity."
The cornerstone of the Ma·s onic structure is Truth.
The truths of Freemasonry are purposely veiled in allegory a nd
symbol, and their deeper meanings do not appear upon the surface of
the ritua l. Our ceremonies are full of cunningly hidden suggestions of
these immortal truths-so much <SO that one is almost inclined at times
to claim for Freemasonry an inspiration from the Great Architect
Himself.
The symbols and ceremonies of Freemasonry have more than one
meaning. They rather conceal than disclose the truth. They hint it only ,
at least; and their varied meanings are only to be discovered by reflection
and study. Truth is not only symbolized by light, but as the ray of light
is separable into different rays of different colors, so is truth separable
into kinds. It is t~e province of Masonry to teach all truths-not moral
truth alone, but political and philosophical, and even religious truth . so
far as concerns the great and essential principles of each.
What is truth? If we could answer that question we could be gods ,
a nd kn ow the secrets of the universe. Truth is the great object of
Masonic study-the age long ques t of man. It is the reward promised
to those who are faithful, when their spiritual temple is completed.
"Truth," said one of the most ancient Indian sects of philosophers.
"is the Eternal Attribute of G od," and this expression has been han ded
down to us through the long succession of ages in the lessons of
Freemasonry, wherein we are taught, "Truth is a divine attribu te and
the fou ndation of every virtue."
" It is no proof of a man's understanding to be able to affirm
whatever he pleases: but to be able to discern that what is true
is true, and that wha t is false is false, this is the mark of intelligence." Swedenborg
Moral truths are distinguished from other tr uths by a singular characteristic ; so soon as we perceive them, they appear to us a s the rule
of our conduct.
The doctrines of Masonry are the most beautiful that it is possible

164

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

to imagine. They breathe the simplicity of the earliest ages, animated
by the love of a martyred God. That word which the Puritans translated
" Charity," but which is really "Love," is the keystone which supports
the entire edifice of this mystic science. Love one another. teach one
another. help one another. That is all our doctrine, all our science, all
our law. We have no narrow-minded prejudices; we do not debar from
our society this sect or that sect; it is sufficient for us that a man worships God, no matter under what name or in what manner. Ah!, rail
a gainst us, bigoted and ignorant men, if you will. Those who listen to
the truths which Masonry inculcates can readily forgive you. It is
impossible to be a good Mason without being a good man.
"Today's challe nge, then, to our Fraternity is to apply more completely its principles within our ranks; that duty we owe to God, that
loyalty we owe to our country; that fellowship we owe to our neighbor
and brother. That doctrine, in real action, will influence scores of others
beyond the boundaries of our organization, not only of the present
generation, but also the coming generation. We are charged to assume
that leadership.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON SOJOURNERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The year of 1965 has been a very encouraging year for your Committee. The program that was initiated last year has received added
momentum and a total of 922 Sojourners affiliated with our Lodges from
other Jurisdictions, an increase of 69 over last year. This is the greatest
number of Sojourner affiliations recorded since separate statistics have
been maintained. Incidentally, there were 1,438 California Masons who
affiliated within the Jurisdiction.
The Sojourners, M aster Masons from other Jurisdictions, are with
us in ever increasing numbers. The task of locating them and bringing
them into the fold of California Masonry offers a great and a year round
challenge to each and every one of us. This challenge, if accepted with
imagination and enthusiasm, can produce very satisfying and lucrative
results. Just think, last y ear our 922 affiliates contributed $23.050 to our
Homes and nearly $3.800 in per capita taxes to the Grand Lodge. In
each succeeding year this same number will pay a minimum of $14,000
in Lodge d ues. the annual per capita tax and an untold sum in contributions to the Home Endowment Fund.
The 1965 program was a continuation of the one adopted last year.
It was published to all Lodges with the suggestion that each Master
implement the program and initiate plans to aggressively:
Seek out the Sojourner and extend him a cordial invitation to visit;
Develop and present interesting and instructive programs;
Insure that the visitor is given a friendly greeting and is made to feel
that his visit was worth while;
Follow up the visit with a personal contact and a friendly invitation
to return;
Extend a sincere and friendly invitation to participate fully in California Masonry by affiliation.
My thanks to the Grand Master for his assistance in drafting the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

167

leaflet " Participation." Copies have been made available to all Lodges
and it has been very well received. A copy given to a Sojourner, coupled
with a friendly greeting, will do much to create a favorable impression.
A second printing of 50,000 copies has been made and are available for
the asking-use them.
M a ny of our Lodges had outstanding Sojourner programs that contributed materially to our all time high. M ar Vista U.D., Newport Beach .
was outstanding with 23 affiliations. Given special mention in 1963 and
1964. the following are again cited for their affiliations: Consuelo No. 325
-8; Oak Plains No. 789-8, a nd Home No. 721-6. The following

No. 242-11; Stanislaus No. 206-I O; Ionic No. 520--1 O; Los Angeles
No. 42-9; Menorah No. 623-9 and El C ajon Valley No. 576-8.
The outstanding Masonic District is No. 635, Newport Beach, with

were both given honorable mention in 1963 and 1964. The following
were given special mention in 1964 and again merit a cita tion: No. 508,
