1965. The Net Ga in of 87. ·s hown for 1965, is a small but welcome increase over the Net Gain of 5 shown for last year. This net increase is
due primarily to a decrease in the number of withdrawals coupled with
an increase in the number Raised and the number of Sojourner Affiliations. The added interest in the Sojourner program has had a material
bearing on the Net Gain and further increases can be expected if added
effort is put into the Sojourner program to sell "Participation."
The Sojourner often asks: " Why should I affiliate? I don't like to
pay your $25 contribution to the Homes; your dues are much higher than
back home; I have a sentimental attachment to the Lodge where I was
raised.''

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

168

169

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

These reasons for non-affiliation are answerable, but many Sojourners will not listen to the answers. This is regretted. The contribution to
the Homes is essentially an insurance premium against possible adversity
in old age-especially for the widow who may be left destitute. He may
have paid a similar fee back home, but will his widow want to go back
to a Home in the cold and snow after living out here for a few years?
Too many similar cases happen each year.
Yes, our dues are higher than in many Jurisdictions, although it is
noted that many have raised their dues in recent years. Everything is
higher in California and well worth it. California offers more and one
must pay for what he gets. So, if it is a matter of cost that keeps a Sojourner from affiliation, there is not much we can do but leave that one
alone and look for others who are not so cost conscious.
The sentimental reason can readily be solved by taking a Dual
Membership. The Jurisdictions permitting this are listed on the leaflet
"Participation." With Dual Members hip the Sojourner can keep his
home ties and enjoy Masonry with us through affiliation.
The Most Worshipful William Holman. P.G.M. of Minnesota recently met a Minneapolis Mason in Santa Ana who seemed overjoyed
at meeting him and said: "I have lived here over ten years but I still
keep my membership back home. You belong to University Lodge in
Minneapolis, don't you?"
Brother Holman came right back: "No. I belong to Silver Cord in
Santa Ana and you should belong to a Lodge in California, too. I still
hold membership back there, but I belong here and you should, too."
These words of Brother Holman off er an excellent answer as to the
"why". Coming from a Past Grand Master of another Jurisdiction, his
answer presents a strong boost for affiliation.
A man who has Masonry in him and is desirous of obtaining the most
from his membership will want to BELONG where he lives so he can
participate to the fullest without the fear of being called a "free loader."
If he is only a card carrying Mason there is usually little that can be
done to convince him he should BE LONG a nd time and effort might best
be spent on more fertile soil.
During the year, your Committeemen have made numerous visitations
to promote the Sojourner program and have received many comments
a nd s uggestions. The points most generally emphasized are submitted
for your earnest consideration:
Each Master should appoint an active, energetitc Sojourner Committee to implement, develop and carry on the Sojourner program for
the Lodge. Many Masters fail to appoint such a Committee or develop
a Lodge program to attract Sojourners. An occasional social or educational program ; an open meeting with entertainment; a picnic or a dance
can do much to increase attendance as well as a ttrac t Sojourners. Such
varied programs will take imagination and effort but will produce won-

derful results. The members of your Grand Lodge Committee are available to assist you in developing a Lodge program.
A personal contact is worth many letters. A telephone committee to
contact members and Sojourners alike, for special meetings, will produce
astonishing res ults. A car pool to assist those who cannot drive at night
can also prove very helpful.
How many of us have taken the time to greet a man who wears a
M asosnic ring or pin? A friendly greeting can often develop into a true
M asonic friendship and may also develop into an affiliation. Let's keep
our eyes open and extend a friendly greeting to a stranger in our midst.
M any Sojourners state they are afraid they cannot pass an examination for admission. At times the Lodge Examining Committee endeavors
to extract the Candidate's Lecture from the applicant. This of course is
not good or necessary. Masters and Inspectors can remedy this situation
by periodic and proper instruction.
Many Sojourners, after filing an application for affiliation. have been
subjected to grillings by a Personnel Committee and have been required
to answer the full list of questions on the application form by members of
the Investigating Committee. This is considered extremely bad manners.
Reason and common sense dictate a ' 'warmer" approach. Again, proper
instruction by Masters and Inspectors can remedy this situation.
RECOMMEND that the proper conduct of an investigation by an
Examining Committee and by the members of a n Investigating Committee be covered in appropriate schools of instruction.
In many cases Grand Lodge letters asking for cooperation to seek out
the Sojourner ai;id endeavor to bring him back into "Participation" have
met with little or no response. The Sojourner program is intended to
bring back into the fold. those wandering Sojourners who have lost
contact with Masonry as well as to secure affiliations.
RECOMMEND that this matter be taken up in Schools of Instruc~
tion and that the Lodge officers be enjoined to pursue the Sojourner
program with diligence.
During the past year you r Committeemen have visited Masonic
clubs. under various names, in industry. senior citizen communities and
in cities alongside our regular Lodges. The clubs are mostly composed of
Sojourners with a sprinkling of our own members. They are basically
social in character and seem to fill a void left by our regular Lodges.
Some maintain a close liaison with the loca l Lodge and participate in its
activities.
These groups are a source of great potential strength for Masonry in
California and need only the sanction and guidance of Grand Lodge to
fill what is now a vacuum and to attract many into "Participation" tha t
otherwise would be lost to the Fraternity.
RECOMMEND that the Grand Master have this ma tter of

"Masonic Clubs" studied with the purpose of adopting regulations that
will recognize these social organizations, as Masonic in character, and
give them support, recognition and guidance.
Your Committee feels that the funds appropriated in the past have
been a material aid in increasing our affiliations.
RECOMMEND that such funds, as this Grand Lodge may consider
justifiable. be appropriated for 1966 so the Committee may continue to

We who have had the pleasure and privilege of working on this

EXHIBIT "B"

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Masonic Information Committee has held two meetings this past
year, a fact which in itself should be worthy of reporting to this body.
Such has never happened before. Similar meetings are planned for the
coming year.
I might mention that the recommendations which are made in this
report are the result of these meetings. All recommendations are the
result of Committee action .
Our first consideration was on the matter of a policy recommendation
covering the handling of public media releases. Our Committee recommends that these be on a local level wherever and whenever possible. We
feel that. with the possible exception of such purely statewide matters as
the Grand Lodge Communication, for example, that contact with the
press and radio, and the preparation of releases to all media, should be
in the hands of the constituent Lodges.

With this in mind, the Committee has prepared and sent to the
Masters of all constituent Lodges two publications to serve as a guide in
the preparing and placing of news releases. The first publication is one
which was written by our present Grand Master several years ago. the
one entitled "If Freemasonry Is Good, Let Us Talk About I t." The
points stressed in this booklet, that all stories be prepared and judged on
the basis of Oigpity. Quality and Substance, are ones that should govern
all our contact with the public. and media serving the public.
The second booklet was written by Brother William R. Latta. a
public relations counsel in Southern California, and one of the founders
of our Masonic Press Club of Los Angeles. He is also a past president of
that organization. The title of his booklet is "Let's Talk About Freemasonry.'' and. in very brief form, outlines how the objectives enunciated
in the firs t booklet might best be accomplished. It is hoped that the
Mastef\s, and the Wardens, of all our constituent Lodges will read both
these booklets carefully.
During the coming year. the Committee proposes the publication of
a third booklet, this one consisting of a number of carefully prepared
and thoroughly edited sample news s tories. These. we hope, might serve
as a guide, in the preparation of your news stories. A special subcommittee of professional news men is preparing this guide for you. We
hope to have it ready at an early date.
The Masonic Information Committee, in cooperation with the two
Masonic Press Clubs. is proposing to hold a Public Information Con fer-

would be invited to speak to the conference, and thus, as is our aim,
assist in more clearly directing our own efforts in the path of Dignity,
Quality and Substance.
The Committee wishes to express its appreciation to the Grand
Master for his understandi ng of our problems, and to the Grand Secretary and his staff for the assistance given us over the past year. It is
hoped that next year's Committee will enjoy the same cooperation.
Before closing, the Committee is reminded of a joint meeting which
was held this past year, at which representati ves of the Education.
DeMolay. Public Schools Week. and Constitution Observance Committees attended. It is our feeling that this was most helpful. and that
they shou Id be continued.

TRIAL RECORDS NOS. 1052, 1469, 1554, 1637,
1649, 1652, 1675, 1703, AND 1754
Petitions for restoration have been referred to the Committee on
Grievances in the foregoing trial records.
Petitioner in Trial Record No. 1469 has withdrawn his petition.
These petitions are supported by letters of recommenda tion. usually
from friends of the petitioner, and in most cases we have some information as to the feelings of the former Lodges of these petitioners.
As pointed out in our reports many times in the past, restoration
by Grand Lodge does not restore a petitioner to membership in a Lodge.
but only to the rights and privileges of Masonry in general. and the
petitioner becomes a Mason at large. similar in status to one who has
taken a dimit from a Lodge. To gain membership he must petition some
Lodge for affiliation. (not necessarily his former Lodge). and be
elected by unanimous vote.
We therefore often recommend restoration by Grand Lodge so that
the petitioner may subject his desire for membership to the Lodge of
his choice, and we trust that our recommenda tion will not prevent
that Lodge making the usual investigation of the applicant.
Where it seems apparent that the petitioner could not be affiliated
with his former Lodge that factor tends to lead us to deny restoration
by Grand Lodge.
We have carefully considered all the files and we offer the following resolution:
RESOLVE D : That the petitions for restoration in the following
trial records be granted:
No. 1554, Mendocino Lodge No. 179.
No. 1649, Sequoia Lodge No. 349.
No. 1652, The Gardens Lodge No. 621.
No. 1675, Garvanza Lodge No. 492.
No. 1703, Monte Vista Lodge No. 655.
and that the petitions in the following trial records be denied:
No. 1052, Henry S. Orme Lodge No. 458.
No. 1637, Inglewood Lodge No. 421.
No. 1754, Inglewood Lodge No. 421 .
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1842
The accused of San Buenaventu ra Lodge No. 214 was charged
two separate times in the Justice Court of Ojai Judicial District with
the crimes of issuing checks with insufficient funds on deposit and
failure to provide for his wife and family, both charges being misdemeanors, and in each case he pleaded guilty. Thereafter he was
charged in his Lodge with unmasonic conduct. The specifications of the
charge allege specifically that he pleaded guilty to the misdemeanor
charges.
The accused wrote an equivocal letter in answer to the notice sent
to him by the Master of the Lodge in which he admitted the plea of
guilty to the misdemeano rs but attempted to explain the reasons therefor. The Trial Master treated the letter as a plea of guilty and the
accused was found guilty of unmasonic conduct without trial and
suspended.
The specifkation s were improper in that the specifk acts of issuing
checks without sufficient funds and failing to support his family should
have been alleged as those are the acts of unmasonic conduct, pleading guilty to misdemeano r charges is not. The accused admitted only
the pleas of guilty and not the acts which would indicate he did not
have an opportunity to enter the proper plea.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVE D: That the purported suspension of the accused in
Trial Record No. 1842 be reversed and set aside and the matter remanded to the Lodge with direction to proceed to have charges and
specifications prpperly set forth and proceedings taken thereon.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1859
A member of Traver Lodge No. 294 was charged with improper
and lewd conduct with several young girls. He pleaded not guilty in
the Lodge and a commission met to try him. He appeared before the
meeting of the commission and stated that he was being accused for
improper motives but partially admitted the facts. He said he would
not appear at the trial and left the place. Witnesses were sworn a nd
supported the charge. Accused was found guilty and ordered suspended.
Our committee feels that conduct such as was proved at the trial
in this case merits expulsion.
We offer the following resolution:
RESOLVE D: That the finding of guilt in Trial Record No. 1859
be approved but that the penalty be raised to expulsion and that accused is hereby expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1867

and was committed to a correction al institution . N otice of intended
expulsion under Section 732 C.M.C. was given by the Lodge. The
accused wrote a letter d emanding a Masonic Trial and pleaded not
guilty. Trial was set for July 22. 1965. The accused wrote a number
o f letters stating that he would be released from the correction al institution the forepart of Septembe r and asking that the trial be continued for sixty days until Septembe r 23 so that he could personally
appear and present facts showing his innocence . H is request was
denied and at the trial he was not present or represente d. T he only
evidence was certified copies o f his conviction in the state courts and
he was found guilty and the sentence was expulsion.
He has appealed and personally appeared before your Committe e.
It appears that the accusation s grew out of matrimonial difficulties of
the accused. It also appears that the rules of the correction al institution
prevented his writing any statement of facts justifying his conduct or
proving the contrary.
While it is a general rule that the date of a trial is set for the convenience of the Commissi oners and the Trial Masters. and that the
Lodge does not have to wait until the accused is released from a correctional institu tion. reasonable continuan ces should be allowed under
Section 719 C.M.C. It is the opinion of the Committe e that under the
circumstan ces of this particular case the request of the accused for a
continuan ce of sixty days to enable him to present his defense was
reasonable and should have been granted. We therefore present the
following resolution :
RESOLV ED: That the purported expulsion of the accused in
Trial Record No. 1875 be reversed and set aside, and the matter
remanded to th~ Lodge with directions to proceed to retry the case
before a commission after a proper summons served on the accused.
Adopted.
Respectfully submitted .

A member of San Fernando Lodge No. 343 was charged with
unmasoni c conduct in that he had written several letters and had made
numerous statement s to the general effect that the women or girls of
the Eastern Star, Job's Daughters and Rainbow Girls should let their
hair down a nd take care of the Masons sexually. This seemed to be
an obsession with him. Among others. he wrote to our Grand Secretary,
the Grand Secretary of the York Rite Bodies, and made similar statements to the Mother Advisors of the Rainbow Girls.
He pleaded not guilty and was tried by a commission. He appeared
at the trial without counsel and was given every considerat ion by the
Trial Master. He admitted writing the letters and making the statements. and persisted in his expression s of opinion concernin g the
duties of the women and girls toward all Masons.
He was found guilty and suspended .
We feel that this man has no place in Masonry. We offer the
following resolution :
RESOLV ED : That the finding of guilt in Trial Record No. 1867
be affirmed, but that the penalty be raised to expulsion and that the
accused be expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1869
A member of Kit Carson Lodge No. 784 was charged with adultery
and non-suppo rt of minor children. He pleaded not guilty in the Lodge
and was tried by a commission. He was found guilty of the specifications and of unmasonic conduct and expelled.
Accused filed an appeal and, although not technically correct, we
have given it considerat ion.
The undispute d evidence supports the findings of the trial commission. The accused himself gave the informatio n for a birth certificate
of a child listing himself as the father. the mother not being his wife.
Court document s show that he was convicted of contempt for failing
to pay support for his children as ordered by a court.
We offer the following resolution :
RESOLV ED : That the finding of guilt and the expulsion of the
accused member of Kit Carson Lodge No. 784 are ratified. affirmed
and approved.
Adopted.

REPORT OF COMMI TTEE ON RETIRE MENT PLAN
To the Most W orshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California :
In 1954, the Retiremen t Pens ion Plan was inaugurate d fo r the
employees of the Masonic Homes of California , the Grand Lodge of
California and affilia tes, to provide a retiremen t life income for employees in addition to Social Security benefits. upon a ttaining the age of
sixty-five (65) .
The plan has certain requireme nts to be eligible for membersh ip.
The employee mus t have been in our employ for a period of two (2)
years and attained the age of thirty ( 30) years.

182

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

In I 964, the original plan was amended to change conditions for
early retirement from age fifty-five ( 55) plus twenty ( 20) years of
service to age fifty-five ( 55) and fifteen (I 5) years of service.
At the present time 119 employees are covered by the plan. One
hundred sixty-six are ineligible due to insufficient length of service.
The employees contribute to the plan three ( 3) percent of their
regular annual salary, a nd the employer contributes an amount to make
the plan actuarially sound. During the year 1964 the employees contributed $15,293.00. The employer contributed $44,684.00, which is
about a three to one ratio. Net investment income for 1964 amounted to
$54,942.00.
The assets have grown from a modest beginning to $744,210.00 as
of December 31, 1964.
The pension payments to retired employees, ending December 31.
1964 amounted to $10,057, covering 12 employees.
During the current year 1965. twelve ( 12) employees have already
retired, and there will be two ( 2) more eligible for retirement before
the end of the year, making a total of 14 retirees for this year.
During the year 1966, four ( 4) additional employees will be eligible
for retirement under the plan.
Respectfully submitted,
L. HAROLD ANDERSON
ALFRED F. BRESLAUER
PHIL N. MYERS
PAUL F. PFLUEGER

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
OF THE
MASONIC CLUB AT THE UNIVERSITY
BERKELEY, CALIFORNIA
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
Your Board in submitting this report fully recognizes the success
of the Club at Berkeley is due to the combined efforts of all California
Masons, the students, and the University.
We, who are most closely associated w ith the operation of the
Clubhouse, are sincerely appreciative of the personal interest and s upport of the Grand M aster, Theodore Meriam, and the Officers of
Grand Lodge.
A foundation for evaluating the information submitted in this
report can be found in the By-laws of the Masonic Club at Berkeley.
a corpora tion in the state of California.
"The Corporation sh a ll be conducted for the exclusive benefit of
the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free a nd Accepted Masons of

183

the State of California and subject to its laws, rules, and regulations.
"The purpose of the Corporation is to provide a 's ocial club for members of the student-body, faculty , and staff of the University of California, Berkeley. California, w ho are M aster Masons, their sons,
daughters. wives, and widows; also friends a nd guests as approved by
the Board of Directors."
~ur B~ard has continued to encourage and sponsor promotional
act1v1bes with the goal of increasing membership. The fall semester
1964 had a full program including a Friendship dinner. coffee hours,
a square dance. Faculty dinner. a weekend for U .C.L.A. Clubhouse
members, and a Christmas party for children. The spring semester had
theater parties, a Faculty dinner, Sunday nite suppers. and an Easter
party for underprivileged children. In addition to having the Right
Worsh~pful Myron Smith speak at the Fall Initiation and the Right
Worshipful John Porter speak at the Spring Initiation the students were
very pleased to be able to informally spend time one afternoon with
the Most Worshipful Theodore Meriam.
This last semester we have stressed the facilities available at the
Clubhouse and arranged to have resources that will attract the quality
of student we want associated with our organization. The most widely
used of these items is a set of foreign language dictionaries and
chemistry and physics handbooks. An additional help to our students
a re the two loan funds. The small loan fund for short term loans in
small amounts has been used nineteen times and the Altenberg Loan
Fund for la rger amounts has had five recipient·s this year.
Two major i;:hanges have been made by the students this last
semester: girls are now allowed in the pool room and the Student
Constitution has been updated. The significant long term changes in
the constitution are the discarding of the old pledge program for
entering students and the creation of a "Big Brother and Big Sister"
program to help get all acquainted. M embership now stands at 143.
The Masonic Club President for the fall semester, John Spencer, wrote
the following to entering students :
" I would like to welcome you to Berkeley. Cal is a w onderful school
full of learning, fun, tradition, and a tremendous place to spend your
next few years. However, with its 27,500 students. it also can be a
very lonely place. I would like to give you an opportunity to meet people, relax, and have a good time."
Roy Cross. President for the ·s pring semester, stated in his report:
"My main goal was to build up a basic foundation for the coming
fall semester.... As for improvements in the future I think a scholarship
program should be set up to promote good grades .... This would be
on the basis of grades alone with no consideration of need."

MEMORIAL SERVICE

Lodges suffered losses. Two hundred twelve Lodges lost one each;
seventy-five Lodges had two losses; twenty-one Lodges lost three; eight
Lodges lost four; and one Lodge lost five members who were members of
Grand Lodge. This year there appears to be a larger number of Lodge
Officers among those who have passed on. Nine Lodges report losing
their Masters and nine Lodges lost Wardens. The remainder of the
four hundred sixty-two were Past Masters.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In Masonry we are often reminded of the brevity of life and the
inevitableness of death. The "Hour-Glass" reminds us "how swiftly the
sands run, and how rapidly our lives are drawing to a close!" Man
wastes away. "Today he puts forth the tender leaves of hope; tomorrow
blossoms and bears his blushing honors thick upon him; the next day
comes a frost which nips the shoot; and when he thinks his greatness is
still aspiring, he falls like autumn leaves to enrich our mother earth." Or
::behold what havoc the scythe of time makes among the human race!"
We must soon be cut down by the all-devouring scythe of time, and be
gathered into the land where our fathers have gone before us."
While we "do not sorrow as those without hope," yet when we go
over the names of the departed as they come in from the Lodges we
cannot escape a measure of sorrow. Some of our brethren who have
gone were in the prime years of life. We reasonably hoped that they
might have been with us for many years. But "God has led our dear
ones on, and He can do no wrong." Many of our brethren whose names
appear in this report were of riper years. They labored abundantly for
many years, but now their work is done, and they are forever with their
Lord. For some the Angel of Death was indeed a kind messenger sent to
liberate them from suffering, and they are now where there is "no more
pain, neither sorrow nor crying."
All of us will know some names, and many of us will rem ember many
whose names are here. They were ·r espected men with whom we have
worked and had rich fellowship. We .are sad at the separation, yet we
are deeply thankful for the memories of shared lives and the belief that
there is a larger life beyond.
The statistics of our report are somewhat overwhelming. During the
past Masonic Year four hundred sixty-two of our members have passed
away. This number appears to be the largest in the history of this Grand
Lodge. This is what we can expect as the number of our Lodges increases
and the membership grows larger. Three hundred seventeen of our

Among the departed was one of our well known and beloved Past
Grand Masters, fohn Randle Moore. He was Chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee up to the time of his death. An eulogy for Brother
Moore will be given by Past Grand Master Guy B. Mize.

fames Leo Halley, who had served this Grand Lodge on various committees, and as a Trustee of our Masonic Homes, died on February 7,
1965. An eulogy for Brother Halley will be given by his friend, Past
Grand Master L. Harold Anderson.
Glenn C. Holmes, former Junior Grand Steward and committeeman,
was raised in the Celestial Lodge above on January 1, 1965. Glenn
Holmes was born in Marion, Iowa, on January 2, 1893, and spent the
earlier years of his life in that state. He received the degrees of Masonry
in Capital City Lodge No. 312 of Iowa and was raised a Master Mason
on May 27, 1919. Havi ng moved to California, he affiliated with Mission
Lodge No. 169 of this jurisdiction on June 1, 1932. On October 29, 1938,
he affiliated with Dos Palos Lodge (now No. 681) as a charter member,
and served that Lodge as its Master in 1941. In October, 1941. he was
appointed Junior Grand Steward by Grand Master Frank M. Smith and
served in that of6ce for one year. He served as Chairman of the Committee on Charters from 1944 to 1955. Retiring to live in Carmel. he
became a plural member of Carmel Lodge No. 680 and retained tha t
status until his death. Interested in community welfare, he was elected
Councilman of the City of Mendota and served some time as Mayor
of that city. He was interested in people, especially when there was an
opportunity to help. During World War II he and his wife opened their
home to homesick and lonely young men and women stationed at a
military base not far away. This was typical of the acts of this kindly,
good humored brother. He passed away January 1st, one day short of
his seventieth birthday, but he will live on in the hearts and minds of his
brethren, and of the many to whom he proved a helpful friend in ti mes
of need. He heeded his Master's command, "Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself," and created kindliness in the hearts of others.
Rufus Bernhard von KleinSmid. California lost a valued elder
statesman, scholar, and educator when Doctor von KleinSmid passed
away on July 9, 1964. He was for many years the very well known and
highly respected President of the University of Southern California and
held high rank among educators in this country. He was a member of

192

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

James A. Garfield Lodge No. 566, having been raised a Master Mason
on April 10, 1902. He had thus been a member of the fraternity for over
sixty-two years. He had served as Grand Orator of this Grand Lodge.
Doctor von KleinSmid lived a long life, rich in great achievements. He
contributed much to the life of his fellow men. and he will live on in the
lives of many students who came under his influence and others who had
close association with him. We honor his memory and are proud that he
was a member of our fraternity.

Milton Ho{fe Sharp, for many years Inspector of the 210th District,
passed away December 12, 1964. Brother Sharp was a member of
Buckeye Lodge No. 195, having been raised in that Lodge on May 13,
1943. He went through the chairs and served as Master of his Lodge;
after which, on February 1, 1954, he was commissioned Inspector of the
210th District. He served in that position until March, 1964, for over
ten years. For faithful service, and work well done, we pay our tribute
of respect to our departed brother.
Isaac M cGu ffin, one of our older members, was gathered to his
fathers on January 27, 1965. Brother McGuffin was a member and Past
Master of McKinley Lodge No. 347. He was raised on April 24, 1901,
and at the time of his death had been a Mason for sixty-three years and
nine months. In 1908, when Brother Oscar Lawler was Grand Master, he
was commissioned " Inspector" and served for years in that office. For
extended, faithful service we honor him.
"Now the laborer's task is o'er

Now upon the farther shore
Lands the voyager at last."

Noel W. R oser, Sr. On July 11, 1965, San Bernardino lost a very
able and beloved member of the Craft in the passing of Noel W. Roser,
Sr. at the comparatively early age of 53 years. Brother Roser was a
native of Lansing, Illinois, and came to California over 25 years ago.
He received the degrees of Masonry in_ Damascus Lodge No. 648 in
1945 and with great devotion and ability served as a n officer of that
Lodge and was its M aster in 1952. When it was a pparent that a second
Lodge was needed in San Bernardino, Brother Roser was chosen to be
the Charter Master of Golden Valley Lodge (now No. 796) in 1959.
Under his able leadership as Master, and then for three years as
Secretary, that Lodge has grown and prospered. He was active in other
Masonic bodies, having progressed to the position of Deputy Grand
Commander of the Grand Commandery, Knights Templar of California.
Owing to his illness he was unable to go on to the office of Grand
Co~~an~er. H~ was also active in Scottish Rite and had filled many
positions m Shrme groups. His work in DeMolay was outstanding for

GRAND LODGE OF CA LIFORNIA

193

over ten years. He served as Chapter Dad and was a member of the
Advisory Council.
For many years he was a Supervisor of Personnel and for the last
three years had served in that capacity with the Etiwanda Steel Co. As
a citizen. he was Chairman of the C ity of Rialto's Personnel Board. He
was also a member of the Method ist Church. Funeral services were held
in San Bernardino under the d irection of Damascus Lodge No. 648 and
Golden Valley Lodge No. 796. Also participating were the Gra nd
Commander of Knights Templar and other Grand Commandery Officers.
As a testimony of the esteem in which Brother Roser was held , over
"100 persons attended the services. A bro ther of ability and devotion , he
contributed much to Masonry and his fellow men. His early removal
leaves a gap in the ranks hard to fill. Our sympathy goes out to his wife
and son, and other members of his family.
Samuel Leslie Hawken. Just as we were completing this report word
was received that Brother Les Hawken had passed away in his sleep at
the H alekulani Hotel. Honolulu, while vacationing in the Hawaiian
Islands. He died of a heart attack on Monday. September 20, 1965. He
was 82 years of age. Vice President of Garnett Young and Co., and a
resident of Burlingame. Brother Les had a long and distinguished career
in M asonry. A member of Burlingame Lodge No. 400. he was raised in
that Lodge on July 30, 1918, and served as W orshipful Master in 1924.
Les served as a member of the Burlingame Masonic Hall Association
from 1925 and was a Trustee until the time of his death. In this Grand
Lodge he was a well known figure. Appointed Inspector on January 27,
1925, he served the 364th District until his resignation on December 31,
1959- for almos t j5 years. For a number of years his name headed the
list of Inspectors as the senior member in point of service of that distinguished corps. We know of only one man- the late Clark Shaw of
Long Beach-whose length of service as Inspector exceeded that of
Les Hawken. He will be greatly missed in his Lodge, his City. and this
Grand Lodge. Many officers. past and present, of the Lodges in the
364th District will long remember the helpfulness of this faithful brother.
While we are all saddened by his passing, we are deeply thankful that
he was so long with us and so much a part of us. Our sympathy goes out
to his wife and two sons who survive him.
There are many names on the list of four hundred sixty-two which
well merit attention, but neither time nor space will permit. The complete list will be made a part of this report. All these brethren served for
such periods as God permitted them. Each according to his strength
and talents. A record of their achievements would be voluminous. No
one can measure the influence they had upon their brethren, their cities
and the State. We bow in reverent tribute to their memory and humbly
pray that we be rededicated to the God and the causes they so nobly
served.

We end our report with the words of a prayer :
"Almighty God, with whom do live the spirits of those who depart
hence in the Lord and with whom the souls of the faithful after death
are in strength and gladness, we give thee hearty thanks for the good
examples of all those thy servant·s who, having finished their course in
faith, do now rest from their labor. And we beseech thee that we, with
all those who have finished their course in faith, may have our perfect
consumation and bliss in thy eternal and everlasting glory. Amen."

Board of Trustees for the Masonic Homes.
"He not only lived but flourished-a man who invested well the
amount of time allotted to him. H is last office held in the Scottish Rite
was that of A lmoner, the dispenser of alms. With compassion for all in
need or oppressed, honesty and integrity were the warp and woof of his
personality.
"In countless ways he has influenced for good thousands of men
and women whose lives he has touched.
"'James Leo,' as we loved to call him, had a quiet gentle strengtha simple and all-pervading beauty of spirit that marked him as one of
nature's elect.
"Inspiring leader, able administrator, competent executive, w ise
counselor, gallant and fearless warrior for truth an d right, faithful
friend , always ·r eady with wit and humor, devoted husband, father,
grandfather-and all-around family man of the first order.
"We shall remember him forever as truly a man set apart with rare
and blessed endowments. He was always an optimist-always a man of
hope; never doubting the ultimate victory of Right, Truth and Justice.
H e breathed and lived our Masonic precepts to a d egree we rarely
observe.
"Now, at one bound, he has passed over into posterity. and thus has
consigned himself to the guardianship of memory.
"A mighty tree has fallen in our midst leaving a large and empty
space against the sky.
"We humbly pray that his soul and spirit will be forever blessed by
Him who is the Father of us all."
I can only add a thought with reference to James Leo Halley, a truly
self-made man:
"When it was difficult to be cheerful. he was cheerful. When it was
hard to be patient, he was patient. When he couldn't have been blamed
if he had quit, he didn't quit. When he would have liked to speak his
mind, he kept silent. When it would have been easy to be disagreeable,
he stayed agreeable. When he could have ducked duty, he took duty on.
When a man who could be trusted was needed, he could be trusted! " A
great man, a devoted family man, a dedicated Mason, and a good true
friend.

J.

EULOGY
JAMES LEO HALLEY

By L. Harold Anderson
It is my privilege and pleasure to present to you the eulogy given
our esteemed brother, James Leo Halley, a member of Richmond Lodge
No. 375, on February 10, 1965. at the California Masonic Memorial
Temple in San Francisco by the Reverend M. Jay M inkler, a member of
Fairmount Lodge No. 435:
"James Leo Halley rose from humble beginnings to a degree of
eminence in the city of his birth, at a time when a strong voice of
reason and restraint was helpful to the entire community. He was not
afraid of hard work and was willing and anxious to act upon his convictions. He also possessed the qualities of courage and imagination so
necessary to progress and new development.
"Throughout his long career of public service on the Board of
Supervisors, he recognized the need for sincere and mutual relationships with all his fellow citizens. Man lives by and through such
relationships.
" In this way our distinguished brother suceeded in building a strong
homely American philosophical linkage with people of all faiths and in
all conditions of social. economic and political status.
"Death for such a man is not the great leveler. Death, rather, gives
us, the living, the opportunity to measure the eminence of the man to
whom we pay final respects.
"Although a veteran of World War I. his fraternal service-s are
more intimately and personally remembered; especially by all who have
had any connections with Masonic life in California.
" Past Master of Richmond Lodge. Past Venerable Mastei: Lodge of
Perfection, and 33° Mason of the San Francisco Bodies of the Scottish
Rite. Past Grand Patron of the Order of the Eastern Star of the State
of California. Past Potentate Islam Temple of the Shrine: and most

OBSER VATIO NS
OBSERVA TION

No. l

In recent years, and especiall y in the last several years, the Grand
Lodge has been receiving a constant ly increasin g number of invitation s
to lay the cornersto nes of public schools and public buildings . It is, of
course, our desire to be able to accept all such invitatio ns. However , the
number is rapidly reaching the point where scheduli ng of these
ceremon ies to accommo date both the local authoriti es and the Grand
Lodge Officers is becomin g difficult indeed. I believe that we should
consider the possible establish ment of a special cornersto ne ceremon y
team in the Bay Area and also in Southern Californ ia in order that
we may have less difficulty in being .able to readily accept the invitations which are offered to us. I am not suggesti ng that the Grand
Lodge Officers would not participa te but rather that we would be
able to provide two, or even three, cornersto ne ceremon ies in different
parts of C alifornia at the same time. When possible, of course, the
necessar y stations would be filled by the elected and appointiv e
Grand Lodge Officers but their non-atte ndance should in no way
interfere with our a bility to provide a top-qual ity cornersto ne ceremon y
which would be complete ly represen tative of the Grand Lodge of
Californ ia.

The Committ ee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand M aster observes that:
( 1 ) The Grand Lodge has received an increasin g number of invitations to lay the cornersto nes of public schools and public buildings .

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORN IA

201

( 2) That it is the desire of the Grand Lodge to accept all such
invitations.
( 3) H owever, the number of invitation s received is rapidly approachin g the point when scheduli ng of these ceremon ies to accommo date the local authorities is becoming increasin gly difficult.
( 4) The Grand Master s uggests that the Grand Lodge consider the
possible establish ment of a special cornersto ne ceremon y team in the
Bay Area , and also in Southern Californ ia in order to more readily
accept the invitation s offered.
( 5) This would enable the Grand Lodge to provide two, or even
three, cornersto ne ceremon ies in Californi a at the same time.
Your Committ ee on Policy and General Purposes agrees with the
Grand Master and offers the followin g motion:
We move tha t it be the policy of the Grand Lodge that there be two
or more groups in different parts of the State which are qualified and
ready to perform the ceremon y of laying of cornersto nes when directed
by the Grand Master to do so.

The Committ ee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committ ee on Jurisprud ence concurs in the suggestio n of the
Grand Master tha t the Grand Lodge should be able to provide two or
even three cornersto ne ceremon ies in different parts of the Jurisdict ion
a t the same time. We desire merely to make the observat ion that there
is but one Grand Lodge and that it can be opened for a ceremon y only
once at the same time, conseque ntly the second or third cornersto ne ceremony in a differen t place must be performe d without opening Grand
Lodge. This, of coarse. is permissible under our adopted Book of Ceremonies.
Adopted .
OBSERVA TION

No. 2

During the course of service as Grand Master, one necessar ily attends a good many receptions for the Grand Master. In many instances
these reception s are formal affairs, confined to members of the Lodge
or Lodges involved, and are conducte d in what has become a very
tradition al manner. I have found that there is a greater enthusias m and,
I trust, a greater impact on Masonry in a commun ity when the reception
for the Grand Master is held as an open affair with the wives, families
and guests of the members of the Lodges present so that all may hear
the message of the Grand Master. I believe that the effectiveness of the
visit of the Grand Master to any commun ity can be greatly enhance d
if his appearan ce and presenta tion may be public, and I suggest that
wheneve r it is feasible and practical the reception for the Grand
Master should not be a closed affair.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

202

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
There has been referred to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes a comment by the Grand Master which is neither a decision
nor a recom.mendation and which he has therefore quite properly called
an observation.
. ~he observation which is the subject of this report and recommendation is nu~bere~ 2, and its substance is stated adequately in its last
sentence: I believe that the effectiveness of the visit of the Grand
Master to any community can be greatly enhanced if his appearance
and presentation may be public. and I suggest that whenever it is feasible
and practical the reception for the Grand Master should not be a closed
affair."
Certainly no one who is acquainted with the Grand Master and
~as o?se~ed his outsta nding talents in meeting the public and in expressing h1.s views, whether in respect to Masonic matters or otherwise. would
question for a moment the effectiveness of such personal contacts.
~our Committee is concerned, however, lest the great appeal of such
public appearances might militate agains t the cherished opportunities of
~aster Masons. to me~t and greet their Grand Master in their Lodges
m accordance with ancient custom. Only in tiled Lodges may the special
honors due the G~and Master be extended. Only in tiled Lodges may
the members be given. the . most. ~eaningful information concerning the
state of the Craft which hes w1thm the special competence and knowledge of the Grand Master. These are precious Masonic privileges and
not community matters.
. While. therefore, your Committee rejoices in such public presentations as may be found feasible by the Grand Master from time to time
it feels impelled. for the reasons stated, to recommend that the Grand
Lodge affirm its special regard for its Grand Master by maintaining the
p~esent. policy that whether the appearance of the Grand Master at any
given time or place shall be public or in a tiled meeting shall be determined in each instance by the Grand Master a fter consultation with
the local brethren.
We move the adoption of this report.
~he Committee on Ritual indicated its concurrence in the recommendation.
Adopted.

No. 3

. On sever~! occasions during this past year I have been asked questions concernmg the eligibility for the degrees of Masonry on behalf
of men who are not of a Protestant denomination. Because of these
Ee.el. that I should state very emphatically that religious
questi~ns
~enommat1on 1s m no way a criterion for Masonic eligibility. No man
is b~rred from. Masonry because of religious faith. Only that man who
demes the existence of a Supreme Being is ineligible to become a

!

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

203

Mason. In this respect, any Mason who exercises the privilege of casting a negative ballot because of religious denominational prejudice is
committing an unmasonic act, even though the fact of his action may
be known only to himself. Religious discrimination has no place wha tever in the structure of Freemasonry, and this must be understood by all
Master Masons .
Received.
OBSERVATION No. 4
It has been brought to my attention on several occasions during
this past year that in some Lodges the conduct of the officers and
members during the refreshment period in the banquet hall following
the conferring of a degree has been lacking in the dignity and the
propriety which should be expected on such occasions. I want to point
out that the dignity and quality of a Masonic gathering is not confined
to that portion of the gathering which is held behind tiled doors. It is
incumbent upon every presiding Master that he supervise and conduct
all Masonic gatherings of h is Lodge in such a manner that there will
be at all times a n atmosphere of complete propriety. Crudeness and
ribaldry have no place in any Masonic gathering.
Received.
OBSERVATION No. 5
It has been my observa tion in my several years of association with
the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes that many of our constituent Lodge officers do not clearly understand the admission requirements for the Masonic Home at Union City. Although the requirements
have been explained on many occasions. problems continue to arise
because of misinformation or misunderstanding. It should be clea rly
emphasized that no Lodge officer should make any statement. either
directly or implied. which would tend to cause a potential applicant
for admission to the Home to believe that his or her admission is
ass ured. Necessarily there is a thorough investigation by a professional ly trained representative of the M asonic Home for each application.
Occasionally. the inves tigation discloses facts concerning the applicant
which are not known by officers of the Lodge sponsoring the applicant
and thus awkward and even embarrassing situations can result when
a n application must be d enied after the applicant has been encouraged
by statements of Lodge officers. I want to urge each of you to be
thoroughly familiar with the rules of admission to both of our M asonic
Homes and to recognize that admission to either of the homes is a
privilege and not a right.
Received.

OasERVATION

No. 7

It has been my experience this yea r in much reading of the California Masonic Code tha t the time is rapidly approaching when there
should be an updating of our Code. T wo things are necessary. One
is to eliminate from the Code those items of duplication and of
obsolescence that quite obviously need not be in the Code. Secondly.
our present Code refers. in many insta nces. to the Ross Digest. This
former volume of M asonic law is not a lwa ys available to one who
is searching the California Masonic Code for the answer to a problem.
I believe that our entire law should be contained in one volume. I have
no definite recommendation as to how to proceed with such a project.
I merely want to comment at this time tha t, as time goes along , the
need for modernization of the California Masonic Code becomes more
pressing.
Received.

DECISIONS
(The C ommittee on furispruden ce has read and considered the Gra~d
Master's decisions. We find them to be clear, accurate and_w~ll considered. We report separately on Decision No. 7, but at this time move
the approva l of Decisions Nos. 1 through 6 and recommend a yes vote. )
DEc 1s10N No. 1
I was a sked as to the eligibility for a Masonic funeral of a brother
who ha d taken a Dimit from a Lodge in our Jurisdiction and then
some years later had applied for affiliation but, prior to the time _of
possible election, he had passed away. Since the brother ~oluntanly
took his Dimit and there had been no charges of unmasomc conduct
found against him at any time, and since we must assume that his
application for affiliation was because of a sincere desire to return to
active Masonic membership, I believe we must rega rd the deceased
brother in at least the same light as we would a member suspended
for non-payment of dues since a Lodge may, in its discretion, bury a
member suspended for non-payment of dues. If there be no other
offenses established against him it would seem reasonable that a Lodge
might. in its discretion. provide a Masonic funeral service for a brother
who has applied for return to active membership but through the
ci·rcumstance of death had not completed the process. I therefore
ruled that a Masonic fun eral service could be provided in these
circumstances.
Adopted.
DEc 1s10N No. 2
I was asked as to the propriety. as well as legalitry, of enclosing
tickets for a DeMolay Breakfast in a letter sent to members of a
Lodge urging their attendance at the Breakfast. I ruled that to enclose
tickets either with a Lodge Trestleboard or in a direct letter to members
of a Lodge would be considered as using pressure to sell the tickets
and thus would be illegal under our law. It is perfectly proper to announce in a Tresleboard or by direct letter to members of a Lodge
that a D eMolay Breakfast is to be held as a fund-ratsing proj~c~ and
thus an invitation is extended to members of the Lodge to part1c1pate.
Their choice, however. should be free of any implication of requirement
to purchase a ticket.
Adopted.
D Ec1s10 N No. 3
The question was presented : C ould a subordinate organization of
a Lodge a ccept the gift of a substantial block of tickets from a racetrack in order that the tickets might be sold to members of the Lodge
and the proceeds then go to the subordinate organization of the Lodge?
I ruled tha t this would be illegal. The organization must be considered
as though it were the Lodge itself. Our Law is clear that no Lodge can

206

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

accept any of the proceeds or profits of any gambling enterprise. This
provision does not require that the gambling itself be unlawful. In my
opinion, the selling of tickets to a racetrack would be aiding an enterprise which is conducting gambling. It is also my opinion that the proposed scheme was basically contrary to established M asonic policy.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Decision number 3 of the Grand Master, that a subordinate organization of a Lodge could not accept the gift of a block of tickets from a
race track and sell them to members of the Lodge was referred to the
Com mittee on Policy and General Purposes. With commendable restraint, we believe, the three members of the legal profession serving on
the Policy Committee see only a legal point involved and on questions
of law they continue to remain mute - as a Committee, that is.
Adopted.
DEc1s10N No. 4
I was asked whether it was proper for a Lodge to use its funds for
the purchase of clothing for the grandson of a deceased member of
that Lodge who has been admitted to the Masonic Home for Children
at Covina. Our Law does not cover this point but I am certain that
when this Grand Lodge broadened the eligibility rules for entrance to
the Children's Home. there was no thought of any differentiation in the
aid and assistance that could be extended to any child who might enter
under the broader eligibility rules. I therefore ruled that it was a
proper expenditure of Lodge funds to provide suitable clothing for the
boy. The same Lodge also asked if the Lodge might reimburse itself
for the funds expended for the child's clothing from the father'·s weekly
contribution to the Home on behalf of his son. (The father of the boy
was not a M ason). The answer was "no" because the contribution of
the father is deemed to be a direct contribution to the daily cost of
support of his son at the Home.
Adopted.
DEcrs10N No. 5

I was asked if the interior of a ballot box must be padded. There
is nothing in the California Masonic Code which prescribes the exact
form of a ballot box. I believe that it is completely proper and probably
obviously necessary that the ballot box should be lined with some
material that would so deaden the sound as to make it impossible for
anyone nearby to even estimate whether a cube or ball had been deposited in the box. Our ballot is strictly secret. Thus, every reasonable
precaution should be taken so that there will be no opportunity for
any member present to be able to ascertain in any way how another
brother has voted. I therefore ruled that the ballot box in question
should be suitably lined with a n appropriate material which will sufficiently deaden the sound of the fall of the cubes or balls.
Adopted.

DEc1s10N No. 6

The question was asked if a Lodge could present a trowel as a gift
from the Lodge to the candidate. M y answer was that it could do so
but that the expenditure for purchase of the trowel must come from
the refreshment fund . not from the general funds of the Lodge. This
was the intent and the effect of a preceding decision which established
that a trowel cannot be purchased with general funds of a Lodge.
Adopted. NOTE: R esolution No. 9, page 237, supersedes.
DECISION No. 7

My opinion was asked whether a resident of California, who while
in the military service of the United States had been made a Mason
in a regular Lodge under a foreign jurisdiction, could be permitted to
visit a Lodge in this jurisdiction.
I held that under Section 551 of the California Masonic Code,
having received the degrees from a foreign source, without proper
permission of the Lodge nearest his place of residence, he could not
be recognized as a Mason until such Lodge (nearest his place of
residence) shall have ·received him as a member. However. he is not
a cla ndestine Mason.
While it was once held that such Lodge could as a condition for
receiving his application demand t he payment of the full fee for the
three degrees ( CMC. Sec. 551b). nevertheless, it is my opinion that
a later decision and report of the Jurisprudence Committee ( R. D ..
Sec. 576; Proc. 1900, p. 866; Cf. R.D .. Sec. 577, Proc. 1912, p. 158) is
much more in a~cord with our Masonic philosophy. and that it would
be unfair for the Lodge nearest his place of residence to make any
charge, beyond its affiliation fee, for receiving him as a member. To
require him to pay again for degrees regularly received elsewhere
would be to penalize the innocent brother, who was ignorant of the
rules of Masonic juris diction.
It is my opinion, therefore, that under these circumstances it would
be highly improper for the Lodge to charge more than the affiliation
fee for receiving him as a member.
(In connection with this Decision I want to recommend that our Law
be changed to make it possible for a California resident who, while in
the military service, has been made a Mason in a regular Lodge under
a foreign jurisdiction to be considered as having properly become a
Mason. A man in the military service does not have control of his
place of actual residence and although his legal residence may remain
in California for all practical purposes his residency is where the
military authorities place him. If he is deemed eligible for membership
in a Lodge within the jurisdiction where he is performing his military
service, and this is a jurisdiction with whom we are in fraternal accord.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRANO LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

then we should not place this Master Mason in a technically unwelcome
status upon his return to California. He should be recognized as a
regular member of the Lodge which he has joined.)

The Committee on f urisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence reports on the Grand Master's
Decision No. 7 as follows:
This decision is that a resident of California who, while in the military service of the United States, was made a Mason in a regular Lodge
under a foreign jurisdiction cannot be permitted to visit a Lodge in this
jurisdiction.
We believe that this decision is in strict conformity to Section 551
of the C.M.C .. which provides that such person cannot be recognized
as a Mason until the Lodge nearest his residence shall have received
him as a member.
In addition, the Grand M aster held that under such circumstances,
it would be highly improper for the Lodge nearest his residence to charge
the brother more than the affiliation fee for receiving him as a member.
This also we believe to be in accordance with the law as set forth in
Section 551. as construed in previous decisions and reports adopted by
this Grand Lodge.
We move that the decision be approved.
The Grand Master has recommended that Section 551 be changed
to recognize such a person as having properly been made a Mason. To
effect this change in the law, we offer the following resolution :
RESOLVED that Section 551 of the C.M.C. be amended to add
thereto the following:
"However, any Lodge shall recognize as a Ma·s on a person who,
while in the military service of the United States, has received
the degrees of Masonry in a regula r Lodge under a jurisdiction
recognized by this Grand Lodge in which he is stationed at the
time of receiving the degrees and in accordance with the laws of
such jurisdiction."
We move the adoption of the resolution and recommend a yes vote.
The Grand Master's decision was adop ted.
Amendment to Section 551 C .M.C. adopted by 5/ 6 vote.

RECO MMENDATION No. 1
At the 1964 Communication this Grand Lodge authorized the Grand
Master to appoint a special committee to study and make recommendations concerning possible modification of our laws respecting liquor.
The report of that committee has been submitted to the Grand Master
and I have chosen to include it in this message. The committee consisted
of:
Phil N. Myers, P.G.M.. McCloud Lodge No. 430.
Norman Smith, Barstow Lodge N o. 682.
John A. Sickenberger, West Lake Lodge No. 392.
Samuel I. Jacobs, Doric Lodge No. 216.
John Williams. Sequoia Lodge No. 349.
Herewith is the full report of this committee :
To the Most Worshipful Theodore Meriam
Grand M aster of M asons in California:
" The undersigned Committee, appointed by you in compliance with
the resolution adopted by the 1964 Grand Lodge Communication.
respectfully s ubmits the following report:
It is the opinion of the C ommittee that the provisions of the California Masonic Code should be revised and amended in the following
particulars :
( l) An ordinance be adopted reading substantially as follows:
"A Masonic Lodge shall not hold meetings in, own
or lease a building containing a liquor establishment, except that a tenant in such a building who is engaged
primarily in the business of selling other merchandise
may sell bottled liquors incidentally to the sale of such
other merchandise; provided, however, that such tenant
shall not be permitted to display dominating or offensive
advertising in connection with the sale of such bottled
liquor on the exterior of a building owned by the Lodge.
nor may a Lodge be a tenant in a building where such
dominating or offensive advertising is displayed."
( 2) Section 408b of the California Masonic Code, which was
Grand Master H eald's Decision No. 7 adopted at the 1964
Communication, adequately covers the situation therein provided. and we recommend no change.
( 3) An ordinance be adopted reading substantially as follows :
"A Masonic Lodge may hold a purely social evening, open installation of officers. or meeting where business is transacted incidentally, in a public hotel, restaurant, or other establishment serving liquor, provided
that no liquor is served or consumed during the meeting or meal."

Grand Lodge of California will not be in violation of California law if they are complying with the law of the Grand
Lodge of the foreign jursdiction when they are actually in
such foreign jurisdiction.

conflict with the above should be amended or modified.

Masters and/ or other presiding officers of any organizations
requiring Masonic connection should not tolerate conduct
on the part of members which is contrary to the principles
of Freemasonry, and to this end they should use their good
offices to avoid the creation of any opportunity which might
easily degenerate into an occasion which would bring reproach upon our Fraternity.

RECOMMENDATION No. 2
A review of the membership returns over the past several years
reHects a steady increase in the number of instances where the Lodges
are granting advance remission of dues to a disproportionate number
of their members. The latest tabulation shows 25 cases where such
remissions have covered over 4 % of the membership of the particular
Lodge. Of these, the percentage was fi ve or more in sixteen instances
and one of the Lodges included in the above remitted, in advance.
the dues of 14% of its members.
The Grand Secretary has called attention to the above tendency in
severa l of his annual reports. Each time he has pointed out that such
a procedure by the Lodge is based upon the provisions of Section 577
of the Code, but involves a misunderstanding of the intent of that section. As covered by annotation 'h' of the section, eligibility for remission in advance occurs only where payment of his dues would involve
a definite hardship to the member.
It would not appear as probable, in these times, that 5 % of the
members of each of sixteen Lodges would suffer real hardship by the
payment of dues or that, in the extreme case cited, 14% of that Lodge's
membership is in such financial distress that Section 577 needs to be
applied.
In order that we may seek a better general understanding of the
regulations it is my recommendation that the incoming Grand M aster
appoint a committee of not more than three members to study the
matter of unwarranted remission of dues and report its findings and
recommendations to the 1966 Annual Communication.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes urged adoption o f the
recommendation.
Adopted.

RECOMMENDATION No. 3

At the 1964 Communication of our Grand Lodge the report of the
Special Committee on Committee Structure was adopted. By this adoption certain policies suggested in the report were approved. The Deputy
Grand Master, in selecting committee personnel for the for thcoming
Grand Lodge year. has implemented these policies enthusiastically and
extensively. as will be observed when the committee appointments are
announced la ter this week. However, both time and circumstance have
prevented complete implementation of the recommenda tions concerning
committee structure adopted by Grand Lodge last year. Definitions o f
the duties of each committee need yet to be refined before they can be
submitted for legislative action and inclusion in the California Masonic
Code. Certain committee consolidations which were recommended and
which do not require legislative action have been effected; others have
not, and it is my recommendation that the incoming Grand Master
appoint a special committee to study furthe r the suggested consolida~
tions which have not been put into effect in order that it may be d early
determined that such consolidations will be of rea l benefit to our Grand
Lodge work. The recommendations of last year's special committee
were far reaching in their effect and scope and it has taken more time
than had been anticipated to put them all into effect; thus the work
must be continued.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes urged adoption of the
Grand Master's recommendation. In this connection it proposed that
the renewed recommendation of the Committee on Constitution Observance in its report that it be made a Standing Committee be a matter
for consideration by the Special Committee on Committee Structure.
The Committee on Jurisprudence indicated its concurrence in the recommendation of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The Grand Master's recommendation was adopted.

PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO THE ORDINANCES
MASONIC PLAQUE OR SIGN WITH EMBLEM
AT ENTRANCE TO CITY
1964 Resolution ( 5)

This resolution considered at the 1964 Annual Communication failed
to receive a 5/6ths vote, but did get a simple majority. The matter is up
for reconsideration at the 1965 session. See S ection 783 CM.C . It requires a 2/ 3rds vote for adoption.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Masonic Lodges are proud of their existence as evidenced by their display of emblems on Temples, notices of meetings and
activities in newspapers; and
WHEREAS, the Grand Master's Special Commission on Masonic
Practices has stated "that we are failing dismally and disastrously to
inform the public of today what Masonry is and what it .stands for. Far
worse than opposition, we face wide ignorance of the very existence of
our Fraternity"; and
WHEREAS', there appears to be no valid reason why a Masonic
Lodge should not be allowed if it so desires to place at the entrances of
a city or town a dignified and well maintained sign or plaque exhibiting
a Masonic emblem and giving the name and number of the Lodge, and
or where and when it meets thus notifying traveling Masons and the
public in general that there is an active Masonic Lodge in that city or
town.
RESOLVED, that subsection S of Sec. 333 C.M.C. be repealed.
Respectfully submitted,

Ref erred to Committ ees on Jurisprud ence and on Policy and General
Purposes .

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Committ ee on Jurisprud ence, in the interest of economy of time.
has reported on both Resolutio ns Nos. 7 and 18 ( 1964) in one report
and the report largely consists of stating the differences between the
two resolutio ns. It is true. as stated in the report of that Committ ee,
''These two resolutio ns are wholly different in content." Because they
are different. the Committ ee on Policy and General Purposes will discuss
them separate ly.
We shall turn our attention first to Resolutio n No. 7 ( 1964) because it was presente d and numbere d first last year and for the more
cogent reason that everythin g which the proponen ts of Resolution
No. 18 ( 1964) seek to accompli sh thereby will be accompli shed if
Resolutio n No. 7 ( 1964) is adopted.
Let us, therefore , consider No. 7 ( 1964) and after you have voted
thereon. we shall turn to the other resolution.
This resolutio n was referred to the Committ ee on Policy and General
Purposes during the 1964 Commun ication. The Committ ee recomme nded
that the resolutio n be adopted. A written ballot was taken. The resolution received more than a majority "yes" vote. but the vote did not reach
the required five-sixths, hence the resolutio n is again before us. and the
Committ ee has re-exami ned the argumen ts for and against it.
The enacting clause of the resolutio n is quite brief and reads as
follows: "that Section 334 C.M.C. be amended to add the following
words at the end of the section: A Lodge shall have the authority to
inform its members by United States mail in the Lodge Bulletin or
otherwis e of the names of applican ts for the degrees and it shall have
the authority to so inform its members as to the names of candidat es and
the dates of conferra l of the several degrees. "
We shall discuss the two types of notices separate ly. but it should
be pointed out that the proposed amendm ent as to both types is permissive, it does not require Lodges to give either notice; it permits each
Lodge to decide for itself to give one. both or neither of the notices.
Your Committ ee is aware that notices of applicati ons to receive the

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORN IA

221

degrees are mailed to their members by many English. Canadia n , Australian Lodges; also by Lodges in New Jersey. Massach usetts and we
believe in other jurisdicti ons in the United States.
One obvious and valuable end which ·such a notice would serve
would be to bring the applicati on to the attention of any member of the
Lodge who might know o f any disqualification of the applican t. U nder
the present prohibiti on against such notices. the member knowing of the
disqualification may know nothing of the applicati on unless he is
present at the particula r Stated M eeting at which it is read or the particular Stated Meeting when a ballot is taken. The situation may be different in smaller communities, but in a medium or large city in which
every Lodge has city-wide jurisdicti on, we cannot be too zealous in
affording our Lodges every reasonab le means of ascertain ing whether
its applican ts are worthy or unworth y. This resolutio n appears to your
Committee to be a step in that direction .
A more pleasant aspect of the proposed amendm ent is that such a
notice would inform a member of the Lodge who was an acquaint ance of
the applican t, but perhaps not in close enough contact with him to otherwise learn, that the applicati on was being made. Again it would seem
that this would redound to the welfare of the Lodge and to the happines s
of the member who was the acquaint ance.
The argumen ts against the amendm ent are that we have never done
it before, therefore we should not do so now. This argumen t is one that
may be urged against every proposed change. If it is accepted as being
sufficient of itself, progress cannot be made along any line.
It may be sai~ that such a notice might, on some occasion come to
the attention of a non-Mas on. We ask, ls your Lodge receiving applications which it would be ashamed to have known by non-Mas on s? Are
there men applying to our Lodges who would be ashamed to have it
known that they were knocking at the door of Masonry ? We hope not,
but if either is the case we ought to find it out.
The second notice which the amendm ent would permit a Lodge to
give to its members, if it desired to do so, would be tha t, for example on
Novemb er second, F irst Degrees would be conferre d on John Smith and
William Brown, that on Novemb er ninth Second Degrees would be
conferre d on Paul Jones and Harry White and on Novemb er sixteenth
a Third Degree would be conferre d on Donald Thomas . It certainly
would be a service to the members of the Lodge who were friends of
one or more of these candidat es to be advised that their friend was to
receive a degree. It would permit such members to know in advance and
to arrange their personal engagem ents so that they might attend the
conferral .
We do not believe that there is any risk involved that the informat ion
in the notice would be of value to any solicitor because the amendm ent
does not contemp late the publicati on of addresse s or occupati ons.

FINANCING OPERA TIONS OF MASONIC HOMES
(3)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, it is the duty and obligation of all Master Masons to
aid and assist distressed, worthy Brother Master Masons, their widows
and orphans; and
WHEREAS, less than half the Masons in California act upon this
obligation and voluntarily make annual contributions to the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund; and
WHEREAS, it is manifestly unfair to expect half the Masons to
carry all the burden of the Homes; and
WHEREAS, the accumulation of money in the Endowment Fund
and the magnitude of that Fund is such as to act as a deterrent to some
Masons with regard to the needs of the Homes; and
WHEREAS, the interest earned by the Fund does not, nor will it
in the foreseeable future, provide adequate income to operate the Homes,
which fact has made it necessary to institute a per capita tax to augment
this income and further to conduct an annual appeal for funds to
enlarge the corpus of the Fund; and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge and its constituent Lodges are faced
with a continuous and increasing expense necessary to operate this
fund raising activity of the annual drive for contributions to the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund; and
WHEREAS. the Masonic Homes ought to be the charge and care
of all Masons throughout the year and not merely during a short time
period designated for fund raising
BE IT NOW THEREFORE RESOLVED. that the operations of
the Masonic Homes be conducted hereafter on a more nearly current
basis.
That this end be achieved by setting the per capita levy for the
Masonic Homes annually by the Grand Lodge to provide 75% of the
approved operating budget of the Masonic Homes, thus assuring that
all Masons will share equally in supporting the Homes.
That the balance of funds required to operate the Homes be taken
from the annual income of the corpus of the Masonic Homes Endowment
Fund.
That the capital requirements of the Masonic Homes. when authorized and approved by the Grand Lodge. be met by using the annual
income from the corpus of the Fund above that required to fund the
operating budget.
That any income from the corpus of the Fund, not utilized within
two years for either of the purposes stated, be returned to the corpus
of the fund to be governed by the rules thereunto applying.
That modus operandi of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board be

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

227

directed to obtaining bequests and gifts to the corpus of the Fund by
means other than an annual appeal to the members for contributions.
That Section 247 C.M.C. be amended by adding the words "Capital
requirements" immediately following the word "maintenance."
That Section 249 C.M.C. be deleted from the C.M.C.
Respectfully submitted,
E. S. HAYS, M., No. 761
THELO A. PERROTT, P.M., No. 761
HERBERT E. SIMONS,
J. WILLIAM CARL, M., No. 346
P.M., No. 761
ToM J. McW1LLIAM,
P.M., No. 761
JoHN J. WILLIAMS, P.M., No. 761
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Polioy and General
Purposes, and Finance; also to the Masonic Homes Endowment Board
and the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 3 proposes a •s omewhat radical change in the concept,
or manner, of securing funds for operating expenses of the two Homes
maintained by this Grand Lodge.
We think that the regulations set out in our Code, with reference to
the Masonic Homes Endowment Board, i.e .. Article V. Sections 241-250,
inclusive, developed and strengthened over a long period of years with
the consent at all times of Grand Lodge, are reasonable and, to the
greatest extent possible, equitable. The present per capita assessment
for operating expenses of the Homes faHs equally on each member of
the Fraternity through the annual levy of each Lodge. It is our considered judgment that too many of our Lodges could not meet a substantial increase in the total per capita tax to be paid out of the dues
of members which this resolution would entail-unless our members,
through action in their respective Lodges, would uniformly agree to a
substantial increase of present dues.
Your Committee does agree with the proponents of this re·solution
that each member of the Fraternity should do his full share in this most
worthy charity.
We recognize that charity emanates first from the heart and secondly
from the pocketbook, and we recognize the difficulty of equalness in
giving. Let him who can, and so desires, give in proportion to his means.
The example so set cannot but help influence liberality in giving by
others. Such is the history of our Endowment Fund as it has moved
steadily forward in purpose and results.
Finally, it is to be observed that procedures followed by this Grand
Lodge are, to a very great extent, comparable to those followed by other
Grand Lodges which maintain Homes, by religious organizations, by
secular organizations which have projects for the unfortunate and by
charitable foundations.

PROCEED INGS OP THE

Your Policy and Genera l Purpose s Commi ttee recomm ends a no
vote on the resolution.
The Commit tee on Jurisprudence:
Resolution No. 3 was referred to the Commi ttee on Jurispru dence
and we submit our report as follows:
Resolution No. 3 propose s that Grand Lodge annuall y provide an
operatin g budget for the Masoni c Homes by levying a per capita tax
upon all constitu tent Lodges . The amount of these taxes thus assessed
upon the Lodges is to be 75 % of the total operatin g budget as thus fixed
by Grand Lodge for the Masoni c Homes. The remaini ng 25 % to be
taken from the annual income received from the corpus of the Masoni c
Homes Endowm ent Fund.
The Resolut ion further propose s to amend Section 247 C.M.C. and
to repeal Section 249 C.M.C.
The effect of the propose d amendm ent to Section 247 would be to
permit the income from the Endowm ent Fund to be used for capital
requirem ents as well as maintai ntenanc e. The Section now provide s that
such income can only be used for mainten ance purpose s.
The present Endowm ent Fund was built up and created by contributions from many sources. These contribu tors donated to the Fund
upon the knowled ge and represe ntation that the corpus of the Fund
would forever remain intact, the income alone to be used for mainten ance
purpose s. They are entitled to have the Fund used for the sole purpose
for which it was created . and for which they donated . In our opinion it
would be an unwarr anted and illegal breach of trust to now change the
purpose s for which said funds can be used after millions of dollars have
been thus donated to it.
The Commit tee on Jurispru dence is opposed to this Resolut ion.
The Commit tee on Finance , the Masoni c Homes Endowm ent Board.
and the Board of Trustee s of the Masoni c Homes concurr ed in the
recomm endatio n of the Commi ttees on Policy and General Purpose s a nd
on Jurispru dence.
A majority voted against the resolution.
