Resolution No. 4 propose s an amendm ent to Section 283 Californ ia
Masoni c Code, to provide for .. perman ent," fixed per capita upon Lodges
for the conferri ng of degrees . for Grand Lodge constitu tional requirements, for Grand Lodge general activities, for support of the Masoni c
Homes of Californ ia and for the use and benefit of the Californ ia
M asonic Memori al Temple . The several levies provide d for in the resolution total $4. l 0 per capita plus $1.00 for each degree conferr ed during
the year. It should be noted that the total suggest ed per per capita levy,
with complete detail, is a part of the report made to Grand Lodge by the
Commi ttee on Finance at each Annual Commu nication of Grand Lodge.

230

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDING S OP THE

The resolution also proposes the elimination of that portion of Section 283 which gives Grand Lodge authority to levy additional per
capita levies if such in its judgment are necessary. Striking this portion
of the Section is an effort to bind future sessions of Grand Lodge something which cannot be done and would only make it necessary to enact
new special legislation at every Annual Communica tion.
This resolution, suggesting fixed, inflexible annual per capita levies
should be defeated because it is impracticabl e. While much of Grand
Lodge expenses can be determined in advance, resolutions are brought
to the floor of Grand Lodge for your consideratio n at each Annual
Communica tion anti, if approved by you. may and frequently do require
appropriatio ns in excess of any income which could be provided on
fixed per capita levies.
It is in the province of members of Grand Lodge when considering
resolutions to give weight to financial considerations as well as to the
merit of ·s ubjects under discussion. Obviously. if you as members of
Grand Lodge approve legislation requiring the expenditure of Grand
Lodge funds, the means for implementin g your judgment must be
available.
We move adoption of the resolution and your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommend s a no vote.

The Committee on Finance:
There was referred to the Finance Committee Resolution No. 4
which seeks to amend Section 283 C.M.C., which is the section of our
Constitution and Ordinances under which you are given the authority
to vote such sums for the support of Grand Lodge activities, and to
support the operation of our Masonic Homes as, from time to time,
you may deem necessary.
The resolution would completely eliminate the discretion you now
hold in these matters and fix the amounts at those presently in effect.
The proponent of the resolution gives three reasons for his proposal:
First, that the amount of the per capita is obscurely published; second.
that changes in the per cap ita may be made with little or no forewarning; and, third, that it is inconsistent for certain amounts to be fixed,
while others are left to your discretion.
The Proceedings of Grand Lodge, including action on per capita,
are published annually and a copy sent to every Lodge. The resolution
mentions some difficulty experienced by Masters and Wardens relating
to knowledge of action on per capita. We would simply like to point
out that the information is not only available in the Proceedings , but
also point out that when the matter of per capita is reported by this
Committee on the floor of Grand Lodge, every M aster and Warden
present hears it thoroughly discussed every year without exception, in
complete detail, with reasons given for each recommende d amount before the matter is submitted for vote.

231

It would be impossible to forewarn delegates on the per capita. The
amount to be submitted can be determ ined only during Grand Lodge
after the budget is completed and after you Masters and Wardens and
Past Masters decide what you want to do with resolutions w hich
directly affect the total per capita. Witness last ·y ear when on Thursday
of Grand Lodge Week you voted to distribute our magazine to all
Masons and a 25 cent per capita to s upport it . The only other substantial
per capita increase in recent years also came last year w hen Grand Lodge
approved a 50 cent increase in the per capita for the Masonic Homes.
The record will show that thi·s Committee. in previous ann ual reports
to Grand Lodge, repeatedly forewarned that such an increase would ,
in all probability, be necessary.
The third reason for the proposal, that of inconsistenc y in having
fixed and flexible amounts in the Section, is, in our opinion, without
merit and very impractical in its application. The basic fact is: Control
over this flexibility is at all times in your hands. This resolution would
remove the flexibility. fix all amo unts, and repeal your discretionar y
power. The control will remain in your hands, but with this difference=. In
future any changes would require a 5/ 6ths vote. As stated, we thmk
this would be impractical. and would unnecessari ly tie your hands.
We assume that you wish to support Grand Lodge activities and the
Homes with the funds that are required, and that you have the good
judgment to do so without requiring a 5/ 6ths vote when changes are
req uired.
We strongly recommend a no vote on this resolution.
The Committee on f urisprudence:
This resolution seeks to amend Section 283 of the California Masonic
Code.
As now effective, that section provides that each constituent Lodge
shall make the following contribution s:
I. For every degree conferred during the year the sum of $1 .00.
2. For each Master Mason on the Lodge rolls the sum of SOc.
3. For each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of June 30 such
per capita sum as the Grand Lodge shall levy for its general activities.
4. For each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of June 30, such
per capita sum as the Grand Lodge shall levy for the suppor t of the
Masonic Homes of California.
5. For each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of June 30, the
sum of $1.00 for the use and benefit of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple.
It will be noted that a s it now stands this section leaves to the discretion of you brethren in Grand Lodge assembled. in subsection 3 the
per capita to be levied for the general activities of Grand Lodge. and
in subsection 4 the per capita to be levied for the support of the Masonic
Homes.

232

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Resolution No. 4 proposes that the amount of the per capita for
Grand Lodge general activities be fixed at $1.00, and the per capita for
the Masonic Homes be fixed at $1.50.
While we have grave doubt as to the advisability of establishing
statutory limitations of the per capita for these two purposes, because
any change in these fixed limitations at any session of Grand Lodge
would require formal legislation, this is a matter for other committees
to recommend - namely Policy a nd General Purposes, Finance and
Masonic Homes.
However, Resolution No. 4 is not in proper form. In its subsection
2nd it adds to the present language of subsection 2nd the words: "for
Grand Lodge constitution al requirement s."
After an examination of our Constitution , we find these words, "for
Grand Lodge constitution al requirement s," to be ambiguous and uncertain. We must conclude that the resolution is not in proper form
and recommend that it be not adopted.
A majority voted against the resolution.

USE CHARTE R PHOTOCO PY ON ALL OCCASIO NS
(5)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREA S, the original charter is considered the most important
and the most treasured document of a constituent lodge. and
WHEREA S, the original charter as issued by the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California, if lost, stolen or destroyed, can never
be replaced, and
WHEREAS , Prudence directs that every possible precaution and
every possible protection should be afforded the original charter at all
times, and
WHEREA S, the original charter of a constituent lodge should
never be unnecessari ly exposed to any danger of loss. theft, destruction,
accident. injury. etc., and
WHEREA S, Grand Lodge in recognition of the risks involved in
unnecessari ly exposing original lodge charters to any danger has
permitted the use of photostatic copies. instead of the original charter,
at any time - except at the installation of officers, and
WHEREA S, due to recent hazardous experiences in moving the
original charter from its permanent protective place, such as bank vaults.
etc., to transport it to lodge for annual installations , particularly so on
long durations of risks as weekends and holidays, is considered as
undue a nd unnecessary risk to such an important and irreplaceabl e
document,
. ~E IT THEREFO RE RESOLVE D. that photostatic copies of the
ong1nal charter of a constituent lodge, when properly and officially
processed through Grand Lodge, may be used instead of the original
on all occasions, and

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered
Resolution No. 5, which would permit the use of a photostat of the
charter on all occasions.
We sympathize with the concern expressed in this Resolution and
urge each of our Masters to heed the injunction of the Installing Officer to carefully preserve the charter and to duly transmit this evidence
of authority to his successor in the Master's chair.
We feel in concert with the Grand Lecturer that the charter should
be used at the annual Install<1tion of Officers. The presence of the
charter is not only consistent with our ritual but also evidences to the
incoming Master the continuing authority of this Grand Lodge. Additionally it is conceivable that unless periodic effort is made to bring
the cha rter to this ceremony this priceless instrument may well be lost.
We believe that the balance of risk weighs heavily to retaining the
present custom.
The Committee on Ritual authorizes us to state that they concur in
this report.
The Committee on Jurispruden ce authorizes us to report that they
see no question of law and will therefore have no report.
We move the adoption of the Resolution but urge a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This resolution proposes that no Master Mason be permitted to
display any emblem or emblems of any organization requiring Masonic
membership as a prerequisite above the square and compass on any
sign. building, tower or anything used for the display of such items.
It is the opinion of the Jurisprudence Committee that the resolution
as presented is couched in confusing language and could be carried to
ridiculous extremes such as to apply to a jeweler who is a Mason and
displays Masonic emblems for sale.
To eliminate this confusion we submit the following substitute
legislation to carry out the intent of the proponents of Resolution No. 7.
NOW. THEREFORE . BE IT RESOLVED that a new section be
added to the California Masonic Code to read as follows:
"334.1 That no Master Mason be permitted to display any
emblem or emblems , representing organizations requiring Masonic membership as a prerequisite, or purporting to be Masonic
in nature above the square and compass of the Blue Lodge on
any sign, building or tower."
In order to place the substitute resolution before Grand Lodge we
move its adoption, but urge a no vote on this resolution.
The Committee on Commercialism indicated its concurrence in the
recommendations.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Resolution, although involving somewhat technical and extensive language and the proposed amendment of Section 246 and 403
of the C.M.C.. is essentially very simple in nature. It merely permits
the purchase for Masonic investment purposes of preferred stocks, and
evidences of indebtedness of corporations whose common stock is fully
listed and registered on a National Securities Exchange. even though
the preferred stocks, or evidences of indebtedness, may not themselves be
so listed and registered.
It would appear that necessary and proper safeguards for investments are maintained under the proposal and that the policy expressed
under the "Prudent Man Rule," adopted by Grand Lodge in 1951, is
also being maintained.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes moves adoption
of the Resolution and recommends a Yes vote. We are authorized to
state that the Cpmmittees on Jurispruden ce and Finance concur; and
that the Committee on Jurisprudence states that the Resolution, if
adopted, will effectuate the purposes of the proponents.
Adopted 5/6 vote.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This amendment would correct an existing inequity among Masters
who die during their term of office by adding the words "including a
Master who died before September 29, 1961" to Section 490 of the
California Masonic Code.
In 1961 a Lodge was authorized, by resolution . to designate a
Master who died during his term of office as a Past Master. Since this
amendment was not made retroactive it does not apply to those Masters
who died prior to September 29, 1961. and thus creates two classes
of Masters who have died while in office. Such distinction was, we
believe, contrary to the intent of Grand Lodge in adopting the 1961
amendment. There should be a single application of the rule to all
those who fall within its provisions.
The Committee on Jurisprudence advises that the language of the
proposed amendment, if adopted, will accomplish the purpose of its
sponsors.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes moves the adoption
of Resolution No. l 0 and recommends a yes vote.
The Committee on f urisprudence indicated its concurrence in the
recommendation.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General P urposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes reports as follows:
This resolution would increase the present ten mile residence requirement as set fo rth in Section 522 C.M.C. to twenty-five miles.
If adopted, this resolution would create a circle fifty miles in diameter
within which each Lodge could accept applications for the degrees
without any waiv~r of jurisdiction being required.
In the San Francisco area for example a Lodge situated in Oakland
could accept without waiver an applicant residing on the peninsula
south to Palo Alto as well as north of San Rafael and Vallejo. In the
Los Angeles area a Lodge in Whittier could accept applications without waiver from the entire San Gabriel Valley, the greater part of Los
Angeles City. the many communities of Orange County and the cities
of the Long Beach complex.
W e believe that Masonry thrives best and serves best where it is
an integral part of the civic and community life. Our Public Schools
programs and our Constitu tion Observance programs largely revolve
about the community.
To fragment the identity of our Lodges will not in our opinion
strengthen either the Lodge as a unit or Masonry as an institution .
The Committee on Jurisprudence has authorized this Committee to
report that they see no point of law involved and will therefore have
no report.
We move the adoption of the resolution but urge a no vote.
A ma jority voted against the resolution.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, rapidly changing population densities and modern
travel facilities require many men to travel hitherto unheard-of distances to their places of business. and
WHEREAS. it is sometimes more convenient for a prospective
candidate to attend a Lodge closer to his business than to his home
residence, and
WHEREAS, a more important factor than distance in the promotion of good attenda nce of new candidates is the existence of strong ties
of friendship between himself and other members, and
WHEREAS. the present ten-mile limit residence requirement set
forth in Section 522 C.M.C. needlessly delays the acceptance of many
otherwise excellent candidates,
THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED that Section 522 of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:

Anything in these Ordinances to the contrary nothwithstanding, without any waiver of any sort being sought or obtained, an

MAURICE A. HARB AND, P.M., N o. 120
Referred to Committees on Jurisprude nce, and on Policy and General Purposes.
The Committe e on Jurispruden ce:
In presenting this report, your Committe e on Jurisprude nce desires
to raise and to rely upon a point of order.
This resolution is an attempt to abrogate the requireme nt of unanimous ballot on applicatio ns for membership by providing that a~ application "shall not be rejected unless three or more cubes appear i.n the
b allot box." Your Committe e is of the opinion that this would v10late
the Ancient Landmark s, and that the Grand Master should declare
the resolution rejected on that ground. The powers of the Grand Lodge
itself are limited by a strict adherence to the Ancient Landmark s of the
Order, and every member of this Grand Lodge, on his installatio n as
Master, agreed that it is not in the power of any man or body of men
to make innovation s in the body of Masonry.
Dr. Albert G. Mackey defined the landmarks as "those ancient and
therefore universal customs o f the Craft which either gradually grew
into opera tion as rules of action, or if once enacted by any compete~t
authority were enacted at a period so re~ote t.~~~ no account of their
origin is to be found in the records of history.
A custom or rule of
action to constitute a landmark must have existed from time whereof
the memory of man runneth not to the contrary." And "as a Gra~d
Lodge has no power to enact a landmark, so it has no power to abolish
or detract from one."
In the Old Regulatio ns of 1721, it was provided in Article VI. as
follows :
"But no man can be entered a Brother in any particular Lodge,
or admitted to be a member thereof, without the unanimou s consent of all the members of that Lodge then present, when the candidate is proposed, and their consent formally asked by the Master; and they are to signify their consent or dissent in their own
prudent way, either virtually or in form , .but wit~ unanimity ; nor
is this inherent privilege subject to a d1spensat10n; because the

members of a particular Lodge are the best judges of it; and if a
fractious member should be imposed on them, it mig ht spoil their
harmony, or hinder their freedom, or even break or disperse the
Lod ge." ( C.M.C., App .. p. 355)
This was affirmed by our Grand Lodge in I 853 in the following
lang uage:

245

"But the ancient Constituti ons point out the req uisites which
a candidate for Masonry must possess; one of w hich is that no
man shall be made a Ma son without the unanimou s consent of
the members present of the Lodge to which he may petition. The
opposition of one member is sufficient to reject a candidate. and,
say the ancient Constituti ons. 'this is an inherent right, not subject to a dispensation '."
This was an "inherent right" even in 1721, which means that it
was an essential, a permanen t and inseparabl y existing right; not derived
from another or received from another; and therefore was co-existen t
with Freemaso nry itself.
The existence o f this rule in 1721 as an "inherent privilege" means
that it is actually more ancient than certain of the Landmarks mentioned
in Dr. Mackey's list of twenty~flve. While not so mentioned , it is
neverthele ss recognized by his Eighth Landmark relating to the pre~
rogative of the Grand Master to make Masons at sight "in a regular
Lodge by unanimou s consent of the members present."
However, D r. Mackey did not claim that the 25 Landmarks in his
list were exclusi've of others, and several years before 1850 when Dr.
Mackey suggested his list, the Grand Lodge of New York had stated
31 "cardinal principles " which were considered by it as Ancient Landmarks, one of which was "that a candidate must be proposed in open
Lodge at a stated meeting and can only be accepted at a stated meeting
following, by the scrutiny of a secret ballot and by an unanimou s vote";
and it went on to say that "besides these, there are various landmarks
which constitute the framewor k of the governme nt of the F raternity"
and various duties and rights more fully set forth in the "Ancient
Cha rges" which are a part of the C onstitution s of Freemason ry. T here
are many other jurisdictio ns which hold that the "Old Charges" contain
the Landmark s.
We therefore recommen d that the Grand Master declare this resolution rejected because it is in violation of the Ancient Landmark s of
the Order.
Following the report of the Committe e on Jurisprude nce the Grand
Master declared the resolution rejected because it is in violation of the
Ancient Landmark s of the Order.

WHEREAS. by complying with Section 579 of the California
Masonic Code it causes the Secretary extra work and the Lodge unnecessary expense; and
WHEREAS. it seems to be the same Brethren who are notified each
year; and
WHEREAS. a Brother should know that he is delinquent if he
is still interested in Masonry and wants to be a Mason; and
WHEREAS. a Brother has two years after being suspended, and
this should be ample time, to pay his arrearages of dues and be restored
without any questions being asked;
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED. that Section 579 of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"579. SECRETARY TO SEND NOTICE. In case any
member shall have refused or neglected to pay his regular dues
during a period of twelve months, the Secretary shall notify him,
BY ORDINARY MAIL. deposited in the U. S. Postoffice addressed to him at his last known address. at least sixty ( 60)
days in advance, that unless at the Stated Meeting specified
either his dues be paid, or sickness or inability to pay be shown
as the cause of such refusal or neglect. he will be suspended from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry."

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution proposes that when a member shall have ref used or
neglected to pay his regular dues during a period of 12 months, the
Secretary shall notif.y him by ordinary mail at least 60 days in advance
of his proposed suspension. This would eliminate the present requirement that notification be by registered letter or certified mail.
Your Committee feels the statement of the Committee on Jurisprudence in 1873 is still true:
Masonic law imposes on every member of a Lodge the duty of paying his dues and prescribes a penalty for wilfully neglecting payment.
Before imposition of such penalty it is a basic tenet of justice that the
accused shall have his day in court and that he shall not be subject to
penalty until he has been advised of the facts against him .
It is also true that, while the member has an obligation to his Lodge
in the payment of dues, the Lodge has an obligation to be certain that

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

.

This resolution, No. 17. as amended would_delete from Sect10n 6_9~.4
C.M.C., relating to default cases in Masonic charg~s, the provision
allowing the accused to obtain a copy of the proceedings.
f
Since the release of such a copy would endanger the secrecy o :
Masonic proceeding, and ·since the accused has, in the case sup.Pose .
already defaulted, there would appear to be no re~son to require the
Lodge to prepare an additional copy of the proceedings.
Your Committee on Poky and General Purposes fa vors the amended
resolution and urges a yes vote.

The Committee on f urisprudence:

.

This resolution proposes an amendment to Section ?92.4,. which
deals with instances of charges of unmasonic conduct, in wh_Kh the
accused. after being served with a copy of the charge. a~d notice that
he should file his plea of guilty or not guilty thereto, fails to file such
pleaThe section as it stands provides that on his application, after having
so failed to answer, the accused may ask for and be given a copy of the
whole record, including the Master's findings, the penalty fixed by the
Master, and his report to the Grand Secretary..
f h
We see no reason for giving to a defaulting accused a copy o t e
Master's findings and conclusion. The accused who fails to answe~ ~as
had his chance to be heard and no good would be served by giving
him a copy of the whole record.
.
.
We believe that the effect which Brother Ross intends, and which
we approve, would be arrived at if the Grand Lodge would adopt the
following amended Resolution:

. Our present ordinanc es provide that if a proposed amendment re,

an our procedur es.

PERMIT USE OF CANDLE OR TAPER

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 21 proposes to authorize Lodges to use candles
instead of electric lights near the altar, if they desired to do so. The
report of the Ritual Committee has already called attention to the fac ts .
tha t Lodges may so do if they wish and some have, should remove any
doubt if such existed in any local a rea. The proposed resolution does
not propose any change in the existing policy. A yes vote would accomplish nothing and a no vote might later be construed to be a prohibition
against the use of candles. The resolution is moot-a legal form the
Policy Committee should not utter.
I move that Resolution No. 21 be laid on the table.
Grand Lodge tabled the resolution.

(22)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & AM. of California:
WHEREA S . a copy of the Bible upon which the candidate is
obligated in the Third Degree should be given to the candidate at tha t
time. accompanie d by a presentation speech by the Master or some one
designated on the Master's behalf;
THEREFO RE BE IT RESOLVE D, that the Master. or Brother
designated by the Master, present to the candidate who has been raised,
as a gift from the Lodge, a Holy Bible which ·should be accompa nied by
a prescribed presentation speech to be prepared by the Grand Lodge
Committee on Ritual. For example, the following presentation speech is
used in another jurisdiction:
''My Brother1 s), I have been requested by our Worshipful M aster
to present to you this Holy Bible-a gift from your Lodge. You will
recall that on your first a ppearance in this Lodge you were presented
with a lambskin or white leathern apron. and on the second with the
three precious jewels, the meaning of which was explained to you at
the time. And now, my friend(s), you are to receive the third g ift- the
greatest gift of all- the HOLY WORD of GOD.
"The HOLY BIBLE res ts upon the Altar of every Masonic Lodge,
supporting the S quare and Compasses. This BOOK, beloved by so
many generations, is our VOLUME of SACRED LAW and a
GREAT LIGHT in M asonry. The BIBLE opens when the Lodge
opens; it closes when the Lodge closes. No Lodge ca n transact its own
business , much less initiate candidates into its mysteries unless the
BOOK of HOLY LAW lies open upon its Altar. Thus the BOO K of
the WILL of GOD rules the Lodge in its labors. as the Sun rules the
day, making its work a worship.
"No Mason needs to be told what a great place the BIBLE has in
the Masonry of our day. It is central. sovereign, supreme-th e great and
dazzling light of moral truth, the master light of all our seeing. From

258

PROCEEDIN GS OP THE

the Altar it pours forth upon the E ast. the West, and the South. its
white light. of Spiritual Vision, moral law and immortal hope. Upon
the BIBLE every Mason takes solemn vows of loyalty. of chastity and
of charity. pledging himself to the practice of Brotherly Love, and as he
renews these vows with every new made brother, the lanugage and
imagery of the BIBLE becomes more familiar and eloquent'. and its
mu sic becomes a part of his very soul. Nor is it strange that this should
be so. As faith in GOD is the cornerston e of the Craft, so. naturally,
the BOOK which tells us the purest truth about GOD rests upon our
Altar. and as it supports the Square and Compasses. literaUy. upon the
Altar. so does it literally support the superstruc ture of Freemaso nry.
For all of Masonry is founded upon the Divine Laws contained in this
HOLY BOOK.
"But the BIBLE is not only a foundation rock. It is also a quarry
we find the truths which make us men. As in ages gone by,
which
in
rays of sunlight were stored up in vast beds of coal for t~e use of ~an.
so in this BOOK the light of Moral Truth is stored to light the mmds
and warm the hearts of mankind with the knowledg e that GOD has
made us for himself: and that our hearts will be restless, unhappy and
lonely until we learn to rest in HIM whose will is our peace.
" He hath showed thee. 0 Man, what is good, and what doth the
Lord require of thee. but to do justly. to love men:y and to walk humbly
with thy GOD.
"Have no other GODS but me;
Unto no image bow the knee.
Take not the name of GOD in vain;
Do not the Sabbath Day profane.
Honor thy father and mother too;
And see that thou no murder do.
From vile adultery keep thou clean;
And steal not though thy state be mean.
Bear not false witness-s hun that blot;
What is thy neighbor 's-covet not.
" Therefore , all things whatsoeve r ye would that man should do

"And now, my brother(s ), this BOOK is yours, and with it the

The Committe e on R itual:
The Committe e on Ritual. to which has been presented Resolution
No. 22. reports as follows:
Briefly. the resol ution proposes the adoption of a Bible presentati on
lecture, a nd the presentati on of a Bible to every candidate obligated in
the Third Degree.
We are opposed to the adoption of this resolution for several
reasons.
1. We object to the lengthenin g of the time required fo r the work
and exemplification of the Third Degree.
2. As previously stated, we object to the addition of more material
for the officers of the Lodge to commit to memory.
3. The adoption of this resolution would compel the purchase of
Bibles for every brother obligated in the Third Degree, and would constitute an entry into the area of religious practice in the Lodge, creating
an infringeme nt on the right of free choice of the individual. Our sole
requireme nt for membersh ip is that a man is "a believer in God and a
future existence, " and on this basis we receive applicants embracing
religions other than Christiani ty.
And finally. the resolution would make mandatory the expenditu re
of Lodge funds for this purpose.
We move the adoption of the resolution . but recommen d a no vote.
The Committe e on Policy and General Purposes concurred in the
recommen dation.
A majority voted against the resolution.

memorial type service to be used by constituten_t Lodg.e~ when requested
by a deceased brother's family. This would be m addition to the present
form of funeral service.
.
.
your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which this
resolution has been referred reports as follows:
.
The Grand Lodge presently permits the use of our funeral s_e~v.1ce
for a deceased brother Mason lost at sea and there is no proh1b1t1on
against using the funeral service in other cases where the body of the
deceased brother is not present.
We do not believe there is sufficient demand to justify having two
types of Masonic funeral services.
T o require that the officers of the constituent Lodges learn and
become proficient in two types of funeral services wou.ld add a ~urde_n
to their already heavy schedule of ritualistic work which we believe is
both unnecessary and inadvisable.
We therefore urge a no vote.
The Comm ittee on Ritual:
The Committee on Ritual to which has been presented Resolution
No. 23. reports as follows:
.
.
This resolution proposes that a suitable memorial servtce to be
adopted. in addition to our present funeral service, to be used as a
memorial type service.
.
During our 1962 Communication , in repo~ting on ~ resolution for
the adoption of a graveside service. the Committee on Ritual stated that
"we do not believe there is either justification or reasonable demand for
having more than one M asonic Funeral Service, applicable to all cases
.". We still hold this conviction.
Our present funeral service is of such a nature that it may be used
even though the body of the deceased brother is not present.. Further,
by the adoption of Section 605g, permitting the funeral servtce for a
deceased Mason lost at sea and whose body was not recovered; and

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

261

Section 605i, which permits our funeral service for one whose body has
been willed to a university and therefore is not present a t the servicethis Grand Lodge has adequately spelled out its attitude as to the flexi~
bllity of our funeral service and its use even though the body of the
deceased brother is not present.
In view of the previous actions of this Grand Lodge broadening the
use of the funeral service, we do not see the necessity for an additional
service or ritual. We, therefore. oppose the adoption of the resolution.
We move the adoption of the resolution, but recommend a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge F. & A. M. of California:
An audit of the finances of Grand Lodge and its agencies for the
fiscal year ending June 30, 1965. has been completed as required by our
Code. Copies of the audit have been furnished the members of this
Committee and examined in detail. In our opinion the reports correctly
state the financial position of Grand Lodge.
For the fiscal year under consideration, Grand Lodge had tota l
revenue of $423,074.00 and total expense of $388.989.00, leaving net
revenue of $34,085.00. This favorable result reflects careful use of
Grand Lodge funds by everyone involved and deserves commendation.
However, a substantial portion of this surplus resulted from unavoidable
delays in the completion of programs by several committees. These
funds must be included in appropriations for the new fiscal year so that
the programs may be carried out.
GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT
The Grand Treasurer's Report was referred to and examined by
this Committee. We find all items having to do with fin ance in accord
with the audit and recommend approval.
EXCESS E XPENDITURES OVER BUDGETED APPROPRIATIONS
During the last fiscal year the Grand Master, with the approval of
the Chairman of the Finance Committee, approved appropriations
totaling $3,135.00 in excess of certain budgeted items. These items are
detailed in the audit. There was sound reason for this action in every
case and we recommend approval.
"CALIFORNIA FREEMASON" MAGAZINE
In line with the decision at the last Grand Lodge Communication ,
the transition in the distribution of our official publication, California
Freemason. has been made from a limited list of paid subscribers to a
mailing to all regular members of Lodges in this jurisdiction. supported
by a per capita tax of 25 cents.
Without going into detail. the change-over resulted in a deficit to
Grand Lodge for the last fiscal year of $11,837.00. This deficit was after

262

PROCEEDIN GS OP THE

transferrin g $35,945.00 from "Californi a Freemaso n Reserve" to the
general funds of Grand Lodge. You should keep in mind in this connection that the 25 cent per capita you vo ted to support this distributio n
was for the fisca l year ending June 30. 1965. These funds, therefore,
were not in hand until after that date, but are now available to support
the distributio n in the n ew fiscal year.
We are unable to determine accurately at this stage the cost o f a
full year's publicatio n and distributio n of the magazine under the new
system. The revenue from the 25 cents per capita may fall short of
covering costs by some $10.000.00. H owever, we a re recommen ding
that the per capita remain at 25 cents until we have another year's
results before us. at which time a more accurate determina tion can be
made on the necessity of increasing this per capita.
We recommen d approval of the transfer of $35,945.00 from "California Freemaso n Reserve" to general funds. There are some $4,000.00
remaining in this reserve to cover possible future claims for refunds of
past subscriptio ns paid in advance.
LIBRARY COMMISSI ON

The budget for the last fiscal year included a capital appropriat ion
of $5,750.00 to purchase a display case to house the Model of King
Solomon's Temple. By good manageme nt the Library Commissi on was
able to save a portion o f this appropria tion. They requested and received
approval of the expenditu re of this saving on additional book shelves.
Inasmuch as this was also a capital expenditu re ""e do not feel the
action requires Grand Lodge approval and it is reported as a matter of
record only.
The Commissi on is requesting a modest increase in operating budget,
and $2,315.00 capital appropriat ion for a new museum display case to
replace a very old and obsolete case now in use in the museum. We are
including these amounts in the appropria te sections of the budget for
the new fiscal year.
MASONIC HOMES

The members of the Finance Committe e have received and examined
the Report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes. We have consulted
with the Chairman o f the Board from time to time. We are in accord
with their conclusion that no increase should be requested in the present
per capita of $1.50.
H owever, you should be aware of the fact that the Homes had an
operating deficit in the last fiscal year of approxima tely $600.000.00.
This deficit was covered by a transfer from reserves. The net amount of
the reserve account remained the same, however, because of bequests
received during the year which could properly be added to reserve
account.
It is apparent that the cost of operating our Homes is not going to

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

263

d line in the foreseeabl e future. It is equally apparent that the Homes
ecnot always expect to cover operating deficits by transfers from reca~es and that it will be necessary for G rand Lodge to take a realistic
~~:w of the situation and devise means by which the income of the
Homes can be increased.
We offer the following resolution :
RESOLV ED. that the sum of $1.50 per capita be levied for the
fiscal year ending June 30, 1966. the proceeds to be paid to the
Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California .
SALARIES

You will be pleased to know that in the la st fiscal year, of the
salaries appropria tion of $93.000.00, only $84.292.00 was expended .
This was due almost entirely to the efficient manageme nt of the Grand
Lodge offices and staff by the Grand Secretary, Most. Worshipf~l
Edward H. S iems. From time to time he has made adjustmen ts m
salaries of the members of the staff. bringing them along with increases
where they are warranted ; but because of greater efficiency in overall
operations in the area of automatio n and work schedule he has been
able to reduce the total numbers of the staff. mainly by not finding it
.
necessary to replace those who left by retirement or otherwise.
Those of us who have had occasion to contact the office on busmess
or personal visitation -and this includes Lodge Secretar!e s and ~any
members of Committe es and Boards-a re impressed with the air of
quiet efficiency and ease with which the enti re operation . i~ con~ucted .
Brother Siems accepted this job five years ago at a cr1t1cal time when
his predecess or was forced to retire due to physical disability. and. we
should add . at ·some financial sacrifice on his part from the salary he
commande d in the business field. At the time he took over this job five
years ago the salary was $20,000.00 and it has remained the same. We
feel that this is entirely inadequat e. Although we are a fraternal. nonprofit organizati on, and make no pretense of competing with the business world. we do feel that an increase in this salary is deserved and
more than justified. We recommen d an increase to $25.000.00 per ye.ar.
effective Novembe r 1, 1965. We have discussed this recommen dation
with the Grand Treasurer , the Grand Master and the Deputy Grand
Master. It has their unanimou s approval. This increase will not req uire
any enlargeme nt over last year in the budget appropria tion for salaries.

You will be pleased that the above estimates of income and expense
for the current fiscal year show a small surplus. Such net revenue serves
to increase the General Funds of Grand Lodge, or. in other words. our
Reserves. We should endea vor to make this standard procedure, first,
because it is sound fiscal policy, and secondly, for the less obvious
reason that each year we reduce our reserves by capital appropriations
for new equipment and replacement of worn out and obsolete items.

268

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

A comparison of the new budget with that of the preceding year
shows that, for this year at least, we are making some progress in
holding the line on expenses. There were fifty-seven items in last year's
budget. For the new year the amounts for thirty remain the same,
eleven are increased for a total of $9,600.00, fourteen are reduced for a
total of $20,630.00 and three items are eliminated entirely in the amount
of $3,945.00. The result is a net reduction of $14,975.00.
In the light of ever-increasing cost of goods and services, this favorable trend is the product of the efforts of all your brethren to whom
you intrust the responsibility of spending your money in the broad
advancement of the welfare and growth of Masonry in this jurisdiction.
We offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That for the purposes of paying the expenses of
Grand Lodge. a per capita aggregating $4.10 be levied for the fiscal
year ending June 30, 1966, divided as follows:

JOHN RANDLE MOORE

By Guy B. Mize
Once again the Almighty Fiat has gone forth and with it there was
removed from our midst on March 28, 1965, our beloved brother, Past
Grand Master John Randle Moore. A continuing series of heart attacks
proved more than his rugged spirit could bear and he slipped away in
his sleep to eternal rest. Faithful to the end to his love of Masonry.
John attended the Annual Meeting of the Los Angeles Board of Relief
only seven days prior to his passing , so that he could enjoy the fellowship of the 1800 Masons present at the breakfast. W a rm, indeed, were
the many greetings given him by so many of his brethren, happy to have
him in their midst. And, although physically tired from the meeting,
he returned to his home in Corona Del Mar, uplifted by the Masonic
fellowship which he had sought and obtained.
It was my great privilege to know John as one of my closest, personal
friends. He was my Inspector in the old 86th Masonic District during
most of the years I served as an officer of my Lodge. I was honored to
be selected to follow him as Inspector when John was chosen in October,
1944, to be Junior Grand Warden of this Grand Lodge. In the succeeding
years, he was always available to me as I assumed other Masonic duties.
and he offered me wise counsel - but only when asked to do so.
During my term as Grand Master, John Moore was a pillar of
strength with his profound knowledge of Masonic law and customs.
There were occasions when we did not agree while considering a problem. but as long as our disagreements did not involve a compromise of
principle. there could be no breach of our friendship.
It was natural that I would turn to John Moore to serve me personally in legal matters and I always felt secure in his advice. I shall be ever
grateful that our paths in life crossed and that I could know him as a
true friend and brother.
On October 13. 1947, John Randle Moore stood before his brethren
assembled for the 98th Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California to
give an account of his stewardship as Grand Master for the year then
ending.
True, indeed, were the attributes penned by the biographer who
wrote for the Proceedings of that year:
"John Moore has preserved and perpetuated the finest tra ditions of
the office of Grand Master during his incumbency in that exalted station.
"On matters of policy he has s teadfastly adhered to the Ancient
Landmarks and has found a way to be progressive and modern within
their limits.
"On matters of law he stated at the outset of his term that he would

277

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

not knowingly violate nor permit to be violated the law of Grand Lodge
.
and he has kept his pledge.
"He has brought to problems of administration a careful. studious
mind and has been painstaking in his search for the essentials necessary
to a proper solution.
" Kindly, considerate, social. and so friendly that all brethren :vere
at ease in his presence. John will be affectionately remembered as My
Grand Master' by all who served with him."
In his message to Grand Lodge, John Moore said:
"My services have now come to judgment at your hands. I have
not the temerity or the vanity to argue that my acts this year have
contributed to the progress of Masonry, but I shall be compensated
and flattered if. in your wisdom, you find that they have not interrupted
or impeded it, and that it will continue to flow, unde.r God, slowly,
.
serenely and harmoniously into time."
In these two statements, we gain insight into the character of this
great Mason and his unwavering fidelity to the trust imposed in hi~.
Yes, John Moore has placed himself indelibly in the records of California Freemasonry - and his passing brings sorrow to many across
this country and in every country where M asonry is known. His friends
elsewhere were legion and in his extensive travels he always found
time to pursue Masonic interests so that he could bring to this Grand
Lodge important and timely reports on the condition of Freemasonry
in other climes.
John was born September 13, 1893 in Johnsonville, Tennessee, the
son of James Randle and Dora (McCauley) Moore, both parents of
Irish descent. His forebears were early settlers of North Carolina a nd
participants in the Revolutionary War against the Britis h. He attended
grammar school in Tennessee and high school in Campbell, Missouri.
Entirely on his own in the securing of an education, ambitious for an
education, and willing to w ork and strive for it, he worked on a farm,
cut timber. operated a lathe in the manufacture of axe handles, worked
as a carpenter, carried newspaper and laundry routes, clerked in a mercantile store and, in 1917 upon graduating from high school, became
principal and teacher in a two-room school at Gibson, Missouri, where
he received a salary of $60 per month. By this time, the ruggedness and
simplicity of his character which was to remain with him all his life was
clearly established.
John's record was so outstanding that upon his application for
officer's training in World War I, the Superintendent of the Campbell
High School was constrained to write a letter of endorsement to the
commanding general where John's application was being processed.
Quoting briefly from the letter, how interesting and prophetic were
these statements:
"It is a rare pleasure, indeed, to a school teacher to be called upon
to speak in behalf of a young man such as John R. Moore. He has a

commanding appearance and personality. Whatever he has been or
is he will be leading. I voice the sentiments of this entire city when I
say that John Moore is one of the strongest men in our town physically, mentally, and morally. He is one of America's choice products and will serve his country with honor."
Such was the opinion of a man who wrote those words on May 5,
1917. Such is our opinion today.
John Moore went on to serve his country in W orld War I as a
Second. Lieutenant, Company I, I 9th Division, U nited States Army.
Immediately following his military service, he enrolled in the University of Missouri and then graduated from the University of C olorado.
He was admitted to the practice of law in Colorado in 1922 and in
California in 1923. Professionally, he prac ticed law in Los Angeles
for more tha n 40 years including several years as trust officer of a Los
Angeles bank and 15 years as State Inheritance Tax Appraiser and
Referee. In I 956 he was a participant in the White House Conference
on Education held in Washington, D . C.
!ohn was married to Tekla Bender on October 12, 1922, they
having met as students at the University of Colorado. He is survived
by Mrs. Moore, a son. John Bender, a daughter, Edith Bear, five
grandchildren in whom he took great delight, and four sisters. Unquest_ionably, the greatest joy in John's life was his family and
happiest he was when surrounded by them. This was so evident to all
who had the privilege of knowing John intimately. T hen, too, he had
the pleasure of receiving his son Bender into his law practice in I 952
and they practiced law together under the firm name of M oore and
Moore. On the 9ccasion of John's first official visit as Grand Master,
in . ~is o~n Lodge, Meridian N o. 667, he had the rare priviledge of
raising his son, Bender, to the sublime degree of Master Mason.
Other than his law practice. John's chie f business interest was with
Forest Lawn Memorial Park in Glendale. serving as a member of the
Council of Regents, as a member of the board of directors of Forest Lawn
Memorial Park Association and as P resident of the Board of Trustees of
Forest Lawn M emorial Cemetery Association.
.Other organizations claimed John's interests and he belonged to the
society. Sons of the R evolution; American Legion; Los Angeles Bar
Association; State Bar of California; Kappa Sigma; Phi Delta Phi;
and the Los Angeles Club of Rotary International.
Other than his family, Joh n's greatest love was Masonry and it was
in its vineyards tha t he served for so many years with s uch great
distinction.
. ~aised in Four fvl ile Lodge No. 212 at Campbell, Missouri. John
d1m1tted to and bec:ime a charter member of Meridian Lodge No. 667,
Glendale, in 1928. H e served as Master of the latter Lodge in 1933
and then ensued a continuous service to Grand Lodge culminating in
his election to the office of Grand M aster on October 18, 1946. But

CORRESPONDENCE REPORT
ANNOUNCEMENT
Reviews of the Proceedings of other Grand
Lodges have appeared quarterly in the "California Freemason," copies of which have been sent
to each Grand Lodge. This program will be continued.
The "California Freemason" is issued quarterly
and each copy carries additional reviews. Hence,
they do not appear in these Proceedings.
